chapters.title: Counting steps (Big-O and reading the limits)
chapters.tagline: Before you write a line, the input size tells you which algorithm is allowed
goals: Count how many steps a loop takes, as a function of n
Name the common growth rates: 1, log n, n, n log n, n², 2ⁿ
Read a problem's limits and know the slowest solution that still passes
Replace a double loop with one pass, using a little maths
chapters.prelude:
import time

def timed(fn, *args):
    """Run fn(*args) and return (result, seconds)."""
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
Two correct programs can differ by a factor of a million in speed. Timing them on your laptop with 10 items tells you nothing: both finish instantly. What matters is how the work grows when the input gets bigger. That's what Big-O describes: drop the constants, keep the shape.

A computer does roughly 10⁸ simple steps a second (pure Python is slower, nearer 10⁷). Every problem on LeetCode or Codeforces states its limits, like 1 ≤ n ≤ 200 000, and a time limit of 1 or 2 seconds. Put those together and you know what kind of solution the setter expects before you've read the rest.

blocks.name: ds-bigo
blocks.title: How fast each kind of algorithm grows
blocks.goal: Solve all three puzzles: for each limit on n, pick the most work you can afford in about a second.
blocks.intro: Click any bar to see an example of that kind of algorithm and how long it would take.

blocks.html: Count how many times the innermost line runs. A loop over range(n) runs n times; a loop inside a loop multiplies.
Every pair (i, j) with i < j is counted once: n(n−1)/2 pairs. That's about n²/2, and Big-O drops the ½: it's O(n²).

blocks.q: How many times does the loop body run, as a function of n? while n > 1: n = n // 2
blocks.why: Each step halves n. Starting from a million, you reach 1 after about 20 halvings, because 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶. Halving is the signature of O(log n).

blocks.q: for i in range(n): for j in range(0, n, 2): ... What's the Big-O?

opts.t: O(n² / 2), which is different from O(n²)

blocks.why: The inner loop runs n/2 times for each of n values of i: n²/2 steps. Constant factors like ½ are dropped, so it's O(n²). (They still matter in practice, but they never change which bar you're on.)

blocks.q: for i in range(n): j = 1; while j < n: j *= 2. What's the Big-O?
blocks.why: The outer loop runs n times; the inner one doubles j, so it runs about log₂ n times. n × log n.

blocks.html:
This table is worth memorising. It's the first thing strong competitors look at.

Largest nMost work you can affordWhat it usually means
n ≤ 10O(n!)try every ordering
n ≤ 20O(2ⁿ · n)try every subset
n ≤ 500O(n³)three nested loops
n ≤ 5 000O(n²)every pair
n ≤ 10⁶O(n log n)sort, heap, binary search
n ≤ 10⁸O(n)one pass
n ≤ 10¹⁸O(log n) or O(1)maths, or halving

blocks.title: allowed
blocks.prompt: Write allowed(n) that returns the most work you can afford for that largest input size, as one of these strings, using the table: "n!", "2^n", "n^3", "n^2", "n log n", "n", "log n".
blocks.tests:
assert allowed(8) == "n!"
assert allowed(18) == "2^n"
assert allowed(400) == "n^3"
assert allowed(2000) == "n^2"
assert allowed(200_000) == "n log n"
assert allowed(10**6) == "n log n"
assert allowed(5 * 10**7) == "n"
assert allowed(10**18) == "log n"
hints: Check the thresholds from smallest to largest and return the first one that n fits under. A list of (limit, kind) pairs keeps it short.
blocks.starter:
def allowed(n):
    return "n"

sections.title: One pass instead of two loops

blocks.html: The most common speed-up in all of DSA: instead of looking back at every earlier item, remember a summary of what you've seen so far (the smallest, the sum, the count). Then each new item costs O(1).

blocks.title: best_profit
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. prices[i] is a share's price on day i. You may buy on one day and sell on a later day, once. Write best_profit(prices) returning the most money you can make (0 if every choice loses money). n can be 200 000, so trying every pair (buy day, sell day) is too slow.
blocks.tests:
assert best_profit([7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4]) == 5, "buy at 1, sell at 6"
assert best_profit([7, 6, 4, 3, 1]) == 0, "prices only fall: don't trade"
assert best_profit([2]) == 0
assert best_profit([3, 3, 3]) == 0
assert best_profit([1, 9, 0, 5]) == 8, "the later low (0) doesn't beat 9 - 1"
big = list(range(5000, 0, -1))
r, secs = timed(best_profit, big)
assert r == 0
assert secs < 0.25, f"took {secs:.2f}s on 5 000 days: that's the O(n²) double loop. Keep the lowest price so far instead."
hints: On each day, the best sale is today's price minus the lowest price before today. Keep that lowest price in a variable as you walk.
Two variables, one loop: lowest = min(lowest, p) and best = max(best, p - lowest).
blocks.solution:
def best_profit(prices):
    lowest = float("inf")
    best = 0
    for p in prices:
        lowest = min(lowest, p)
        best = max(best, p - lowest)
    return best

blocks.title: The largest and second-largest in one pass

blocks.html: The decoys show the trap: when a new maximum arrives, the old maximum becomes second. Overwrite first before saving it and it's gone.

blocks.title: missing_number
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. nums holds n different numbers from 0..n, so exactly one number in that range is missing. Return it, in O(n) time and O(1) extra space (no set, no sorting).
blocks.tests:
assert missing_number([3, 0, 1]) == 2
assert missing_number([0, 1]) == 2
assert missing_number([1]) == 0
assert missing_number([9, 6, 4, 2, 3, 5, 7, 0, 1]) == 8
big = list(range(20000)); big.remove(12345)
r, secs = timed(missing_number, big)
assert r == 12345
assert secs < 0.2, f"{secs:.2f}s: `k not in nums` scans the whole list each time, so this is O(n²)"
hints: 0 + 1 + … + n = n(n+1)/2. The total of what's there is sum(nums). The difference is the missing number.

blocks.html: k not in nums looks like one step but it's a hidden loop over the list. Spotting hidden loops (in on a list, list.index, list.remove, slicing, string += in a loop) is half of Big-O in Python.

blocks.q: Which of these is not O(1) in Python?
blocks.why: in on a list checks items one by one: O(n). On a set or dict it's O(1) on average, because they hash. That's the whole of chapter 3.

blocks.title: pair_products
blocks.prompt: Codeforces style. Given a list a of up to 2·10⁵ integers, return the sum of a[i] * a[j] over all pairs i < j. The double loop is 2·10¹⁰ steps. Find an O(n) way.
blocks.tests:
assert pair_products([1, 2, 3]) == 1*2 + 1*3 + 2*3
assert pair_products([5]) == 0
assert pair_products([]) == 0
assert pair_products([-1, 4, 2, -3]) == -4 - 2 + 3 + 8 - 12 - 6
big = list(range(1, 4001))
r, secs = timed(pair_products, big)
s = sum(big); assert r == (s * s - sum(x * x for x in big)) // 2
assert secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s: too slow, that's the O(n²) double loop"
hints: Each x gets multiplied by every number before it. That's x * (sum of the earlier numbers). Keep the running sum.
Another route: (a₁ + … + aₙ)² = Σaᵢ² + 2·Σ_{i<j} aᵢaⱼ, so the answer is (sum(a)**2 - sum of squares) // 2.
blocks.solution:
def pair_products(a):
    total = 0
    seen = 0
    for x in a:
        total += x * seen
        seen += x
    return total

blocks.code:
calls = 0
def f(n):
    global calls
    calls += 1
    if n > 1:
        f(n // 2)
        f(n // 2)
f(16)
print(calls)

blocks.html: Each call makes two calls on half the size. The levels have 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 calls: 31 in total, about 2n. Not every recursion is slow; it depends how fast the problem shrinks. (Chapter 5 builds this from scratch.)

blocks.q: A problem: "1 ≤ n ≤ 18. Choose some of the n items so their weights sum to exactly W." What does the limit tell you?

opts.t: Trying every subset is allowed: 2¹⁸ ≈ 260 000 subsets

blocks.why: n ≤ 20 is the setter saying "brute force over subsets is fine." Small limits are a hint, not an accident.

blocks.title: A "will it scale?" checker for a team's code
blocks.client: A start-up whose search page was fast in testing and timed out on launch day with 50 000 users
blocks.brief: Build scale.py that takes a function and an input generator, runs the function at sizes n = 1 000, 2 000, 4 000, 8 000, … (stopping when one run takes more than 2 seconds), and reports the growth: "looks like O(n²): at your production size of 50 000 this takes about 40 s". Fit the slope of log(time) against log(n): a slope near 1 is linear, near 2 quadratic. Add it to the test suite so a slow change fails the build.
blocks.why: Performance bugs pass every functional test and only show up at real sizes. Doubling the input and watching the time is how engineers spot O(n²) before users do; the same idea (benchmarks in CI) runs at every large tech company.
milestones: Time a function at doubling sizes, with a cut-off
Estimate the exponent from the timings
Predict the time at a production size
Fail loudly when the exponent jumps between two versions
stretch: Repeat each timing a few times and take the minimum (noise only ever makes things slower)
Tell n log n apart from n (it needs a wider range of sizes)

blocks.title: growth_exponent
blocks.prompt: Write growth_exponent(sizes, seconds): given input sizes and how long each run took, return the slope of the best straight line through the points (log n, log t) (least squares), rounded to 1 decimal. A slope of 2.0 means time grows like n².
hints: On a log-log plot, t = c·nᵏ is a straight line with slope k. Least-squares slope: Σ(x−x̄)(y−ȳ) / Σ(x−x̄)².
blocks.solution:
import math

def growth_exponent(sizes, seconds):
    xs = [math.log(n) for n in sizes]
    ys = [math.log(t) for t in seconds]
    mx, my = sum(xs) / len(xs), sum(ys) / len(ys)
    slope = sum((x - mx) * (y - my) for x, y in zip(xs, ys)) / sum((x - mx) ** 2 for x in xs)
    return round(slope, 1)

blocks.title: predict_time
blocks.prompt: Write predict_time(n0, t0, k, n): a run at size n0 took t0 seconds and time grows like nᵏ. Return the predicted seconds at size n, rounded to 2 decimals.
blocks.tests:
assert predict_time(8000, 0.64, 2, 50000) == 25.0
assert predict_time(1000, 0.5, 1, 4000) == 2.0
assert predict_time(100, 0.01, 3, 1000) == 10.0
hints: Ten times the input with k = 2 is a hundred times the time: t0 * (n / n0) ** k.
blocks.starter:
def predict_time(n0, t0, k, n):
    return t0
blocks.solution:
def predict_time(n0, t0, k, n):
    return round(t0 * (n / n0) ** k, 2)

blocks.q: s = "" then for w in words: s += w. In the worst case, what can this cost for n words?

opts.t: O(n²) characters copied, because strings can't be changed in place

blocks.why: Each += may build a brand-new string and copy everything so far. "".join(words) copies each character once: O(total length).

blocks.q: An O(n²) solution takes 1 second at n = 10 000. About how long at n = 100 000?
blocks.why: 10× the input, squared: 100× the time. Doubling n doubles an O(n) program and quadruples an O(n²) one.

blocks.q: Which grows fastest as n gets large?
blocks.why: Any exponential beats any polynomial in the end. 2ⁿ passes n¹⁰ at about n = 59 and never looks back.

blocks.q: a.sort() followed by one loop over a. Total?
blocks.why: Add the steps: n log n + n. Keep only the biggest term: O(n log n).

blocks.q: for i in range(n): if i in seen_set: ... where seen_set is a Python set. Total?
blocks.why: A set lookup is O(1) on average (it hashes), so n lookups cost O(n). With a list instead of a set, the same line would be O(n²).

blocks.q: A problem allows n ≤ 10¹⁸. What kind of solution is it asking for?

opts.t: A formula, or something that halves (O(log n)) like binary search or fast power

blocks.why: You can't even loop to 10¹⁸. The answer must come from maths or from cutting the problem in half each step.

blocks.title: allowed_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: allowed(n) returns the most work you can afford for that n: "n!" up to 10, "2^n" up to 20, "n^3" up to 500, "n^2" up to 5 000, "n log n" up to 10⁶, "n" up to 10⁸, else "log n".
hints: Seven if lines, smallest limit first.
blocks.starter:
def allowed(n):
    pass
blocks.solution:
def allowed(n):
    if n <= 10: return "n!"
    if n <= 20: return "2^n"
    if n <= 500: return "n^3"
    if n <= 5000: return "n^2"
    if n <= 10**6: return "n log n"
    if n <= 10**8: return "n"
    return "log n"

blocks.q: What does Big-O measure, and how do you use a problem's limits to choose an algorithm?
blocks.a: Big-O describes how the number of steps grows as the input size n grows, ignoring constant factors: a loop over n items is O(n), two nested loops over all pairs O(n²), halving each step O(log n), trying every subset O(2ⁿ). A computer does roughly 10⁸ simple steps a second (pure Python closer to 10⁷), so the limit on n tells you the most work you can afford: n ≤ 20 allows 2ⁿ, n ≤ 5 000 allows n², n up to about 10⁶ needs n log n or better, and huge n needs O(log n) maths. To speed something up, keep a running summary (lowest so far, running sum) instead of looking back at every earlier item, and watch for hidden loops like x in list.

chapters.title: Arrays in one pass
chapters.tagline: Keep a small summary as you walk, and swap in place instead of building new lists
goals: Find the maximum-sum stretch of an array in one pass (Kadane)
Use a write pointer to filter an array in place
Rotate and reverse in place with O(1) extra memory
Sort three kinds of value in one pass (the Dutch flag)
chapters.prelude:
import time, random

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
An array is a row of boxes in memory, side by side. Reading a[i] is instant because the computer jumps straight to box i. Most array problems are about walking that row once while carrying a few numbers in your head.

The classic: which stretch of neighbouring numbers (a subarray) has the largest total? Think of a shop's profit and loss per day, and the best run of days to show investors.

blocks.name: ds-kadane
blocks.title: Every stretch, or one walk
blocks.goal: Run try every stretch to the end, then run Kadane to the end and compare how many stretches each looked at.
blocks.intro: Click any number to see why it helps or hurts a stretch.

blocks.html: The idea in one sentence: if the run you're carrying has a negative total, drop it, because adding a negative start to anything only makes it smaller.

blocks.code:
a = [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]
run = 0
for x in a:
    run = max(x, run + x)
    print(run, end=" ")

blocks.html: run = max(x, run + x) is the same rule written another way: either extend the run with x, or start fresh at x, whichever is bigger. The answer is the largest run ever seen (6, for 4 -1 2 1).

blocks.title: Kadane's algorithm
blocks.tests:
assert max_subarray([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]) == 6
assert max_subarray([-3, -1, -2]) == -1
assert max_subarray([5]) == 5

blocks.html: The first decoy is the classic bug: starting best at 0 gives the wrong answer when every number is negative (the best stretch is then the single largest number, not an empty one).

blocks.q: a = [-3, -1, -2]. What should max_subarray(a) return if a stretch must contain at least one number?
blocks.why: The best you can do is the single number -1. A version that starts best = 0 returns 0, which is only right if empty stretches are allowed. Always check the all-negative case.

blocks.title: max_subarray_where
blocks.prompt: An interview classic, one step harder. Write best_stretch(a) returning (total, start, end) for the maximum-sum subarray (inclusive indices). If several stretches tie, return the one that starts earliest, and among those the shortest. a has at least one number and can have 10⁵ of them.
blocks.tests:
assert best_stretch([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]) == (6, 3, 6)
assert best_stretch([-3, -1, -2]) == (-1, 1, 1)
assert best_stretch([2, -2, 2]) == (2, 0, 0), "ties: earliest start, then shortest"
assert best_stretch([1, 2, 3]) == (6, 0, 2)
big = [random.randint(-50, 50) for _ in range(5000)]
r, secs = timed(best_stretch, big)
assert r[0] == sum(big[r[1]:r[2] + 1])
assert secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s: too slow, use one walk"
hints: Carry run and the index start where the current run began. When run is negative, reset run = 0 and start = j before adding a[j].
Only replace best when the new total is strictly bigger: that keeps the earliest, shortest one on ties.
blocks.starter:
def best_stretch(a):
    return (0, 0, 0)

sections.title: Filtering in place: the write pointer

blocks.html: Building a new list costs memory. Many interview questions say "do it in place". The pattern: one index reads every item, another (w, the write pointer) marks where the next kept item goes.

blocks.title: move_zeroes
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. Move every 0 in the list a to the end, in place, keeping the other numbers in their original order. Return nothing; change a itself.
blocks.tests:
a = [0, 1, 0, 3, 12]; move_zeroes(a); assert a == [1, 3, 12, 0, 0]
a = [0]; move_zeroes(a); assert a == [0]
a = [4, 2]; move_zeroes(a); assert a == [4, 2]
a = [0, 5, 0]; b = a; r = move_zeroes(a); assert b == [5, 0, 0] and r is None, "change the list itself, don't return a new one"
hints: Walk with x. Every non-zero goes to a[w], then w += 1. Afterwards, fill from w to the end with zeros.
blocks.starter:
def move_zeroes(a):
    return [x for x in a if x != 0] + [0] * a.count(0)

blocks.title: dedupe_sorted
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. a is sorted. Remove duplicates in place so the first k slots hold each distinct value once, in order, and return k. (What's after slot k doesn't matter.)
blocks.tests:
a = [1, 1, 2]; k = dedupe_sorted(a); assert k == 2 and a[:k] == [1, 2]
a = [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4]; k = dedupe_sorted(a); assert k == 5 and a[:k] == [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
a = []; assert dedupe_sorted(a) == 0
a = [7]; assert dedupe_sorted(a) == 1 and a == [7]
hints: Because it's sorted, a duplicate always sits right after its twin. Compare a[i] with the last value you kept, a[w - 1].
blocks.starter:
def dedupe_sorted(a):
    return len(set(a))

blocks.code:
def reverse(a, lo, hi):
    while lo < hi:
        a[lo], a[hi] = a[hi], a[lo]
        lo += 1
        hi -= 1

a = list("ABCDEFG")
reverse(a, 0, len(a) - 1)
print("".join(a))
blocks.title: Reverse with two pointers

blocks.html: Rotating right by k (the last k items move to the front) looks like it needs a second list. It doesn't: reverse the whole thing, then reverse the first k, then reverse the rest.

blocks.code:
a = list("ABCDEFG")
k = 3
def rev(lo, hi):
    while lo < hi:
        a[lo], a[hi] = a[hi], a[lo]
        lo, hi = lo + 1, hi - 1
rev(0, 6); print("".join(a))
rev(0, k - 1); print("".join(a))
rev(k, 6); print("".join(a))

blocks.title: rotate_bug
blocks.prompt: This rotation works for small k but crashes or gives the wrong answer when k is bigger than the list (rotating 7 items by 10 is the same as rotating by 3), and when the list is empty. Fix it.
blocks.tests:
a = list("ABCDEFG"); rotate(a, 3); assert "".join(a) == "EFGABCD"
a = list("ABCDEFG"); rotate(a, 10); assert "".join(a) == "EFGABCD", "10 steps on 7 items = 3 steps"
a = list("ABC"); rotate(a, 3); assert "".join(a) == "ABC"
a = []; rotate(a, 5); assert a == []
hints: Rotating by n changes nothing, so only k % n matters. Guard the empty list first (% 0 would crash).

sections.title: Three kinds in one pass: the Dutch flag

blocks.html: Sort a list holding only 0s, 1s and 2s, in one pass, in place. Keep three regions: everything before lo is 0, everything after hi is 2, and mid walks the unknown part in between.

blocks.title: Dutch national flag
blocks.tests:
a = [2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0]; sort_colors(a); assert a == [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]
a = [2, 2, 0]; sort_colors(a); assert a == [0, 2, 2]
a = []; sort_colors(a); assert a == []
a = [1]; sort_colors(a); assert a == [1]

blocks.q: In the Dutch flag, after swapping a[mid] with a[hi], why don't we move mid forward?

opts.t: The number that came from hi hasn't been looked at yet, so mid must check it
To keep the loop running longer

blocks.why: Everything after hi was unknown. The swap brings one of those unknowns to mid, and it could be a 0, 1 or 2. (After a swap with lo it's safe to move on: that slot was already checked.)

blocks.title: make_non_decreasing
blocks.prompt: Codeforces style. In one operation you may add 1 to any element. Return the minimum number of operations to make a non-decreasing (each element ≥ the one before it). n up to 2·10⁵, values up to 10⁹.
blocks.tests:
assert make_non_decreasing([3, 2, 5, 1, 7]) == 1 + 4
assert make_non_decreasing([1, 2, 3]) == 0
assert make_non_decreasing([5, 4, 3, 2, 1]) == 1 + 2 + 3 + 4
assert make_non_decreasing([10**9, 1]) == 10**9 - 1
assert make_non_decreasing([]) == 0
hints: Raising an element to exactly the largest value so far is always enough and never wasteful. Carry that running maximum.
blocks.starter:
def make_non_decreasing(a):
    return 0

blocks.title: max_product
blocks.prompt: An interview favourite that breaks Kadane. Return the largest product of a non-empty stretch of a (integers, may be negative or zero). A negative times a negative is positive, so the smallest product so far matters too.
blocks.tests:
assert max_product([2, 3, -2, 4]) == 6
assert max_product([-2, 0, -1]) == 0
assert max_product([-2, 3, -4]) == 24, "two negatives make a positive"
assert max_product([-2]) == -2
assert max_product([0, 2]) == 2
hints: Carry two runs: the biggest and the smallest product ending here. A negative x turns the smallest into the biggest.
blocks.solution:
def max_product(a):
    best = hi = lo = a[0]
    for x in a[1:]:
        cands = (x, hi * x, lo * x)
        hi, lo = max(cands), min(cands)
        best = max(best, hi)
    return best

blocks.title: leaders
blocks.prompt: A warm-up that teaches walking backwards. An element is a leader if it's strictly greater than everything to its right (the last element always is). Return the leaders in their original left-to-right order, in O(n).
blocks.tests:
assert leaders([16, 17, 4, 3, 5, 2]) == [17, 5, 2]
assert leaders([1, 2, 3]) == [3]
assert leaders([]) == []
big = list(range(6000, 0, -1))
r, secs = timed(leaders, big)
assert r == big and secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s: walk from the right, keeping the maximum seen"
hints: From the right, "greater than everything to my right" means "greater than the maximum so far".
blocks.starter:
def leaders(a):
    return [x for i, x in enumerate(a) if all(x > y for y in a[i + 1:])]

blocks.q: What does Kadane's algorithm throw away, and when?

opts.t: The smallest number, at the end
The current run, as soon as its total is negative
The best answer, when a bigger one appears

blocks.why: A run with a negative total can only lower whatever follows, so starting fresh is never worse.

blocks.q: What's the extra memory used by the write-pointer filter?

opts.t: O(k), for the k items kept

blocks.why: It overwrites the same list. That's what "in place" means.

blocks.q: Rotating 1 000 items right by 1 000 003 steps. How many steps actually matter?
blocks.why: Every 1 000 steps brings the list back to where it started: 1 000 003 % 1 000 = 3.

blocks.q: Which problem is not a "carry one summary while walking" problem?

opts.t: Best day to buy and sell a share
Counting how many pairs of equal numbers there are, without extra memory and in O(n), when the numbers are unsorted

blocks.why: The first three each need just one or two running numbers. Counting equal pairs in unsorted data needs to remember which values you've seen: that's a hash map (chapter 3), or sorting first.

sections.title: Real-world project: the best run of days

blocks.title: A "best run" report for a small business
blocks.client: A café owner with three years of daily profit and loss in a spreadsheet, preparing to talk to the bank
blocks.brief: Build bestrun.py daily.csv that prints the best stretch of consecutive days (total, start date, end date), the worst stretch (the deepest loss), and the longest streak of profitable days. Then handle the café's question about the yearly cycle: treat the year as a circle (December wraps into January) and find the best stretch on that circle.
blocks.why: "Best and worst consecutive periods" appear in finance (maximum drawdown), monitoring (longest outage), genomics (high-scoring DNA segments) and sport (best scoring run). Kadane is the engine behind all of them.
milestones: Best stretch when the year wraps around
stretch: Report the best stretch of at least 7 days
Read the CSV in one pass without loading it all into memory

blocks.title: worst_stretch
blocks.prompt: Write worst_stretch(a): the smallest total of a non-empty stretch (the deepest loss).
blocks.tests:

blocks.q: Explain Kadane's algorithm and the write-pointer pattern, and why each is O(n).
blocks.a: Kadane walks the array once, carrying run = the best total of a stretch ending at the current element. For each x, run = max(x, run + x): extend the stretch, or start fresh if the old run was negative and could only drag things down. The answer is the largest run seen. Starting best at a[0], not 0, handles all-negative arrays. The write pointer filters in place: one index reads every element, w marks where the next kept element goes, so nothing is copied to a new list and extra memory is O(1). Both touch every element a constant number of times, so they're O(n), versus O(n²) for trying every start and end. Related in-place tricks: reverse with two pointers, rotate by k with three reversals (k % n), and the Dutch flag with three regions lo/mid/hi.

chapters.title: Hash maps and sets (remember what you've seen)
chapters.tagline: Trade a little memory for a lot of time with O(1) lookups
goals: Explain how a hash table finds a key without searching
Solve "have I seen the partner of this number?" problems in one pass
Count things with a dict and group things by a key
Rewrite a pair condition so equal keys mean a match
chapters.prelude:
import time, random
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)

sections.title: How a hash table finds things without looking

blocks.html: A list answers "is 37 in here?" by checking every item. A hash table (Python's dict and set) computes a number from the key (its hash), uses it to pick a bucket, and only looks in that bucket. With a good hash function and enough buckets, each bucket holds about one item, so a lookup is O(1) on average, however big the table gets.

blocks.name: ds-hash
blocks.title: Two-sum: every pair, or one lookup each
blocks.goal: Run every earlier number until it finds the pair, then run hash set and compare the number of checks.
blocks.intro: Click a bucket to see what decides where a number goes.

blocks.code:
seen = set()
for x in [4, 8, 4, 15, 8]:
    print(x, "seen before" if x in seen else "new")
    seen.add(x)

counts = Counter("mississippi")

blocks.title: Sets and dicts in practice

blocks.code:
d = {1: "a", 1.0: "b", True: "c"}
print(d)

blocks.html: 1, 1.0 and True are equal and have the same hash, so they're the same key: the first spelling is kept, the last value wins. Keys are matched by hash and then ==.

blocks.q: Why can't a Python list be a dict key, but a tuple can?

opts.t: A list can change after it's stored, which would change its hash and lose it in the wrong bucket

blocks.why: The bucket is chosen from the hash at insert time. If the key changed, a later lookup would compute a different hash and look in the wrong bucket. So only immutable things are hashable. Convert with tuple(lst) when you need a list as a key.

blocks.html: For each item, ask: "have I already seen the thing that completes me?" Then store the item. One pass, one lookup each.

blocks.title: two_sum
blocks.prompt: The most famous interview question. Return the indices [i, j] (i < j) of the two numbers in nums that add up to target. Exactly one answer exists. n can be 10⁵.
blocks.tests:
assert two_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9) == [0, 1]
assert two_sum([3, 2, 4], 6) == [1, 2]

assert two_sum([-1, -2, -3, -4, -5], -8) == [2, 4]
big = list(range(0, 12000, 2)) + [7]
r2, secs2 = timed(two_sum, big, 11998 + 7)
assert r2 == [5999, 6000]

blocks.title: count_pairs
blocks.prompt: Codeforces style. Count the pairs i < j with a[i] + a[j] == k. Values can repeat, and n is up to 2·10⁵.
blocks.tests:

assert count_pairs([1, 1, 1, 1], 2) == 6, "4 choose 2"
assert count_pairs([3], 6) == 0
big = [1] * 4000
r, secs = timed(count_pairs, big, 2)
assert r == 4000 * 3999 // 2 and secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s: too slow"
hints: Like two-sum, but instead of returning on the first match, add how many earlier partners there are: keep counts, not indices.
blocks.starter:
def count_pairs(a, k):
    return sum(1 for j in range(len(a)) for i in range(j) if a[i] + a[j] == k)
blocks.solution:
def count_pairs(a, k):
    seen = Counter()
    total = 0
    for x in a:
        total += seen[k - x]
        seen[x] += 1
    return total

sections.title: Turn a pair condition into equal keys

blocks.html: A powerful contest trick: if a condition about a pair (i, j) can be rewritten as f(i) == f(j), then counting good pairs is just counting equal keys.

blocks.title: same_differences
blocks.prompt: Codeforces style. Count the pairs i < j with a[j] - a[i] == j - i. n is up to 2·10⁵.
blocks.tests:
assert same_differences([3, 5, 1, 4, 6, 6]) == 1
assert same_differences([1, 2, 3]) == 3
assert same_differences([1, 2, 1, 2]) == 2
big = list(range(5000))
r, secs = timed(same_differences, big)
assert r == 5000 * 4999 // 2 and secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s: rewrite the condition first"
hints: Move everything about i to one side: a[j] - j == a[i] - i. Now it's "count pairs with equal keys", where the key is a[i] - i.
blocks.solution:
def same_differences(a):
    seen = Counter()
    total = 0
    for i, x in enumerate(a):
        total += seen[x - i]
        seen[x - i] += 1
    return total

blocks.q: Average cost of x in s when s is a Python set of n items?
blocks.why: One hash, one bucket, about one comparison. (Lists are O(n); sorted lists with binary search O(log n).)

blocks.q: Why does two-sum look up target - x before adding x?

opts.t: So a number can't be paired with itself

blocks.why: With target 6 and x = 3, adding first would find the 3 you just stored. Looking up first means you only match earlier numbers.

blocks.q: A hash table's lookup is O(1) on average. When can it be O(n)?

opts.t: When many keys land in the same bucket (collisions), for example inputs built to attack the hash function

blocks.why: If everything collides, one bucket holds all n keys and you're back to a list. Codeforces "anti-hash" tests do exactly this to unprotected hash maps; adding a random salt to keys defeats them.

blocks.q: Which of these needs a dict rather than a set?

opts.t: Has this email address signed up already?
How many times has each email address signed up?
Are there any duplicates in this list?
Is this word in the dictionary?

blocks.why: A set remembers whether; a dict remembers something about each key (a count, an index, a list).

blocks.q: You need "pairs with a[i] + i == a[j] - j". What's the key trick?

opts.t: It isn't an equal-keys condition, because the two sides use different formulas: count a[i] + i values and look up a[j] - j as you go
It can't be done in O(n)

blocks.why: You don't need the same formula on both sides. Walk j, look up how many earlier i had a[i] + i == a[j] - j, then store a[j] + j. Any "f(i) = g(j)" condition is one lookup per element.

blocks.q: How does a hash table give O(1) lookups, and what's the two-sum pattern?
blocks.a: A hash table computes a hash number from the key and uses it to choose a bucket, then only compares against the few keys in that bucket. With a good hash function and a table that grows as it fills, buckets stay tiny, so lookups, inserts and deletes are O(1) on average (O(n) in the worst case, if everything collides). Keys must be immutable, because the bucket is chosen from the hash when the key is stored. The two-sum pattern: walk the array once; for each x, ask whether its partner (target − x) has been seen, then store x. Storing counts instead of indices counts pairs. More generally, rewrite a pair condition so one side depends only on i and the other only on j (for example a[i] − i == a[j] − j), then count with a dict as you walk: O(n) instead of O(n²).

chapters.title: Prefix sums and difference arrays
chapters.tagline: Pay once up front, then answer every range question in O(1)
goals: Build a prefix-sum array and answer any range sum with one subtraction
Count subarrays with a given sum by combining prefix sums with a hash map
Apply many range updates at once with a difference array
Extend prefix sums to 2D grids
chapters.prelude:
import time, random
from collections import Counter
from itertools import accumulate

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
A shop has ten years of daily sales, and the manager keeps asking: "what did we sell between day 1 200 and day 1 450?" Adding up the range each time is slow when there are many questions. Instead, build the running total once: P[k] = the sum of the first k days. Then

sum of days l..r = P[r+1] − P[l]

because everything up to day r, minus everything before day l, leaves exactly the days in between.

blocks.name: ds-prefix
blocks.title: Adding up every range, or one subtraction each
blocks.goal: Answer all six queries with add up every range, then with prefix sums, and compare the work.
blocks.intro: Click a running-total box to see why P starts with a 0.

blocks.code:
a = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2, 6, 5, 3]
P = [0]
for x in a:
    P.append(P[-1] + x)
print(P)
print(list(accumulate(a, initial=0)))
l, r = 2, 7
print(sum(a[l:r + 1]), P[r + 1] - P[l])
blocks.title: Building prefix sums

blocks.html: P[3] − P[3] is the empty range: 0. The leading zero makes every formula work at the edges with no special cases. That's the main reason prefix arrays have length n + 1.

blocks.title: RangeSum
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. Write a class RangeSum built from a list a, with a method query(l, r) returning a[l] + … + a[r] (inclusive) in O(1). There will be 10⁵ queries.
blocks.tests:
rs = RangeSum([-2, 0, 3, -5, 2, -1])
assert rs.query(0, 2) == 1
assert rs.query(2, 5) == -1
assert rs.query(0, 5) == -3
assert rs.query(3, 3) == -5
big = RangeSum(list(range(20000)))
t = time.perf_counter()
for i in range(20000):
    big.query(0, 19999)
secs = time.perf_counter() - t
assert secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s for 20 000 queries: each one is re-adding the range"
hints: Build P in __init__. query is one subtraction.

blocks.title: pivot_index
blocks.prompt: An interview warm-up. Return the first index i where the sum of everything left of i equals the sum of everything right of i (the element itself counts on neither side), or -1.
blocks.tests:
assert pivot_index([1, 7, 3, 6, 5, 6]) == 3
assert pivot_index([1, 2, 3]) == -1
assert pivot_index([2, 1, -1]) == 0, "nothing on the left sums to 0"
big = [1] * 20000
r, secs = timed(pivot_index, big)
assert r == -1 and secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s: slicing and summing for each i is O(n²)"
hints: Right side = total − left − x. Keep left as a running sum.

blocks.html: The most important combination in this chapter. "How many subarrays sum to k?" A subarray l..r sums to k exactly when P[r+1] − P[l] = k, that is P[l] = P[r+1] − k. So as you walk, count how many earlier prefix sums equal current − k. It's two-sum (chapter 3) on prefix sums.

blocks.title: subarray_sum_k
blocks.prompt: One of the most asked interview questions. Count the subarrays of a (integers, may be negative) whose sum is exactly k. n up to 2·10⁴, so O(n²) is too slow in Python.
blocks.tests:
assert subarray_sum_k([1, 1, 1], 2) == 2
assert subarray_sum_k([1, 2, 3], 3) == 2
assert subarray_sum_k([1, -1, 0], 0) == 3
assert subarray_sum_k([3, 4, 7, 2, -3, 1, 4, 2], 7) == 4
big = [0] * 5000
r, secs = timed(subarray_sum_k, big, 0)
assert r == 5000 * 5001 // 2 and secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s: too slow"
hints: seen counts prefix sums so far, starting with {0: 1} (the empty prefix). For each new running sum run, add seen[run - k], then record run.
Sliding windows (chapter 8) don't work here because of negative numbers. Prefix sums + a hash map do.
blocks.solution:
def subarray_sum_k(a, k):
    seen = Counter({0: 1})
    run = count = 0
    for x in a:
        run += x
        count += seen[run - k]
        seen[run] += 1
    return count

blocks.title: divisible_subarrays
blocks.prompt: Interview and contest favourite. Count subarrays whose sum is divisible by k (k ≥ 1; numbers may be negative).
blocks.tests:
assert divisible_subarrays([4, 5, 0, -2, -3, 1], 5) == 7
assert divisible_subarrays([5], 9) == 0
assert divisible_subarrays([-1, 2, 9], 2) == 2
hints: P[r+1] − P[l] is divisible by k exactly when the two prefix sums have the same remainder mod k. Count equal remainders. (Python's % already gives a non-negative remainder for negative numbers.)
blocks.starter:
def divisible_subarrays(a, k):
    return 0
blocks.solution:
def divisible_subarrays(a, k):
    seen = Counter({0: 1})
    run = count = 0
    for x in a:
        run = (run + x) % k
        count += seen[run]
        seen[run] += 1
    return count

blocks.title: product_except_self
blocks.prompt: A top interview question. Return a list where position i holds the product of every element except a[i], without using division, in O(n).
blocks.tests:
assert product_except_self([1, 2, 3, 4]) == [24, 12, 8, 6]
assert product_except_self([-1, 1, 0, -3, 3]) == [0, 0, 9, 0, 0]
assert product_except_self([2, 3]) == [3, 2]
big = [1] * 5000
r, secs = timed(product_except_self, big)
assert r == big and secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s: too slow"
hints: The answer at i is (product of everything left of i) × (product of everything right of i): a prefix product and a suffix product.
blocks.solution:
def product_except_self(a):
    n = len(a)
    out = [1] * n
    left = 1
    for i in range(n):
        out[i] = left
        left *= a[i]
    right = 1
    for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
        out[i] *= right
        right *= a[i]
    return out

sections.title: Difference arrays: many range updates at once

blocks.html: The reverse problem: lots of updates "add v to every element from l to r", then read the final array. Doing each update element by element is O(n) per update. Instead, mark only the edges: D[l] += v and D[r+1] -= v. A prefix sum of D at the end spreads each mark across its range.

assert apply_updates(1, [(0, 0, 7)]) == [7]
lines: for l, r, v in updates:

def car_pooling(trips, capacity):

blocks.html: For a grid, S[i][j] = the sum of the rectangle from the top-left corner to (i−1, j−1). A rectangle's sum is then four lookups: the big corner rectangle, minus the strip above, minus the strip to the left, plus the corner you subtracted twice.

blocks.title: grid_sums
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. Write build(grid) returning the 2D prefix table S of size (rows+1) × (cols+1), and rect(S, r1, c1, r2, c2) returning the sum of the rectangle with those inclusive corners, in O(1).
blocks.tests:
g = [[3, 0, 1, 4, 2], [5, 6, 3, 2, 1], [1, 2, 0, 1, 5], [4, 1, 0, 1, 7], [1, 0, 3, 0, 5]]
S = build(g)
assert len(S) == 6 and len(S[0]) == 6, "S has an extra row and column of zeros"
assert rect(S, 2, 1, 4, 3) == 8
assert rect(S, 1, 1, 2, 2) == 11
assert rect(S, 1, 2, 2, 4) == 12
assert rect(S, 0, 0, 4, 4) == sum(map(sum, g))
hints: Inclusion-exclusion: S[i+1][j+1] = grid[i][j] + above + left − above-left. The query uses the same idea backwards.

blocks.q: Why does the prefix array start with P[0] = 0?

opts.t: To make it the same length as the input
So a range starting at index 0 is P[r+1] − P[0] with no special case

blocks.why: Without it, ranges that start at the beginning need an if. The extra zero is the "sum of nothing".

blocks.q: n = 10⁵ numbers, q = 10⁵ "sum of l..r" queries. Total work with prefix sums?
blocks.why: n to build, then O(1) per query.

blocks.q: "Count subarrays with sum exactly k" when numbers can be negative. Which tool?

opts.t: Prefix sums plus a hash map of how many times each prefix sum has appeared

blocks.why: With negatives, growing a window can make the sum smaller, so windows don't work. Prefix sums turn it into two-sum.

blocks.q: A difference array update "add 5 to positions 3..8" changes how many entries of D?
blocks.why: D[3] += 5 and D[9] -= 5. That's why a million updates are cheap: the prefix sum at the end does the spreading.

blocks.q: Prefix sums need the array to stay fixed. What if values change between queries?

opts.t: Rebuild P after every change, it's fine
You need a structure that supports both updates and range sums in O(log n): a Fenwick tree or segment tree (Part 6)

blocks.why: Rebuilding is O(n) per change. Fenwick and segment trees handle mixed updates and queries.

sections.title: Real-world project: a hotel occupancy planner

blocks.title: How full is the hotel each night?
blocks.client: A 40-room boutique hotel whose booking system lets staff double-book on busy weekends
blocks.brief: Build occupancy.py bookings.csv where each booking has a check-in night and a check-out night (the guest doesn't stay the check-out night). Produce: rooms occupied each night of the year, every night where bookings exceed 40 rooms, the busiest night, and answer "how many room-nights did we sell between two dates?" instantly for the accountant.
blocks.why: Difference arrays power calendar and capacity systems (hotels, cinemas, cloud servers, parking), and prefix sums answer the reporting questions. One pass over the bookings, one pass over the calendar.

Room-nights sold between two dates in O(1)

Draw the year as a heat map

blocks.title: occupancy

hints: +1 on the check-in night, −1 on the check-out night, then a running total.

def occupancy(bookings, nights):

blocks.tests:
rn = RoomNights([1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 0])
assert rn.between(0, 5) == 7
assert rn.between(1, 3) == 5
assert rn.between(5, 5) == 0

blocks.prompt: From memory: subarray_sum_k(a, k) counts subarrays summing to exactly k, in O(n), with negatives allowed.
blocks.tests:

assert subarray_sum_k([1, -1, 1, -1], 0) == 4
assert subarray_sum_k([5], 5) == 1

def subarray_sum_k(a, k):

blocks.q: Explain prefix sums, the prefix-sum + hash-map trick, and difference arrays.
blocks.a: A prefix array P has P[0] = 0 and P[k] = a[0] + … + a[k-1]. Building it is O(n); then any range sum a[l..r] = P[r+1] − P[l] in O(1), because the total up to r minus the total before l leaves just the range. The leading zero removes edge cases. To count subarrays summing to k, note that l..r works exactly when P[l] = P[r+1] − k, so walk once keeping a dict of how many times each prefix sum has appeared (starting {0: 1}) and add the count of run − k at each step: two-sum on prefix sums, which works with negative numbers. Equal remainders mod k give subarrays divisible by k. A difference array does the opposite: to add v to a[l..r], do D[l] += v and D[r+1] −= v; one prefix sum at the end applies every update, so u updates cost O(u + n). In 2D, S[i+1][j+1] = grid[i][j] + above + left − above-left, and a rectangle is four lookups by inclusion-exclusion.

chapters.title: Recursion and the call stack
chapters.tagline: Solve a problem by trusting a smaller copy of it, and remember answers you've already found
goals: Write a recursive function with a base case and a smaller step
Trace the call stack and predict the order things happen
Spot repeated work and remove it with a memo
Turn deep recursion into a loop when the stack would overflow
chapters.prelude:
import sys, time
from functools import lru_cache

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
A recursive function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version, and has a base case small enough to answer directly. The leap of faith: while writing fact(n) = n * fact(n - 1), assume fact(n - 1) already works.

Underneath, each call gets a frame on the call stack (its own n, its own local variables, and where to return to). A call can't finish until the calls it made have finished, so frames pile up and then unwind.

blocks.name: ds-recur
blocks.title: The call tree and the call stack of fib(6)
blocks.goal: Run plain recursion to the end, then run with a memo and compare how many calls did real work.
blocks.intro: Step slowly at first: watch the stack on the right grow as calls start, and shrink as they return.

blocks.code:
def fact(n, depth=0):
    print("  " * depth + f"fact({n}) starts")
    result = 1 if n <= 1 else n * fact(n - 1, depth + 1)
    print("  " * depth + f"fact({n}) returns {result}")
    return result

fact(4)
blocks.title: Watching frames open and close

blocks.code:
def show(n):
    if n == 0:
        return
    print("before", n)
    show(n - 1)
    print("after", n)

show(3)

blocks.html: Everything before the recursive call happens on the way down (3, 2, 1); everything after it happens on the way back up, in reverse (1, 2, 3). That's how the stack lets recursion "remember" where it was.

blocks.q: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?

opts.t: It loops forever, using no extra memory
Each call opens a new frame until Python's limit (about 1 000) and raises RecursionError
Python detects it and stops at the first call

blocks.why: Frames take memory, so infinite recursion runs out of stack. Python sets a limit (sys.getrecursionlimit()) to fail cleanly instead of crashing.

blocks.title: fast_power
blocks.prompt: Write power(x, n) computing xⁿ for an integer n ≥ 0 using only O(log n) multiplications. The idea: xⁿ = (x^(n/2))² when n is even, and x · xⁿ⁻¹ when n is odd. (This is how cryptography raises numbers to 300-digit powers.)
blocks.tests:
assert power(2, 10) == 1024
assert power(3, 0) == 1
assert power(5, 3) == 125
assert power(7, 1) == 7
assert power(3, 200) == 3**200
_, secs = timed(power, 1, 10**7)
assert secs < 0.05, f"{secs:.3f}s: that's n multiplications; halve n instead"
hints: Compute half = power(x, n // 2) once and square it. Calling power(x, n // 2) * power(x, n // 2) makes two calls and loses all the speed.

blocks.title: hanoi
blocks.prompt: The classic. Move n discs from peg a to peg c using peg b, never putting a bigger disc on a smaller one. Return the list of moves as (from, to) pairs. Trust the smaller copy: move n−1 discs out of the way, move the biggest, move the n−1 back on top.
blocks.tests:
assert hanoi(1) == [("A", "C")]
assert hanoi(2) == [("A", "B"), ("A", "C"), ("B", "C")]
assert len(hanoi(10)) == 2**10 - 1
pegs = {"A": list(range(6, 0, -1)), "B": [], "C": []}
for f, t in hanoi(6):
    d = pegs[f].pop()
    assert not pegs[t] or pegs[t][-1] > d, "a bigger disc landed on a smaller one"
    pegs[t].append(d)
assert pegs["C"] == list(range(6, 0, -1))
hints: Three steps: hanoi(n-1, a, c, b) (to the spare peg), the move (a, c), then hanoi(n-1, b, a, c).
blocks.starter:
def hanoi(n, a="A", b="B", c="C"):
    return []

blocks.title: flatten
blocks.prompt: An interview warm-up. Flatten a list that may contain lists, nested to any depth, into one flat list in order.
blocks.tests:
assert flatten([1, [2, [3, [4]], 5], [], 6]) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
assert flatten([]) == []
assert flatten([[[[]]]]) == []
assert flatten(["a", ["b"]]) == ["a", "b"]
hints: For each item: if it's a list, flatten it (the smaller copy) and extend; otherwise append it.
blocks.starter:
def flatten(x):
    return [y for part in x for y in part]

blocks.title: climb_stairs
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. You climb a staircase of n steps, taking 1 or 2 steps at a time. Count the different ways. n up to 80. The plain recursion ways(n-1) + ways(n-2) is the fib tree from the simulation, so it's far too slow at 80: memoize it.

assert climb(1) == 1
assert climb(2) == 2
assert climb(3) == 3
assert climb(5) == 8
_, secs = timed(climb, 30)
assert secs < 0.05, f"climb(30) took {secs:.2f}s: that's the exponential call tree. Add a memo."
assert climb(80) == 37889062373143906
hints: Add @lru_cache(maxsize=None) above the function (or keep a dict yourself). Every climb(k) is then computed once.

blocks.title: grid_paths
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. A robot starts in the top-left of an r × c grid and only moves right or down. Count the paths to the bottom-right corner, with a memo. r and c up to 100.
blocks.tests:
assert paths(3, 7) == 28
assert paths(3, 2) == 3
assert paths(1, 1) == 1
_, secs = timed(paths, 12, 12)
assert secs < 0.05, f"paths(12, 12) took {secs:.2f}s: memoize on (r, c)"
assert paths(100, 100) == 22750883079422934966181954039568885395604168260154104734000
hints: The last move into the corner came either from above (r - 1, c) or from the left (r, c - 1). Memoize on (r, c).

blocks.title: memo_bug
blocks.prompt: This memoized function crashes with TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'. A memo stores answers in a dict, so arguments must be hashable. Fix it so best_sum still takes a list from the caller.
blocks.tests:
assert best_sum([2, 7, 9, 3, 1]) == 12
assert best_sum([1, 2, 3, 1]) == 4
assert best_sum([]) == 0
r, secs = timed(best_sum, [5] * 400)
assert r == 1000 and secs < 0.2
hints: Memoize an inner function that takes only the index i, and let it read the list from the outer function. (Or convert the list to a tuple before calling the cached function.)

sections.title: When the stack is too deep

blocks.html: Python's stack holds about 1 000 frames. A recursion that goes n levels deep fails at n = 10⁵, even with a memo. Contest solutions in Python usually turn such recursions into loops: compute small answers first and build up. That's a bottom-up table, the other face of dynamic programming.

blocks.title: ways_134
blocks.prompt: Codeforces style. Count the ways to write n as an ordered sum of 1s, 3s and 4s (so 1+3 and 3+1 are different), modulo 1 000 000 007. n up to 10⁵, so recursion would overflow the stack: build the answers from 0 upwards in a list.
blocks.tests:
assert ways(1) == 1
assert ways(3) == 2, "1+1+1, 3"
assert ways(4) == 4, "1+1+1+1, 1+3, 3+1, 4"
assert ways(5) == 6
r, secs = timed(ways, 100000)
assert secs < 0.5 and 0 <= r < 1_000_000_007
hints: w[i] = w[i-1] + w[i-3] + w[i-4] (skipping negative indices), starting from w[0] = 1 (one way to make 0: take nothing).
blocks.solution:
def ways(n):
    MOD = 1_000_000_007
    w = [0] * (n + 1)
    w[0] = 1
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        w[i] = (w[i - 1] + (w[i - 3] if i >= 3 else 0) + (w[i - 4] if i >= 4 else 0)) % MOD
    return w[n]

blocks.title: Tower of Hanoi, counting moves only
blocks.tests:
assert moves(0) == 0
assert moves(1) == 1
assert moves(3) == 7
assert moves(20) == 2**20 - 1

blocks.q: How many frames are on the stack at the deepest point of fact(5)?
blocks.why: fact(5) waits for fact(4), which waits for fact(3)… down to fact(1): five frames at once. Stack depth = depth of the recursion, not the number of calls.

blocks.q: Plain recursive fib(n) makes about how many calls?
blocks.why: Each call makes two more, and the tree only gets one level shorter on one side. With a memo it's n + 1 calls doing real work.

blocks.q: power(x, n // 2) * power(x, n // 2) instead of computing half once. What's the cost?

opts.t: O(n): the two calls double at every level, undoing the halving

blocks.why: log n levels, doubling each time: 2^(log n) = n calls. Store the result once.

blocks.q: Which is a good sign that memoization will help?

opts.t: The same arguments are passed to the function many times
The function has two base cases

blocks.why: Memoization only helps when calls repeat. Hanoi has no repeats (every call has different pegs or sizes that matter), so a memo wouldn't help it.

blocks.q: A recursion needs depth 10⁵ in Python. Best fix?

opts.t: Rewrite it as a loop that builds answers bottom-up (or keep your own explicit stack)

blocks.why: Raising the limit can crash the interpreter (the real C stack runs out). Bottom-up loops have no depth at all.

sections.title: Real-world project: what's eating my disk?

blocks.title: A `du`-style folder size report
blocks.client: A video editor whose 2 TB drive is full and who can't tell which project folders are the culprits
blocks.brief: Build du.py FOLDER that walks the folder tree and reports each folder's total size (its files plus all its subfolders), the 10 biggest folders, and the deepest path. A folder's size is only known after all its children are measured, which is exactly the "after the recursive call" part of recursion. Then rewrite the walk with an explicit stack so a ridiculously deep folder tree can't overflow Python's stack.
blocks.why: Disk-usage tools, build systems summing dependency sizes, and compilers walking syntax trees are all recursion over trees. Turning recursion into an explicit stack is how production code avoids stack overflows.
milestones: Total size of a folder, recursively
Size of every folder in one walk
The same walk with an explicit stack instead of recursion
stretch: Skip symbolic links so loops can't trap the walk
Show the tree as an indented report, biggest first

blocks.title: folder_size
blocks.prompt: A folder is a dict: keys are names; a value that's an int is a file's size, a value that's a dict is a subfolder. Write folder_size(folder) returning the total size of everything inside.
blocks.tests:
disk = {"a.mp4": 700, "proj": {"raw": {"c1.mov": 4000, "c2.mov": 3500}, "edit.prproj": 20}, "notes.txt": 1, "empty": {}}
assert folder_size(disk) == 700 + 4000 + 3500 + 20 + 1
assert folder_size({}) == 0
assert folder_size(disk["proj"]) == 7520
hints: For each value: a dict means "recurse", an int means "add it".
blocks.starter:
def folder_size(folder):
    return sum(v for v in folder.values() if isinstance(v, int))

blocks.title: all_sizes
blocks.prompt: Write all_sizes(folder, path="/") returning a dict from every folder's path to its total size. Subfolder paths are the parent's path plus the name and a / (so "/proj/raw/"). Visit each file only once in total (don't call folder_size for every folder).
blocks.tests:
disk = {"a.mp4": 700, "proj": {"raw": {"c1.mov": 4000, "c2.mov": 3500}, "edit.prproj": 20}, "empty": {}}
assert all_sizes(disk) == {"/proj/raw/": 7500, "/proj/": 7520, "/empty/": 0, "/": 8220}
hints: One recursive helper that returns its folder's total (so the parent can add it) and records it in out on the way back up.
blocks.starter:
def all_sizes(folder, path="/"):
    return {path: 0}

blocks.title: memo_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: fib(n) with a memo (a dict you manage yourself, no lru_cache), so fib(90) is instant. fib(0) = 0, fib(1) = 1.
blocks.tests:
assert [fib(i) for i in range(8)] == [0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13]
r, secs = timed(fib, 90)
assert r == 2880067194370816120 and secs < 0.05
hints: Check the memo before recursing, store the answer after. (memo=None then memo = {} avoids Python's shared-default-argument trap.)
blocks.starter:
def fib(n, memo=None):
    pass

blocks.q: Explain how recursion uses the call stack, and when and how to use memoization.
blocks.a: A recursive function answers a small base case directly and otherwise calls itself on a smaller input, trusting that call to be right. Each call gets a frame on the call stack holding its arguments, locals and return point; a frame can only finish after the calls it made finish, so code before the recursive call runs on the way down and code after it runs on the way back up in reverse. Stack depth equals recursion depth, and Python allows about 1 000 frames, so very deep recursion raises RecursionError; then rewrite it bottom-up as a loop or use an explicit stack. When the same arguments recur (like fib, where the call tree has about 1.6ⁿ calls), store each answer the first time in a dict (or lru_cache) and return it on repeats: only one call per distinct argument does work, so fib becomes O(n). Halving the input (fast power) gives O(log n) calls, but only if the half result is computed once.

chapters.title: Sorting and what it unlocks
chapters.tagline: Put things in order once, and a pile of hard questions turns into one easy scan
goals: Explain why merge sort is O(n log n) and insertion sort is O(n²)
Sort by any rule with key= and tuples
Recognise "sort, then scan neighbours" problems
Use counting sort when the values are small
chapters.prelude:
import time
from collections import Counter

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html: Insertion sort is how most people sort cards in their hand: take the next card and slide it left until it fits. Merge sort is how you'd sort a huge pile with friends: split it, everyone sorts a small pile, then merge piles two at a time.

blocks.name: ds-sort
blocks.title: Insertion sort against merge sort, counting comparisons
blocks.goal: Run insertion sort to the end, then run merge sort and compare the comparison counts.
blocks.intro: In merge sort each colour block is one run being merged: the runs double in length every round.

blocks.html: Merging two sorted runs is the key move: look at the front of each, take the smaller, repeat. Each comparison places one item, so merging costs about the total length. Runs double each round, so there are log₂ n rounds: O(n log n) in all. In practice you'll call Python's sorted() (Timsort, a merge-sort cousin), but you need to know what it costs and what it gives you.

blocks.code:
people = [("ana", 31), ("bo", 25), ("cy", 31), ("di", 19)]
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: p[1]))            # by age
print(sorted(people, key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[0])))   # oldest first, then by name
words = ["banana", "Apple", "fig", "cherry"]
print(sorted(words, key=str.lower))
print(sorted(words, key=len))
blocks.title: Sorting by any rule with key=

blocks.code:
nums = [3, 1, 2]
a = nums.sort()
b = sorted(nums, reverse=True)
print(a, nums, b)

blocks.html: list.sort() sorts in place and returns None; sorted() returns a new list. Mixing them up (x = x.sort()) is one of the most common Python bugs.

blocks.q: Python's sort is stable. What does that mean?

opts.t: It never crashes on bad input
Items that compare equal keep their original order
It always takes exactly n log n steps

blocks.why: Stability lets you sort in stages: sort by name, then sort by age, and people of the same age stay alphabetical.

blocks.title: merge_sorted
blocks.prompt: Merge two already-sorted lists into one sorted list in O(len(a) + len(b)) time, the heart of merge sort. Don't call sorted on the result.
blocks.tests:
assert merge([1, 4, 9], [2, 3, 10, 11]) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 9, 10, 11]
assert merge([], [1]) == [1]
assert merge([5], []) == [5]
big_a, big_b = list(range(0, 6000, 2)), list(range(1, 6000, 2))
r, secs = timed(merge, big_a, big_b)
assert r == list(range(6000)) and secs < 0.1, f"{secs:.2f}s: that's a bubble sort, merge from the fronts instead"
hints: Two pointers i and j. Append the smaller of a[i] and b[j], move that pointer. When one list runs out, append the rest of the other.

blocks.title: Merge sort, top-down
blocks.tests:
assert merge_sort([5, 2, 9, 1, 5, 6]) == [1, 2, 5, 5, 6, 9]
assert merge_sort([]) == []
assert merge_sort([1]) == [1]

blocks.title: count_inversions
blocks.prompt: A Codeforces classic. An inversion is a pair i < j with a[i] > a[j]; it measures how unsorted a list is (it's exactly the number of swaps insertion sort makes). Count them for n up to 2·10⁴. Checking every pair is O(n²): instead, count during merge sort. When an item from the right half is taken before the remaining items of the left half, it forms an inversion with each of them.
blocks.tests:
assert inversions([2, 4, 1, 3, 5]) == 3
assert inversions([1, 2, 3]) == 0
assert inversions([3, 2, 1]) == 3
assert inversions([]) == 0
big = list(range(20000, 0, -1))
r, secs = timed(inversions, big)
assert r == 20000 * 19999 // 2 and secs < 1.0, f"{secs:.2f}s: count inside the merge"
hints: When you take right[j] while left[i:] is still waiting, every one of those len(left) - i items is bigger and came earlier: add that many.

blocks.html: After sorting, things that are close in value sit next to each other. Many questions that need every pair (O(n²)) become "sort, then look at neighbours" (O(n log n)).

blocks.title: min_gap
blocks.prompt: Warm-up. Return the smallest difference between any two numbers in the list (at least 2 numbers, up to 10⁴).
blocks.tests:
assert min_gap([30, 5, 20, 9]) == 4
assert min_gap([1, 1]) == 0
assert min_gap([-3, 10]) == 13
import random
random.seed(6)
big = random.sample(range(10**9), 6000)
r, secs = timed(min_gap, big)
s = sorted(big)
assert r == min(b - a for a, b in zip(s, s[1:])) and secs < 0.2
hints: The closest pair in value must be neighbours once sorted. Sort, then compare each item with the next.
blocks.starter:
def min_gap(nums):
    return min(abs(a - b) for i, a in enumerate(nums) for b in nums[i + 1:])

blocks.title: merge_intervals
blocks.prompt: An interview top-10. Merge overlapping intervals [start, end] (touching ones like [1, 3] and [3, 5] merge too) and return them sorted by start.
hints: The loop is right; it just assumes the intervals arrive in order of start. Make that true first.

blocks.title: meeting_rooms
blocks.prompt: Asked at Google and Meta. Given meetings as (start, end) (end is exclusive: a meeting ending at 10 frees the room for one starting at 10), return the fewest rooms needed. Sort the start times and the end times separately and sweep: a start needs a room unless some meeting has already ended.
hints: Walk the sorted starts. Before counting a start, release every meeting whose end is ≤ that start (they're sorted too, so a pointer j is enough).
blocks.starter:
def rooms(meetings):
    return len(meetings)

blocks.title: sort_bug
blocks.prompt: This should return the scores from highest to lowest, but it returns None. Fix it.
blocks.tests:
assert ranking([3, 9, 1]) == [9, 3, 1]
s = [2, 5]
assert ranking(s) == [5, 2]
assert s == [2, 5], "don't change the caller's list"
hints: .sort() sorts in place and returns None. Use sorted(...), which returns a new list and leaves the original alone.
blocks.solution:
def ranking(scores):
    return sorted(scores, reverse=True)

blocks.title: leaderboard
blocks.prompt: Codeforces style. Each player is (name, solved, penalty). Rank by most problems solved, then by least penalty, then by name alphabetically. Return the names in order.
blocks.tests:
ps = [("cy", 3, 120), ("ana", 4, 300), ("bo", 3, 90), ("di", 3, 90)]
assert leaderboard(ps) == ["ana", "bo", "di", "cy"]
assert leaderboard([]) == []
hints: A key can return a tuple; tuples compare item by item. Negate the number you want biggest-first: (-solved, penalty, name).
blocks.starter:
def leaderboard(players):
    return [p[0] for p in sorted(players)]
blocks.solution:
def leaderboard(players):
    return [p[0] for p in sorted(players, key=lambda p: (-p[1], p[2], p[0]))]

blocks.title: largest_number
blocks.prompt: An interview favourite. Arrange non-negative integers so that, written side by side, they form the largest number; return it as a string. [3, 30, 34, 5, 9] → "9534330". Sorting by plain value or plain string fails (try 3 against 30): compare two numbers by which order of gluing is bigger, using functools.cmp_to_key.
blocks.tests:
assert largest_number([10, 2]) == "210"
assert largest_number([3, 30, 34, 5, 9]) == "9534330"
assert largest_number([0, 0]) == "0"
assert largest_number([1]) == "1"
hints: a should go before b when a + b > b + a as strings. Watch out for all zeros: the answer is "0", not "00".
blocks.starter:
def largest_number(nums):
    return "".join(sorted(map(str, nums), reverse=True))
blocks.solution:
from functools import cmp_to_key

def largest_number(nums):
    s = [str(x) for x in nums]
    s.sort(key=cmp_to_key(lambda a, b: -1 if a + b > b + a else (1 if a + b < b + a else 0)))
    out = "".join(s)
    return "0" if out and out[0] == "0" else out

blocks.title: h_index
blocks.prompt: An interview classic. A researcher's h-index is the largest h such that they have at least h papers with at least h citations each. Sort, then scan.
blocks.tests:
assert h_index([3, 0, 6, 1, 5]) == 3
assert h_index([1, 3, 1]) == 1
assert h_index([0, 0]) == 0
assert h_index([10, 10]) == 2
assert h_index([]) == 0
hints: Sorted biggest first, the paper at position h (0-based) is the (h+1)-th best. Keep going while it has at least h + 1 citations.
blocks.starter:
def h_index(citations):
    return len(citations)

sections.title: When values are small: counting sort

blocks.html: Comparison sorts can't beat n log n. But if the values are small integers (ages, grades, letters), you can count each value and write them back out in order: O(n + k) for values in range k, with no comparisons at all.

blocks.title: counting_sort
blocks.prompt: Sort a list of integers in 0..k (k up to 100, n up to 10⁶) in O(n + k) without calling sorted or .sort.
blocks.tests:
assert counting_sort([3, 0, 2, 3, 1, 0], 3) == [0, 0, 1, 2, 3, 3]
assert counting_sort([], 5) == []
assert counting_sort([7], 9) == [7]
import random
random.seed(1)
big = [random.randint(0, 100) for _ in range(200000)]
r, secs = timed(counting_sort, big, 100)
assert r == sorted(big) and secs < 0.25, f"{secs:.2f}s: count each value in ONE pass"
hints: One pass to fill count[x] += 1, then for each value in order, write it out count[v] times.

blocks.title: sort_by_frequency
blocks.prompt: An interview question. Sort the numbers so that the most frequent come first; ties in frequency go smaller value first. Every copy stays in the output.
blocks.tests:
assert by_frequency([4, 6, 2, 6, 4, 4]) == [4, 4, 4, 6, 6, 2]
assert by_frequency([3, 1, 2]) == [1, 2, 3]
assert by_frequency([]) == []
hints: Count first with Counter, then sort with the key (-count, value).
blocks.starter:

blocks.q: Why is merge sort O(n log n)?

opts.t: There are log n rounds of merging, and each round does about n comparisons
It splits the list into √n parts

blocks.why: Runs double each round (1, 2, 4, …, n), so log₂ n rounds; merging a whole round touches every item once.

blocks.q: Insertion sort on a list that is already sorted costs…

opts.t: O(n): each item is compared once with its neighbour and stays

blocks.why: Insertion sort's work equals n plus the number of inversions. Nearly sorted data is its best case, which is why Timsort uses it on small runs.

blocks.q: You need "is there a pair with difference exactly d?" for n = 10⁵. Which plan fits?

opts.t: Sort, then use two pointers (or a set of values)
Counting sort on values up to 10⁹

blocks.why: 10¹⁰ pair checks is too slow; sorting is 1.7·10⁶ and lets you walk two pointers. (Chapter 7 is all about that walk.)

blocks.q: sorted(people, key=lambda p: (-p.age, p.name)) gives…

opts.t: Oldest first; people of the same age in alphabetical order
An error, because you can't negate inside a key

blocks.why: Tuples compare left to right, and negating a number flips its order. (For strings, which can't be negated, sort twice using stability.)

blocks.q: When does counting sort beat sorted()?

opts.t: When the list is nearly sorted
When the values are integers in a small range, like 0..100

blocks.why: O(n + k) only wins when k (the range of values) is small. Values up to 10⁹ would need a billion counters.

blocks.q: Explain how merge sort reaches O(n log n), and what sorting unlocks in problem solving.
blocks.a: Merge sort splits the list in half, sorts each half recursively, and merges the two sorted halves by repeatedly taking the smaller front item; merging costs one comparison per item placed. The halving gives log₂ n levels, each doing about n work, so O(n log n), against insertion sort's O(n²) on shuffled data (though insertion sort is O(n) on nearly sorted data). Python's sorted() is stable and accepts key=, so you can sort by any rule with a tuple key, negating numbers to reverse their order. Sorting unlocks: close values become neighbours (min gap, duplicates, merging intervals), two pointers and binary search become possible, sweeps over sorted starts and ends (meeting rooms), and counting inversions during the merge. When values are small integers, counting sort runs in O(n + k) with no comparisons.

chapters.title: Two pointers
chapters.tagline: Two fingers walking a sorted list, each step ruling something out for good
goals: Walk two pointers inward on a sorted list and prove why it never misses the answer
Use a slow and a fast pointer to rewrite a list in place
Walk two sorted lists side by side
Turn an O(n²) or O(n³) pair search into O(n) or O(n²)
chapters.prelude:
import time

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html: Chapter 3 found a pair summing to a target with a hash set. When the list is sorted, there's a way with no extra memory at all: one pointer at each end.

blocks.name: ds-twoptr
blocks.title: Every pair against two pointers, on a sorted list
blocks.goal: Run every pair to the end, then run two pointers and compare the number of checks.
blocks.intro: Step through two pointers slowly and read each line: every check fades one number out for good.

blocks.html:
Why can't it skip the answer? Say the sum is too small. R points at the biggest number still in play, so L's number plus anything left is too small too: L can't be part of any answer, and moving it loses nothing. The same argument works for R when the sum is too big. That "this one can never work, so drop it" reasoning is the heart of the pattern.

Three shapes of two pointers come up again and again:

ShapePointersTypical problems
Opposite endsL from the left, R from the right, meet in the middlepair sums, palindromes, container with water, 3-sum
Slow and fastboth go left to right; fast reads, slow writesremove items in place, dedupe, compress
Two listsone pointer in each sorted listmerge, intersect, subsequence check

blocks.q: Two pointers on [1, 4, 6, 9] looking for sum 10: the first check is 1 + 9 = 10. Found. What if the target were 13?

opts.t: 1 + 9 = 10 is too small, so L moves right; 4 + 9 = 13 ✓

blocks.why: Too small means L's number is too small even with the biggest partner, so L moves right.

blocks.title: pair_sum_sorted
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 167. nums is sorted. Return the indices (i, j) with i < j and nums[i] + nums[j] == target, or None. Use O(1) extra memory and O(n) time, n up to 10⁵.
blocks.tests:
assert pair_sum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9) == (0, 1)
assert pair_sum([1, 3, 4, 6], 10) == (2, 3)
assert pair_sum([1, 2], 5) is None
assert pair_sum([], 1) is None
big = list(range(0, 12000, 2))
r, secs = timed(pair_sum, big, 11996 + 11998)
assert r == (5998, 5999) and secs < 0.1, f"{secs:.2f}s: that's every pair. Walk inward from both ends."
hints: l, r = 0, len(nums) - 1. Too small → l += 1; too big → r -= 1; stop when they meet.

blocks.title: valid_palindrome
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 125, asked everywhere. A phrase is a palindrome if, keeping only letters and digits and ignoring case, it reads the same both ways. "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" is one. Use two pointers that skip anything that isn't a letter or digit.

blocks.title: container_water
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 11, a top interview question. h[i] is the height of a wall at position i. Two walls and the ground hold water: min(h[i], h[j]) * (j - i). Return the most water any two walls can hold, n up to 10⁵. Start with the widest pair and always move the shorter wall inward (moving the taller one can only make things worse: the width shrinks and the height is still capped by the short wall).
blocks.tests:
assert most_water([1, 8, 6, 2, 5, 4, 8, 3, 7]) == 49
assert most_water([1, 1]) == 1
assert most_water([4, 3, 2, 1, 4]) == 16
import random
random.seed(7)
big = [random.randint(1, 10**4) for _ in range(4000)]

blocks.title: three_sum
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 15, asked at almost every big company. Return every distinct triple [a, b, c] (each sorted, the list of triples sorted) from nums with a + b + c == 0. Sort once, then fix the first number and run the inward walk on the rest: O(n²) instead of O(n³). Skip repeated values so no triple appears twice.
blocks.tests:
assert three_sum([-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4]) == [[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]]
assert three_sum([0, 0, 0, 0]) == [[0, 0, 0]]
assert three_sum([1, 2]) == []
import random
random.seed(15)
big = [random.randint(-10**5, 10**5) for _ in range(450)]
r, secs = timed(three_sum, big)
s = set()
a = sorted(big)
for i in range(len(a)):
    seen = set()
    for j in range(i + 1, len(a)):
        if -a[i] - a[j] in seen:
            s.add(tuple(sorted((a[i], a[j], -a[i] - a[j]))))
        seen.add(a[j])

sections.title: Slow and fast: rewriting in place

blocks.html: The fast pointer reads every item; the slow pointer marks where the next kept item goes. Everything before slow is the answer so far.

Change the list in place (chars[:] = … is not allowed: write with a slow pointer) and return the new length.

blocks.q: What does the inward two-pointer walk need that a hash set doesn't?

opts.t: The list must be sorted (or sorting it must be allowed)

blocks.why: Sorting is what makes "too small → move L" safe. If you need original indices of an unsorted list, a hash set is often simpler.

blocks.q: 3-sum with two pointers costs…

opts.t: O(n²): n choices for the first number, each with an O(n) walk

blocks.why: Sorting (n log n) is swamped by the n walks of length n. Brute force is O(n³).

blocks.q: In "container with most water", why move the shorter wall?

opts.t: The water is capped by the shorter wall; moving the taller one shrinks the width and can't raise that cap
Because the shorter wall is always on the left
To keep the width the same

blocks.why: Every pair using the shorter wall with something further in is worse than the pair you just measured, so that wall can be dropped.

blocks.q: In the slow/fast pattern for removing items in place, what is true at every moment?

opts.t: Everything before slow is the kept items so far, in order

blocks.why: Fast reads every item, slow marks where the next kept item goes. The list's length never changes; you return slow.

blocks.q: is_subsequence("ace", t) with two pointers costs…
blocks.why: One pass over t, advancing the pointer in s on each match.

blocks.q: Explain the two-pointer technique: its three shapes, and why the inward walk on a sorted list never misses the answer.
blocks.a: Two pointers replace a pair search over every (i, j) with a walk where each step discards something for good. Opposite ends: on a sorted list put L at the start and R at the end; if the sum is too small, L's value is too small even with the biggest remaining partner, so L can never be in an answer and moves right; if too big, R moves left. Each step drops one item, so it's O(n) with O(1) memory; fixing one number first gives 3-sum in O(n²), and the same "drop the side that can't help" idea solves container with most water (move the shorter wall). Slow and fast: fast reads every item, slow marks where the next kept item is written, so everything before slow is the answer so far (remove in place, dedupe, compress). Two lists: one pointer in each sorted list, advancing the smaller (merge, intersect, reconcile, subsequence check); merging into the same array goes from the back. Counting with two pointers adds r − l pairs at once.

chapters.title: Sliding window
chapters.tagline: A stretch that grows on the right and shrinks on the left, never going back
goals: Slide a fixed-size window, updating the total in O(1) per step
Grow and shrink a variable window while keeping it valid
Explain why a loop inside a loop can still be O(n)
Spot "longest / shortest / count of subarrays such that…" as window problems
chapters.prelude:
import time
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

sections.title: A window that only moves forward

blocks.html: "Find the longest / shortest / best contiguous stretch such that…" is a sliding window question nine times out of ten. Instead of trying every start and every end (O(n²)), keep one window [L, R]: R moves right to take in a new item, and L moves right to drop items whenever the window breaks the rule.

blocks.name: ds-window
blocks.title: Longest stretch with no repeated letter
blocks.goal: Run restart from every letter to the end, then run sliding window and compare the steps.
blocks.intro: The green bar underneath marks the best window found so far.

blocks.html:
The inner while loop looks like it makes this O(n²), but count moves instead of loops: R moves n times in total and L moves at most n times in total, because neither ever goes back. That's amortised O(n).

Two kinds of window:

KindSizeMoveExamples
Fixedalways kadd the item entering, remove the item leavingmax sum of k in a row, anagrams in a string, moving average
Variablegrows and shrinksR grows it; L shrinks it while it's brokenlongest without repeats, shortest with sum ≥ t, at most k distinct

The variable template:

blocks.code:
s = "abcabcbb"
inside, L, best = set(), 0, 0
for R, c in enumerate(s):
    while c in inside:          # window would break: shrink from the left
        inside.remove(s[L])
        L += 1
    inside.add(c)               # take in the new item
    best = max(best, R - L + 1) # the window is valid here: record it
print(best)
blocks.title: The variable-window template

blocks.q: In the variable window, why is the total work O(n) even with a while inside the for?

opts.t: The while loop runs at most once per step
L only moves forward, so across the whole run the while body runs at most n times in total

blocks.why: Count pointer moves, not loop nesting: R moves n times, L moves at most n times. 2n moves in all.

blocks.title: max_sum_k

blocks.tests:

assert max_sum_k([-1, -2, -3], 2) == -3
assert max_sum_k([5], 1) == 5
big = list(range(20000))
r, secs = timed(max_sum_k, big, 10000)
assert r == sum(range(10000, 20000)) and secs < 0.03, f"{secs:.2f}s: slide the total, don't recompute it"
hints: Start with s = sum(a[:k]). For each new i, s += a[i] - a[i - k].
blocks.starter:
def max_sum_k(a, k):
    return max(sum(a[i:i + k]) for i in range(len(a) - k + 1))
