blocks.q: Which question is a sliding window?

opts.t: Count pairs anywhere in the list adding to k
The longest contiguous stretch whose sum is at most t (all numbers positive)
Whether the list has a duplicate

blocks.why: "Contiguous" plus "longest/shortest/count such that…" is the signal. Pairs anywhere is a hash map or two pointers on a sorted list.

blocks.q: Why does "shortest subarray with sum ≥ target" need positive numbers for the window to work?

opts.t: With negatives, shrinking can make the sum go up, so "shrink while valid" stops being safe
It's slower with negatives but still correct

blocks.why: The window relies on "adding makes it bigger, removing makes it smaller". With negatives you need prefix sums plus a monotonic deque (chapter 12).

blocks.q: In a variable window, when do you record the answer for a longest valid window?

opts.t: After shrinking, when the window is valid again

blocks.why: For longest, record after the window is valid. For shortest, record inside the shrinking loop, while it's still valid.

blocks.q: A fixed window of size k slides over n numbers keeping a running sum. Cost?
blocks.why: One add and one subtract per step.

blocks.q: For counting subarrays (not finding one), after making the window [L, R] valid you add…

opts.t: R − L + 1: every subarray ending at R that starts inside the window

blocks.why: Shrinking a valid window keeps it valid (for "product below k" style rules), so all those starts work.

blocks.q: Explain the sliding window technique: fixed versus variable windows, the template, and why it's O(n).
blocks.a: A sliding window keeps one contiguous stretch [L, R] instead of trying every start and end. A fixed window of size k slides by adding the item entering and removing the item leaving, keeping a running total or count, so each step is O(1). A variable window grows by moving R to take in a new item and, while the window breaks the rule (a repeated letter, more than k distinct, sum too big), shrinks by moving L and undoing that item; then the window is valid and you record it (for "longest" after shrinking, for "shortest" inside the shrink loop while it's still valid). For counting subarrays you add R − L + 1 per R. Though there's a while inside a for, R and L each move at most n times and never go back, so it's amortised O(n). It needs the rule to be monotone: shrinking a broken window must eventually fix it, which is why sum-based windows need non-negative numbers.

chapters.title: Binary search on a sorted list
chapters.tagline: One look at the middle throws away half, so a billion items take about 30 looks
goals: Write lower_bound (first position with value ≥ x) without off-by-one bugs
Use Python's bisect module for counting and inserting

chapters.prelude:
import time
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right, insort

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html: On a sorted list, looking at the middle tells you which half can't hold the answer. Throw that half away and repeat: n → n/2 → n/4 → … → 1 takes about log₂ n looks.

blocks.name: ds-bsearch
blocks.title: Scanning against binary search on 32 sorted numbers
blocks.goal: Run scan from the left to the end, then run binary search and compare the looks.
blocks.intro: Try target 50 too: it isn't in the list, but binary search still says exactly where it would go.

blocks.html: The safest way to think about binary search: don't search for "the target"; search for the first position where a condition becomes true. On a sorted list, A[i] >= x is false, false, …, false, true, true, …, true. Binary search finds the boundary. That position is called lower_bound:

blocks.code:
def lower_bound(a, x):
    lo, hi = 0, len(a)          # the answer is somewhere in [lo, hi]; hi = len(a) means "after everything"
    while lo < hi:
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2
        if a[mid] < x:          # condition false at mid: the boundary is to the right
            lo = mid + 1
        else:                   # condition true at mid: the boundary is mid or to the left
            hi = mid
    return lo

a = [2, 4, 4, 4, 7, 9]
print(lower_bound(a, 4), lower_bound(a, 5), lower_bound(a, 1), lower_bound(a, 10))
blocks.title: The one template to remember

blocks.html: Python ships this as bisect_left(a, x). Its sibling bisect_right(a, x) is the first position with a[i] > x. Between them sit all copies of x:

blocks.code:
from bisect import bisect_left, bisect_right
a = [1, 3, 3, 3, 5, 8]
print(bisect_left(a, 3), bisect_right(a, 3), bisect_right(a, 3) - bisect_left(a, 3))
print(bisect_left(a, 4), bisect_right(a, 4))

blocks.q: lower_bound uses lo, hi = 0, len(a) and while lo < hi. Why is hi set to len(a) and not len(a) - 1?

opts.t: It's a typo that happens to work
The answer can be "after the last item" (x bigger than everything), which is position len(a)

blocks.why: The answer space has n + 1 positions, 0..n. Using len(a) − 1 makes inserting at the end impossible.

blocks.q: About how many looks does binary search need on 10⁶ sorted items?
blocks.why: 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶. Every look halves the range.

blocks.q: On a = [1, 2, 2, 2, 3], what do bisect_left(a, 2) and bisect_right(a, 2) return?
blocks.why: bisect_left: the first position ≥ 2 (index 1). bisect_right: the first position > 2 (index 4). Their difference, 3, is how many 2s there are.

blocks.q: In while lo < hi, why hi = mid (not mid − 1) when a[mid] >= x?

opts.t: mid itself might be the answer, so it has to stay in the range
To make the loop run faster

blocks.why: The condition is true at mid, so mid is a candidate. lo = mid + 1 is safe on the other side, because the condition is false at mid.

blocks.q: What does binary search really need?

opts.t: A yes/no question whose answer goes no, no, …, no, yes, yes, …, yes along the range
The target to be in the list

blocks.why: Sortedness is just the most common way to get that shape. Rotated lists and peaks have it too, and chapter 10 uses it on answers, not indices.

blocks.q: mid = (lo + hi) // 2 in Python, versus lo + (hi - lo) // 2 in C++/Java. Why do those languages prefer the second?

opts.t: lo + hi can overflow a 32-bit int; Python's integers can't overflow

blocks.why: A famous bug that lived in Java's library for years. In Python both are fine.

blocks.q: Explain binary search as "find the first position where a condition becomes true", with the lower_bound template and its pitfalls.
blocks.a: Binary search works on any range where a yes/no condition goes false, false, …, true, true: on a sorted list, "a[i] ≥ x" has that shape. Keep the answer inside [lo, hi] with hi = len(a) (the answer can be past the end). While lo < hi, look at mid: if the condition is false there, the boundary is to the right, so lo = mid + 1; if true, mid could be the answer, so hi = mid. The loop ends with lo = hi at the first true position, after about log₂ n looks (30 for a billion). Python's bisect_left is this lower_bound and bisect_right is the first position > x; their difference counts copies. Pitfalls are off-by-ones: hi = len(a) − 1 forgets the end, hi = mid − 1 can skip the answer, and lo = mid can loop forever. The same template handles rotated lists (condition: a[i] ≤ a[−1]) and peaks (condition: a[i] > a[i+1]).

chapters.title: Binary search on the answer
chapters.tagline: When checking an answer is easy but finding it is hard, guess and halve
goals: Recognise "minimum X such that it works" and "maximum X such that it works"
Write a feasibility check and prove it's monotone
Binary search the answer between safe bounds without off-by-one bugs
Combine a greedy check with binary search (ship capacity, splitting arrays, placing cows)
chapters.prelude:
import time

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

sections.title: Search the answer, not the data

blocks.html:
Some questions ask for the smallest (or largest) value that makes something possible: the slowest eating speed that finishes in time, the smallest ship that carries everything in D days, the biggest gap you can keep between cows. Finding it directly is hard. Checking one guess is easy. And the check is monotone: if a speed works, every faster speed works too.

So the guesses go ✗ ✗ ✗ … ✓ ✓ ✓, which is exactly the shape binary search finds the boundary of (chapter 9).

blocks.name: ds-answer
blocks.title: Koko's bananas: trying every speed against binary search on the speed
blocks.goal: Run try every speed until it finds the answer, then run binary search.
blocks.intro: Click any checked bar to see how its hours were added up. (Bars taller than 16 hours are cut off at the top.)

blocks.html:
The recipe:

  1. Write ok(x): can it be done with value x? (Usually a greedy O(n) loop.)
  2. Check it's monotone: does ok(x) imply ok(x + 1) (for "minimum") or ok(x - 1) (for "maximum")?
  3. Pick bounds where you know the answer lies: lo = something surely too small or the smallest possible, hi = something surely enough.
  4. Binary search for the first x with ok(x) true. Cost: O(check · log(range)).

blocks.title: The template, with a generic check

blocks.q: Why is "slowest speed that finishes in h hours" a binary-search-on-the-answer problem?

opts.t: Because a speed that finishes in time stays fine for every faster speed, so "works?" flips once from no to yes

blocks.why: The piles don't need to be sorted at all. What's sorted is the yes/no answer over the range of speeds.

assert isqrt(r * r) == r
assert isqrt(r * r - 1) == r - 1, "floats can't tell r² − 1 from r²"
hints: Search for the first r with r * r > x; the answer is one less. hi = x + 1 is always too big, so it's a safe upper bound.
blocks.starter:
def isqrt(x):
    return int(x ** 0.5)

blocks.html: For "the largest x that still works", the yes/no pattern is ✓ ✓ ✓ … ✗ ✗ ✗. Search for the first ✗ and subtract one, or round mid up so lo = mid can't loop forever.

blocks.title: aggressive_cows
blocks.prompt: The SPOJ classic (also LeetCode 1552). Stalls are at the given positions; place c cows in different stalls so the smallest distance between any two cows is as large as possible. Return that distance. Check for a distance d greedily: put a cow in the first stall, then in each next stall at least d further on.
hints: ok(d) is true for small d and false for big d. With lo = mid on success, use mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2 (round up) or the loop can get stuck when hi = lo + 1.

blocks.title: Largest x that still works (round mid up)
blocks.tests:
assert last_true(0, 100, lambda x: x * x <= 50) == 7
assert last_true(0, 10, lambda x: True) == 10
assert last_true(3, 3, lambda x: True) == 3

blocks.title: split_array
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 410, a hard one that's the same idea. Split nums (non-negative) into k non-empty contiguous parts so that the largest part sum is as small as possible. Return that sum. (It's the ship problem in disguise: parts are days, the largest sum is the capacity.)
blocks.tests:
assert split_array([7, 2, 5, 10, 8], 2) == 18
assert split_array([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2) == 9
assert split_array([1, 4, 4], 3) == 4
assert split_array([5], 1) == 5
hints: Greedy count of parts needed if no part may exceed cap. If that's ≤ k, cap works (you can always split a part further to reach exactly k).
blocks.starter:
def split_array(nums, k):
    return sum(nums) // k

blocks.title: bouquets
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 1482. Flower i blooms on day bloom[i]. A bouquet needs k adjacent bloomed flowers. Return the fewest days to wait to make m bouquets, or -1 if it's impossible.
hints: ok(day): walk the flowers counting a run of bloomed ones; every time the run reaches k, make a bouquet and restart the run.
blocks.starter:
def min_days(bloom, m, k):
    return max(bloom)

blocks.title: max_median
blocks.prompt: Codeforces 1201C "Maximum Median". a has odd length n. One operation adds 1 to any element. With at most k operations, what's the largest possible median? Sort; to make the median at least m, every element from the middle onward that's below m must be raised to m.
blocks.tests:
assert max_median([1, 3, 5], 2) == 5
assert max_median([1, 1, 1, 1, 1], 5) == 2
assert max_median([4, 1, 2, 4, 1, 2, 4], 7) == 5
assert max_median([7], 10) == 17
hints: The answer is between the current median and the median + k. cost(m) = how much it takes to raise the upper half to at least m. Largest m with cost(m) <= k: round mid up.

blocks.q: Which phrase most strongly hints at binary search on the answer?

opts.t: "The minimum capacity such that it's possible within D days"

blocks.why: "Minimum/maximum X such that [a check passes]" with a monotone check is the signature.

blocks.q: Koko's piles go up to 10⁹ and there are n piles. Cost of binary search on the speed?

opts.t: O(n · log 10⁹), about 30 checks of n each

blocks.why: Each check adds up n piles; there are about log₂(10⁹) ≈ 30 checks.

blocks.q: For ship capacity, why is lo = max(weights) a good lower bound?

opts.t: Any smaller capacity can't carry the heaviest package at all

blocks.why: Good bounds are ones you can justify: lo surely can't be beaten from below, hi surely works.

blocks.q: Searching for the largest x that works with lo = mid on success, why must mid round up?

opts.t: With hi = lo + 1, rounding down gives mid = lo, so lo = mid changes nothing and the loop never ends

blocks.why: mid = (lo + hi + 1) // 2 guarantees progress. Or search for the first failure and subtract one.

blocks.q: int(x ** 0.5) for x around 10⁴⁰ is…

opts.t: Possibly wrong, because x ** 0.5 is a float with about 16 significant digits

blocks.why: Python ints are exact, floats aren't. Binary search (or math.isqrt) keeps everything in integers.

sections.title: Real-world project: how far must the e-bike go?

blocks.title: An e-bike battery planner
blocks.client: A bike-touring company choosing which battery to rent customers for a fixed route with charging stops
blocks.brief: Build battery.py that reads a route (the distances in km of charging points along it, start at 0, finish at the end) and answers two questions: with a battery of range R, how many recharges are needed (charging only when you must)? And what's the smallest range R that gets a rider to the finish with at most k recharges? Show a table of k = 0, 1, 2, … against the minimum range, so the company can price batteries.
blocks.why: Logistics teams size trucks, fuel tanks and data-centre links exactly this way: a greedy check of "does this capacity work?" wrapped in a binary search for the cheapest capacity that does.
milestones: Count recharges for a given range, greedily
Detect routes impossible for that range
Binary search the smallest range for k recharges
stretch: Allow charging stops with different charging times and minimise total time
Plot range against recharges

blocks.title: recharges
blocks.prompt: stops is a sorted list of positions in km: stops[0] = 0 is the start (fully charged), stops[-1] is the finish, the rest are chargers. With a battery range of R km, ride as far as you can and recharge (to full) only at the last charger you can reach. Return the number of recharges, or -1 if some gap between consecutive stops is longer than R.
blocks.tests:
assert recharges([0, 30, 60, 100], 100) == 0
assert recharges([0, 30, 60, 100], 60) == 1
assert recharges([0, 30, 60, 100], 40) == 2
assert recharges([0, 30, 60, 100], 39) == -1
assert recharges([0, 10], 10) == 0
hints: Remember where you last charged. If the next stop is out of reach from there, you must have charged at the previous stop.
blocks.starter:
def recharges(stops, R):
    return (stops[-1] - stops[0]) // R

blocks.title: min_range
blocks.prompt: Return the smallest integer range R that reaches the finish with at most k recharges. More range never needs more recharges, so binary search between the largest single gap and the whole route length.
blocks.tests:
s = [0, 30, 60, 100]
assert min_range(s, 0) == 100
assert min_range(s, 1) == 60
assert min_range(s, 2) == 40
assert min_range(s, 5) == 40
assert min_range([0, 25, 50, 75, 100], 3) == 25
hints: Below the largest gap nothing works, so start lo there (then no -1 case can happen). hi = the whole route with no recharge.
blocks.starter:
def min_range(stops, k):
    return stops[-1] - stops[0]

blocks.title: answer_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: min_speed(piles, h) (Koko) with binary search on the speed, using integer ceiling division.
hints: Bounds 1 and max(piles); works → hi = mid; too slow → lo = mid + 1.
blocks.starter:
def min_speed(piles, h):
    pass

blocks.q: Explain binary search on the answer: when to use it, the steps, and the off-by-one traps.
blocks.a: Use it when a question asks for the minimum (or maximum) value X such that something is possible, checking one X is easy (often a greedy O(n) pass), and the check is monotone: if X works then every bigger X works (or every smaller one, for maximum). The yes/no answers over the range of X then flip exactly once, so binary search finds the boundary in about log₂(range) checks, for O(n · log range) total, even when the range is 10⁹ or 10¹⁸. Steps: write ok(x); justify bounds where lo is the smallest possible answer and hi surely works (ship capacity: max weight to total weight); then while lo < hi, take mid and set hi = mid if ok(mid) else lo = mid + 1. For "largest X that works", set lo = mid on success with mid rounded up, (lo + hi + 1) // 2, or the loop sticks. Keep checks in integers (ceil as (p + k − 1) // k; no float square roots).

chapters.title: Stacks and the monotonic stack
chapters.tagline: Last in, first out, for brackets, undo, and "what's the next bigger thing?"
goals: Use a Python list as a stack with append and pop
Match brackets and evaluate expressions with a stack
Keep a monotonic stack to find the next greater or smaller element in O(n)
Explain the "pushed once, popped once" argument
chapters.prelude:
import time

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
A stack is a pile: you add to the top and take from the top. In Python it's just a list: s.append(x) pushes, s.pop() pops, s[-1] peeks. Both are O(1).

Stacks show up whenever the most recent unfinished thing must be finished first: brackets (the latest ( must close first), undo (the latest change is undone first), function calls (chapter 5's call stack), and expression evaluation.

blocks.title: A stack in three lines

blocks.q: You push 1, 2, 3, pop once, push 4, pop twice. What's left on the stack?

blocks.title: valid_brackets
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 20, the most common stack question. A string of ()[]{} is valid if every opener is closed by the same kind, in the right order. Counting isn't enough: "([)]" has the right counts but is invalid.
blocks.tests:
assert valid("()[]{}")
assert valid("{[()]}")
assert not valid("([)]")
assert not valid("((")
assert not valid("))")
assert valid("")
hints: Push openers. On a closer, the top of the stack must be its partner: pop and compare. At the end the stack must be empty.
blocks.starter:
def valid(s):
    return s.count("(") == s.count(")") and s.count("[") == s.count("]") and s.count("{") == s.count("}")

blocks.title: brackets_bug
blocks.prompt: This bracket checker says "((" is valid. Fix it.
blocks.tests:
assert not valid("((")
assert not valid("[")
assert valid("[]")
hints: Openers left on the stack at the end were never closed.

blocks.title: min_stack
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 155. Write class MinStack with push(x), pop(), top() and get_min(), all O(1). The starter remembers the smallest value ever pushed, which goes wrong after that value is popped. Keep, next to each item, the minimum of the stack up to and including it.
blocks.tests:
m = MinStack()
m.push(5); m.push(2); m.push(7)
assert m.get_min() == 2 and m.top() == 7
m.pop(); m.pop()
assert m.get_min() == 5 and m.top() == 5
m.push(1)
assert m.get_min() == 1
hints: Push pairs (x, min_so_far). The minimum after popping is simply whatever pair is now on top.

blocks.title: eval_rpn
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 150. Evaluate an expression in Reverse Polish Notation: ["2", "1", "+", "3", ""] means (2 + 1) 3 = 9. Numbers are pushed; an operator pops two, applies itself, and pushes the result. Division truncates toward zero (int(a / b)).
hints: Pop b first, then a: the order matters for - and /. Careful, "-11" is a number, not an operator: test with t in "+-*/" only works because operators are single characters.
blocks.starter:
def eval_rpn(tokens):
    return 0

blocks.title: decode_string
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 394, asked at Google. Decode "3[a2[c]]" → "accaccacc": k[...] repeats its inside k times, and brackets nest. When you meet [, push the text so far and the number; at ], pop them and glue.
blocks.tests:
assert decode("3[a]2[bc]") == "aaabcbc"
assert decode("3[a2[c]]") == "accaccacc"
assert decode("2[abc]3[cd]ef") == "abcabccdcdcdef"
assert decode("10[x]") == "x" * 10
assert decode("ab") == "ab"
hints: Numbers can have several digits (num = num * 10 + digit). On ], the popped text goes before the repeated part.
blocks.starter:
def decode(s):
    return s

blocks.html: "For each item, find the next item to its right that's bigger" looks like O(n²). The simulation shows the O(n) way: keep a stack of items still waiting for their answer.

blocks.name: ds-stack
blocks.title: Daily temperatures: scanning right against a monotonic stack
blocks.goal: Run scan right to the end, then run monotonic stack and compare the steps.
blocks.intro: Watch the stack on the right: from bottom to top its temperatures only ever go down.

blocks.html: When a new item arrives, it pops every waiting item smaller than it (it is their next greater element), then waits itself. So the waiting items are always in decreasing order: a monotonic stack. Each item is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total is O(n).

blocks.title: daily_temperatures
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 739. For each day return how many days until a warmer one, or 0 if none, in O(n).
blocks.tests:
assert daily([73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73]) == [1, 1, 4, 2, 1, 1, 0, 0]
assert daily([30, 40, 50, 60]) == [1, 1, 1, 0]
assert daily([30, 60, 90]) == [1, 1, 0]
assert daily([]) == []
cold = list(range(3000, 0, -1)) + [5000]
r, secs = timed(daily, cold)
assert r[0] == 3000 and secs < 0.03, f"{secs:.2f}s: keep a stack of waiting days instead of scanning"
hints: Store indices on the stack (you need them for the distance). While today is warmer than the day on top, pop it and record i - j.

blocks.title: Next greater element for every item (-1 if none)
blocks.tests:
assert next_greater([2, 1, 2, 4, 3]) == [4, 2, 4, -1, -1]
assert next_greater([5, 4, 3]) == [-1, -1, -1]
assert next_greater([]) == []

blocks.title: next_greater_circular
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 503. Same as next greater element, but the list is circular: after the last item, search continues from the start. Walk the list twice (indices 0 .. 2n - 1, using i % n), only pushing during the first pass.
blocks.tests:
assert next_greater_circular([1, 2, 1]) == [2, -1, 2]
assert next_greater_circular([1, 2, 3, 4, 3]) == [2, 3, 4, -1, 4]
assert next_greater_circular([5, 5]) == [-1, -1]
hints: The second pass only resolves items still waiting from the first; it never adds new ones.

blocks.title: remove_k_digits
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 402. Remove k digits from the number string to make it as small as possible. Return it without leading zeros ("0" if empty). Greedy with an increasing stack: while the last kept digit is bigger than the new one and you still may remove, pop it.
blocks.tests:
assert remove_k("1432219", 3) == "1219"
assert remove_k("10200", 1) == "200"
assert remove_k("10", 2) == "0"
assert remove_k("12345", 2) == "123"
assert remove_k("9", 1) == "0"
hints: A bigger digit before a smaller one is always worth removing (it's in a more important place). If removals are left at the end, the digits are increasing: drop from the right.
blocks.starter:
def remove_k(num, k):
    return num[k:] or "0"

blocks.title: largest_rectangle
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 84, a famous hard one. Bars of width 1 have the given heights. Return the area of the largest rectangle inside the histogram. With an increasing stack: when a bar shorter than the top arrives, the top's rectangle can't extend further right, and its left edge is the bar below it on the stack.
blocks.tests:
assert largest_rectangle([2, 1, 5, 6, 2, 3]) == 10
assert largest_rectangle([2, 4]) == 4
assert largest_rectangle([1, 1, 1, 1]) == 4
assert largest_rectangle([]) == 0
r, secs = timed(largest_rectangle, list(range(1, 2500)))
assert r == 1250 * 1250 and secs < 0.03, f"{secs:.2f}s: one pass with an increasing stack"
hints: Append a 0 at the end so everything gets popped. For a popped bar, the rectangle spans from just after the new stack top to just before i.

blocks.title: longest_valid_parens
blocks.prompt: Codeforces 5C / LeetCode 32. Return the length of the longest substring of ( and ) that is a valid bracket sequence. Push indices of (; keep the index of the last unmatched ) at the bottom of the stack as a "wall".
blocks.tests:
assert longest_valid("(()") == 2
assert longest_valid(")()())") == 4
assert longest_valid("") == 0
assert longest_valid("()(())") == 6
assert longest_valid("())(())") == 4
hints: Start the stack with -1. On ), pop; if the stack is now empty, this ) is unmatched, so push its index as the new wall; otherwise the valid stretch ends at i and starts after stack[-1].
blocks.starter:
def longest_valid(s):
    return 2 * min(s.count("("), s.count(")"))

blocks.q: Why is a stack the right tool for matching brackets?

opts.t: The most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed

blocks.why: "Most recent unfinished thing first" is exactly last-in-first-out.

blocks.q: In a monotonic stack for "next greater element", what's true about the stack at all times?

opts.t: It's sorted increasing from bottom to top
Its values decrease (or stay equal) from bottom to top
It holds every item seen so far
It never has more than 2 items

blocks.why: Any smaller item below a bigger new one would have been popped by it.

blocks.q: The monotonic stack has a while inside a for. Its total cost is…

opts.t: O(n), because each item is pushed once and popped at most once

blocks.why: Count pushes and pops over the whole run: at most 2n.

blocks.q: Which problem is not usually a stack problem?

opts.t: Next smaller element to the left

blocks.why: That's a sliding window (chapter 8).

blocks.q: Why store indices rather than values on the stack in daily temperatures?

opts.t: The answer is a distance (i − j), and from an index you can always get the value back

blocks.why: Storing indices keeps both pieces of information.

blocks.title: A text editor's undo and redo
blocks.client: A note-taking app whose users keep losing paragraphs because undo only goes back one step
blocks.brief: Build editor.py with a document and operations type(text), delete(n) (remove the last n characters), undo() and redo(). Each edit pushes an action onto an undo stack; undo pops it, reverses it, and pushes it onto a redo stack; any new edit clears the redo stack. Then add a browser-style history (visit, back, forward) built the same way.
blocks.why: Every editor, drawing app and spreadsheet has an undo stack. Storing small actions instead of whole copies of the document is what keeps undo cheap for huge files.
skills: storing actions instead of whole documents
milestones: Undo with a stack of actions
stretch: Group fast typing into one undo step
Limit the undo history to the last 1 000 actions

blocks.title: editor
blocks.prompt: Write class Editor with text (a string, initially ""), type(s), delete(n) (remove up to n characters from the end), undo() and redo() (each does nothing if there's nothing to undo/redo). A new type or delete clears the redo stack.
blocks.tests:
e = Editor()
e.type("hello"); e.type(" world"); e.delete(3)
assert e.text == "hello wo"
e.undo()
assert e.text == "hello world"
e.undo()
assert e.text == "hello"
e.redo()
assert e.text == "hello world"
e.type("!")
e.redo()
assert e.text == "hello world!", "a new edit clears redo"
e.undo(); e.undo(); e.undo(); e.undo()
assert e.text == ""
hints: Store each action with enough information to reverse it: for a delete, remember the characters that were removed. Undo applies the reverse; redo applies the action again.

blocks.title: browser_history
blocks.prompt: Write class History starting at a home page with visit(url), back(steps) and forward(steps); back and forward move as far as possible and return the current page. Visiting clears the forward history. Use two stacks.
blocks.tests:
h = History("home")
h.visit("a"); h.visit("b"); h.visit("c")
assert h.back(1) == "b"
assert h.back(1) == "a"
assert h.forward(1) == "b"
h.visit("x")
assert h.forward(2) == "x"
assert h.back(2) == "a"
assert h.back(9) == "home"
hints: past holds pages behind you, future pages ahead. Moving back pushes the current page onto future and pops from past.

blocks.title: stack_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: daily(t), days until a warmer day (0 if none), in O(n) with a monotonic stack.
hints: A stack of waiting indices; a warmer day pops and answers them; then it waits too.
blocks.starter:
def daily(t):
    pass

blocks.q: Explain stacks and the monotonic stack: what problems they solve and why the monotonic stack is O(n).
blocks.a: A stack is last-in-first-out: in Python a list with append to push, pop to pop and [-1] to peek, all O(1). Use one whenever the most recent unfinished thing must be finished first: matching brackets (push openers, a closer must match the top, the stack must end empty), undo/redo (two stacks of reversible actions), evaluating postfix expressions, decoding nested strings, and simulating recursion. A monotonic stack keeps indices of items still waiting for an answer, such as their next greater element: each new item pops every waiting item smaller than it (recording itself as their answer) and then waits too, so the stack's values stay decreasing from bottom to top. Each item is pushed once and popped at most once, so despite the while inside the for it's O(n) in total. Variants: increasing stacks for next smaller element and the largest rectangle in a histogram, circular arrays by walking twice, and greedy digit removal.

chapters.title: Queues, deques and the monotonic deque
chapters.tagline: First in, first out, both ends at O(1), and the max of every window in one pass
goals: Use collections.deque as a queue (and know why list.pop(0) is slow)
Simulate processes that take turns with a queue
Keep a monotonic deque for the max or min of every sliding window
Combine prefix sums with a deque when numbers can be negative
chapters.prelude:
import time
from collections import deque

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
A queue is a line at a shop: join at the back, leave from the front. A deque ("deck", double-ended queue) can add and remove at both ends. Python's collections.deque does all four in O(1).

A plain list is a bad queue: list.pop(0) shifts every other item one place left, so it's O(n).

blocks.code:
import time
from collections import deque
n = 60000
a = list(range(n))
t = time.perf_counter()
while a:
    a.pop(0)
print(f"list.pop(0):     {time.perf_counter() - t:.3f}s")
d = deque(range(n))
t = time.perf_counter()
while d:
    d.popleft()
print(f"deque.popleft(): {time.perf_counter() - t:.3f}s")
blocks.title: list.pop(0) against deque.popleft()

blocks.code:
from collections import deque
d = deque([1, 2, 3])
d.append(4)
d.appendleft(0)
d.pop()
d.popleft()
d.rotate(1)
print(list(d))

blocks.q: Which operation is O(n) rather than O(1)?
blocks.why: Inserting or removing at the front of a list shifts everything after it. Deques are built to make both ends cheap.

blocks.title: recent_counter
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 933. Write class RecentCounter whose ping(t) records a request at time t (times only increase) and returns how many requests happened in [t - 3000, t]. Keep a queue and drop old times from the front, so each ping is amortised O(1).
blocks.tests:
rc = RecentCounter()
assert [rc.ping(t) for t in (1, 100, 3001, 3002)] == [1, 2, 3, 3]
def many():
    r = RecentCounter()
    return [r.ping(t) for t in range(0, 4000)]
r, secs = timed(many)
assert r[-1] == 3001 and secs < 0.02, f"{secs:.2f}s: drop old pings from the front instead of recounting"
hints: Append the new time, then popleft() while the front is older than t - 3000. The answer is len(q).

blocks.title: two_stack_queue
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 232. Build a queue from two stacks (plain lists using only append, pop() and [-1]): push(x), pop(), peek(), empty(). Push onto an "in" stack; when you need the front and the "out" stack is empty, pour everything from in to out (which reverses it). Each item moves at most twice: amortised O(1).
blocks.tests:
q = MyQueue()
q.push(1); q.push(2); q.push(3)
assert q.peek() == 1 and q.pop() == 1
q.push(4)
assert [q.pop(), q.pop(), q.pop()] == [2, 3, 4]
assert q.empty()
hints: Only pour when out is empty. Pouring while out still has items would put newer items in front of older ones.

blocks.title: josephus
blocks.prompt: The classic elimination game. People 1..n stand in a circle. Counting starts at person 1; every k-th person is removed, and counting continues from the next person. Return the order people are removed in. Simulate with a deque: rotate(-(k - 1)) brings the k-th person to the front.
blocks.tests:
assert josephus(7, 3) == [3, 6, 2, 7, 5, 1, 4]
assert josephus(5, 1) == [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
assert josephus(1, 4) == [1]
assert josephus(4, 2) == [2, 4, 3, 1]
hints: d.rotate(-m) moves the first m people to the back, so the person you want ends up at the front.
blocks.starter:
def josephus(n, k):
    return list(range(k, n + 1, k))

blocks.title: card_war
blocks.prompt: Codeforces 546C "Soldier and Cards". Two players hold decks (fronts first). Each round both play their front card; the higher card wins, and the winner puts the opponent's card then their own at the bottom of their deck. Someone with an empty deck loses. Return (rounds, winner) with winner 1 or 2, or -1 if the game is still going after 1 000 rounds (it loops forever).
blocks.tests:
assert card_war([1, 3], [4, 2]) == (6, 2)
assert card_war([2], [1, 3]) == -1
assert card_war([5], [1]) == (1, 1)
hints: Two deques; popleft() the fronts; the winner extend([loser_card, winner_card]). Count rounds and give up at 1 000.
blocks.starter:
def card_war(a, b):
    return (0, 1 if max(a) > max(b) else 2)

blocks.html: Chapter 11's monotonic stack answered "next greater". When a window slides, old items also have to leave from the other end, so you need a deque.

blocks.name: ds-deque
blocks.title: Maximum of every window: rescanning against a monotonic deque
blocks.goal: Run rescan every window to the end, then run monotonic deque and compare.
blocks.intro: The deque (under the bars) holds candidates for the maximum, biggest at the front.

blocks.html: Two rules keep it right: a new item pops every smaller-or-equal item from the back (they're older and smaller, so they can never be a window's maximum again), and the front is dropped when its index slides out. The front is always the current maximum.

blocks.title: window_max
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 239, a hard one asked at Amazon and Google. Return the maximum of every window of k consecutive numbers, in O(n). Store indices in the deque so you can tell when the front has slid out.
blocks.tests:

Use prefix sums P (chapter 4): you want the smallest j - i with P[j] - P[i] >= k. Keep a deque of indices with increasing P: pop from the front while it answers the current j (it can't do better later), and pop from the back while its P is ≥ the new one (the new one is smaller and later, so strictly better). blocks.q: Why is collections.deque the right Python queue?

opts.t: It adds and removes at both ends in O(1); a list's front operations are O(n)
It uses less memory than a list

blocks.why: deque.popleft() is O(1); list.pop(0) shifts every item.

blocks.q: In the sliding-window-maximum deque, what order do the values have from front to back?
blocks.why: Any item smaller than a newer one is popped, so what's left decreases. The front is the max.

blocks.q: When does the front of the monotonic deque get removed?

opts.t: When its index slides out of the window

blocks.why: Bigger numbers remove from the back. Only age removes from the front.

blocks.q: Two stacks make a queue with amortised O(1) operations because…

opts.t: Each item is pushed and popped at most twice in total (once per stack)

blocks.why: Pouring can be slow once, but it's paid for by the many cheap operations before it.

blocks.q: Max of every window of k with n = 10⁵ and k = 5·10⁴. Rescanning costs about…

opts.t: 2.5·10⁹: about n − k windows of k each

blocks.why: The monotonic deque does it in about 2n operations.

sections.title: Real-world project: a fair CPU scheduler

blocks.title: A round-robin task scheduler
blocks.client: A home-lab tinkerer whose background jobs (backups, video transcodes, scrapes) keep starving each other on one small server
blocks.brief: Build scheduler.py that simulates jobs arriving with known run times. First, first-come-first-served with one worker: compute each job's waiting time. Then round-robin: each job runs for at most a quantum of time, then goes to the back of the queue if it isn't finished. Compare average waiting time and when each job finishes under both, on a mix of long and short jobs.
blocks.why: Operating systems, web servers and print queues all decide "who runs next" with queues. Round-robin is why one huge job can't freeze your laptop.
milestones: Finish times and averages for both
stretch: Jobs arriving at different times
Priorities with several queues

blocks.title: fcfs_waits
blocks.prompt: Jobs are (arrival, duration), sorted by arrival. One worker runs them in order, each to completion; a job can't start before it arrives. Return each job's waiting time (start − arrival).
hints: Track when the worker is next free. Each job starts at the later of that and its arrival.
blocks.starter:
def waits(jobs):
    return [0 for _ in jobs]
blocks.solution:
def waits(jobs):
    t, out = 0, []
    for arrive, dur in jobs:
        start = max(t, arrive)
        out.append(start - arrive)
        t = start + dur
    return out

blocks.title: round_robin
blocks.prompt: All jobs are ready at time 0: durations[i] is job i's run time. Round-robin with quantum q: take the front job, run it for min(q, remaining), and if it isn't finished put it at the back. Return each job's finish time.
blocks.tests:
assert round_robin([5, 2, 1], 2) == [8, 4, 5]
assert round_robin([3, 3], 10) == [3, 6]
assert round_robin([], 2) == []
assert round_robin([4], 1) == [4]
hints: A deque of job indices and a list of remaining times. Advance the clock by each slice; finished jobs record the clock, unfinished ones rejoin at the back.
blocks.solution:
def round_robin(durations, q):
    left = list(durations)
    finish = [0] * len(durations)
    queue, t = deque(range(len(durations))), 0
    while queue:
        i = queue.popleft()
        run = min(q, left[i])
        t += run
        left[i] -= run
        if left[i]:
            queue.append(i)
        else:
            finish[i] = t
    return finish

blocks.q: Explain queues and deques, and how the monotonic deque finds every window's maximum in O(n).
blocks.a: A queue is first-in-first-out; a deque adds and removes at both ends. Python's collections.deque does append, appendleft, pop and popleft in O(1), while list.pop(0) and insert(0, x) are O(n) because every item shifts. Queues model taking turns: rate counters that drop old times from the front, round-robin scheduling, Josephus elimination with rotate, card games, and (in Part 3) breadth-first search. Two stacks also make a queue with amortised O(1) operations. For the maximum of every window of size k, keep a deque of indices whose values decrease from front to back: each new item pops all smaller-or-equal items from the back (older and smaller, they can never be a maximum again), the front is removed when its index slides out of the window, and the front is the current maximum. Each index enters and leaves once, so O(n) for any k. Two such deques track max and min together; a deque over increasing prefix sums handles shortest subarray with sum ≥ k when numbers can be negative.

chapters.title: Linked-list tricks
chapters.tagline: Nodes and next pointers, fast and slow runners, and reversing in place
goals: Walk, build and edit a singly linked list without losing nodes
Reverse a list in place with prev, cur and next
Use fast and slow pointers for the middle, the nth from the end and cycles
Combine a hash map with a doubly linked list into an O(1) LRU cache

blocks.html:
A linked list is a chain of nodes. Each node holds a value and a next pointer to the node after it; the last one points to None. You only hold the head.

Array (Python list)Linked list
Read item iO(1)O(i): walk from the head
Insert or remove at the frontO(n): everything shiftsO(1): change one pointer
Insert after a node you holdO(n)O(1)

Interviewers love lists because every trick is about not losing your grip on a node before you rewire it. Every lesson here uses build([1, 2, 3]) to make a list and to_list(head) to read one back.

blocks.code:
head = build([3, 1, 4, 1, 5])
node, steps = head, 0
while node:
    print(node.val, "->", node.next.val if node.next else None)
    node = node.next
    steps += 1
print("walked", steps, "nodes")

b = a.next
a.next = b.next
print(to_list(a), b.val, b.next.val)

blocks.html: Reversing is three pointers: prev (the reversed part so far), cur (the node being moved) and nxt (saved before you overwrite cur.next, or the rest of the list is lost).

assert to_list(reverse(None)) == []

blocks.title: reverse_list
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 206, the most-asked list question there is. Reverse the list and return the new head, in O(n) time and O(1) extra memory: rewire the pointers, don't copy the values into a Python list.
blocks.tests:

first = h
r = reverse(h)
assert to_list(r) == [3, 2, 1]
assert r.next.next is first, "rewire the existing nodes instead of building new ones"
assert reverse(None) is None
hints: nxt = cur.next, then cur.next = prev, then step both prev and cur forward.
blocks.solution:
def reverse(head):
    prev, cur = None, head
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    return prev

blocks.title: reverse_between
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 92. Reverse only positions left..right (1-based) and return the head. Walk a pointer to the node before position left (a dummy helps when left is 1), then reverse the next right - left + 1 nodes and stitch both ends back.
blocks.tests:
assert to_list(reverse_between(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]), 2, 4)) == [1, 4, 3, 2, 5]
assert to_list(reverse_between(build([5]), 1, 1)) == [5]
assert to_list(reverse_between(build([3, 5]), 1, 2)) == [5, 3]
assert to_list(reverse_between(build([1, 2, 3]), 3, 3)) == [1, 2, 3]
hints: After reversing the slice, before.next is still the old first node of the slice, which is now its last: point it at cur. Then point before at prev, the new first.
blocks.starter:
def reverse_between(head, left, right):
    return head
blocks.solution:
def reverse_between(head, left, right):
    dummy = ListNode(0, head)
    before = dummy
    for _ in range(left - 1):
        before = before.next
    prev, cur = None, before.next
    for _ in range(right - left + 1):
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    before.next.next = cur
    before.next = prev
    return dummy.next

blocks.title: reorder_list
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 143. Reorder L0 → L1 → … → Ln into L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln-1 → … in place and return the head. It's three tricks in a row: find the middle, reverse the second half, then weave the two halves together.
blocks.tests:
assert to_list(reorder(build([1, 2, 3, 4]))) == [1, 4, 2, 3]
assert to_list(reorder(build([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]))) == [1, 5, 2, 4, 3]
assert to_list(reorder(build([1]))) == [1]
assert to_list(reorder(build([1, 2]))) == [1, 2]
hints: Cut the list after the middle (slow.next = None), reverse what came after, then alternately take one node from each half.
blocks.starter:
def reorder(head):
    return head
blocks.solution:
def reorder(head):
    if not head:
        return head
    slow = fast = head
    while fast.next and fast.next.next:
        slow, fast = slow.next, fast.next.next
    prev, cur = None, slow.next
    slow.next = None
    while cur:
        nxt = cur.next
        cur.next = prev
        prev, cur = cur, nxt
    a, b = head, prev
    while b:
        an, bn = a.next, b.next
        a.next, b.next = b, an
        a, b = an, bn
    return head

b = build([5, 6, 1]); b.next.next.next = shared

blocks.title: add_two_numbers
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 2, a Microsoft and Amazon favourite. Two non-negative numbers are stored as lists of digits, least significant first (342 is 2 → 4 → 3). Return their sum as a list in the same form. Add digit by digit with a carry, like on paper.
blocks.tests:

assert to_list(add_two(build([0]), build([0]))) == [0]
assert to_list(add_two(build([9, 9, 9, 9]), build([9, 9]))) == [8, 9, 0, 0, 1]
hints: Keep going while either list has digits or there's a carry. divmod(s, 10) gives the carry and the digit.
blocks.solution:
def add_two(a, b):
    out = dummy = ListNode()
    carry = 0
    while a or b or carry:
        s = carry + (a.val if a else 0) + (b.val if b else 0)
        carry, d = divmod(s, 10)
        out.next = ListNode(d)
        out = out.next
        a = a.next if a else None
        b = b.next if b else None
    return dummy.next

blocks.q: Why save nxt = cur.next before cur.next = prev when reversing?

opts.t: Once cur.next is overwritten, nothing points to the rest of the list

blocks.why: Rewiring a pointer drops the only reference to what came after. Save it first.

blocks.q: What does a dummy head node buy you?

opts.t: There's always a node before the first one, so head edits need no special case

blocks.why: Return dummy.next at the end, because the real head may have changed.

blocks.q: Slow moves 1, fast moves 2. When fast reaches the end of a 9-node list, slow is at…
blocks.why: Fast covers twice the distance, so slow has covered half.

blocks.q: Why does fast always land on slow inside a loop instead of jumping over it?

opts.t: Because the loop has even length
Fast gains exactly one node per step, so the gap shrinks 1 at a time to 0
Because both start at the head
It doesn't always; you need luck

blocks.why: A gap that drops by exactly 1 each step can't skip 0.

blocks.q: "Find the k-th node from the end in one pass." Which tool?

opts.t: Two pointers with a k-node head start

blocks.why: When the leader reaches the end, the follower is k behind it.

blocks.title: A least-recently-used cache for an image service
blocks.client: A small photo-sharing site whose thumbnail server keeps re-rendering the same popular images
blocks.brief: Build lru.py: a cache with a fixed capacity. get(key) returns the value (or -1) and marks it as just used; put(key, value) stores it, and when the cache is full it evicts the least recently used key. Both must be O(1). A dict finds a node by key; a doubly linked list keeps nodes in use order (most recent at the front), so moving or removing a node is O(1) pointer surgery. Measure the hit rate on a stream of requests where a few images are popular.
blocks.why: Browsers, CDNs, databases and your CPU's cache all evict "the thing not used for longest". This is LeetCode 146, one of the most-asked interview designs at every big company.
milestones: A doubly linked list with dummy head and tail
Hit-rate statistics on a skewed request stream
stretch: A time-to-live on each entry
Compare with Python's functools.lru_cache

def stress():

blocks.q: Explain how linked-list problems are solved: reversing, dummy heads, fast and slow pointers, and the LRU cache.
blocks.a: A singly linked list is nodes with a value and a next pointer, reached from the head. Reading the i-th item is O(i), but inserting or removing next to a node you hold is O(1). The danger is losing the rest of the list when you overwrite a pointer, so save next first: reversal walks prev, cur and nxt, pointing each cur back at prev, and returns prev. A dummy node before the head removes special cases for edits at the front; return dummy.next. Fast and slow pointers solve position questions in one pass and O(1) memory: when fast (2 steps) reaches the end, slow (1 step) is at the middle; a k-node head start finds the k-th from the end; in a loop fast gains one node per step so it lands on slow, and then a pointer from the head and one from the meeting point, moving together, meet at the loop's start. Combining them handles palindromes and reordering (middle, reverse half, compare or weave), and switching lists at the end finds an intersection. An LRU cache pairs a dict from key to node with a doubly linked list in use order, so get, put and eviction of tail.prev are all O(1).

chapters.title: Intervals and sweep lines
chapters.tagline: Sort by an end, turn ranges into events, and sweep once from left to right
goals: Decide whether two intervals overlap with one comparison

chapters.prelude:
import time
import random

def timed(fn, *args):

blocks.html:
An interval [s, e] is a range: a meeting, a booking, a segment of a road. Almost every interval question starts with one test. Two intervals a and b overlap exactly when

a.start < b.end and b.start < a.end

(use <= if touching counts as overlapping). The opposite, "they don't overlap", is easier to see: one ends before the other starts.

blocks.title: The overlap test, and the overlap itself

blocks.q: Intervals are half-open: [s, e) (a booking ending at 5 frees the slot at 5). Do [1, 5) and [5, 8) overlap?

opts.t: No: the first ends exactly where the second starts
Only if they're in the same room

blocks.why: With half-open intervals the test is a.start < b.end and b.start < a.end: 5 < 5 is false.

blocks.html: Chapter 6 merged overlapping intervals after sorting by start. The same idea answers most list-of-intervals questions in one pass.

blocks.starter:
def max_overlap(intervals):
    events = []
    for s, e in intervals:
        events.append((s, -1))
        events.append((e, 1))
    events.sort()

    for _, d in events:
        cur -= d
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best
blocks.solution:
def max_overlap(intervals):
    events = []
    for s, e in intervals:
        events.append((s, 1))
        events.append((e, -1))
    events.sort()
    cur = best = 0
    for _, d in events:
        cur += d
        best = max(best, cur)
    return best

blocks.title: covered_points
blocks.prompt: Codeforces 1000C "Covered Points Count". Segments [l, r] cover integer points (both ends included). Return a list cnt where cnt[k-1] is how many integer points are covered by exactly k segments, for k = 1..n. Coordinates go up to 10¹⁸, so you can't loop over points: sweep events at l (+1) and r + 1 (−1), and between consecutive event positions every point has the same count.
blocks.tests:
assert covered([(0, 3), (1, 3), (3, 8)]) == [6, 2, 1]
assert covered([(1, 3), (2, 4), (5, 7)]) == [5, 2, 0]
assert covered([(5, 5)]) == [1]
_, secs = timed(covered, [(0, 200000), (100, 300)])
assert secs < 0.01, f"{secs:.2f}s: sweep the events, don't visit every point"
r, secs = timed(covered, [(0, 10**18), (5, 10**17)])
assert r == [10**18 + 1 - (10**17 - 4), 10**17 - 4] and secs < 0.01, "sweep the events, don't visit every point"
hints: Before applying an event at x, the points prev..x-1 (that's x - prev of them) all had count cur.
blocks.solution:
def covered(segs):
    n = len(segs)
    events = []
    for l, r in segs:
        events.append((l, 1))
        events.append((r + 1, -1))
    events.sort()
    cnt = [0] * n
    cur, prev = 0, None
    for x, d in events:
        if prev is not None and cur > 0:
            cnt[cur - 1] += x - prev
        cur += d
        prev = x
    return cnt

blocks.q: Explain the main interval techniques: the overlap test, merging, greedy by end, and the sweep line.
blocks.a: Two intervals overlap when each starts before the other ends: a.start < b.end and b.start < a.end (≤ if touching counts), and their shared part is [max of starts, min of ends]. Sorting by start lets you merge, insert or find gaps in one pass, tracking the furthest end so far; two sorted lists intersect with two pointers, dropping whichever interval ends first. To keep the most non-overlapping intervals (or use the fewest arrows), sort by end and greedily keep each interval that starts after the last kept end, because ending earliest leaves the most room. For "how many at once" questions, turn each interval into a +1 event at its start and a −1 event at its end, sort the 2n events (ends before starts at equal times for half-open intervals), and sweep with a running count; the maximum is the number of rooms, and the gaps between events let you count covered points even when coordinates reach 10¹⁸. Cost: O(n log n) for the sort, independent of how large the times are.

chapters.title: Heaps and top-k
chapters.tagline: Always know the smallest (or biggest) item, and keep only the k that matter
goals: Explain how a binary heap stores a tree in a list and why push and pop are O(log n)
Use heapq, including the minus-sign trick for a max-heap
Keep a size-k heap for the k largest, closest or most frequent items
Merge k sorted streams and keep a running median with two heaps
chapters.prelude:
import time
import random
import heapq

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

sections.title: A tree hiding in a list

blocks.html:
A min-heap is a binary tree where every parent is ≤ its children, so the smallest item is at the top. It's stored in a plain list with no pointers: the children of index i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2, and its parent is at (i - 1) // 2.

  • push: add at the end, then swap it up while it's smaller than its parent.
  • pop: take the root, move the last item to the root, then swap it down with its smaller child.

Both walk one root-to-leaf path: O(log n). Turning a whole list into a heap (heapify) is O(n).

blocks.name: ds-heap
blocks.title: Take out the smallest ten times: scanning against a min-heap
blocks.goal: Run scan for the minimum to the end, then run min-heap and compare the comparisons.
blocks.intro: The heap mode draws the list as the tree it represents.

blocks.code:
import heapq
h = [54, 17, 88, 31, 6, 72]
heapq.heapify(h)
print("as a list:", h, "  smallest:", h[0])
heapq.heappush(h, 3)
print("after pushing 3:", h)
print("popped in order:", [heapq.heappop(h) for _ in range(len(h))])
print("3 largest of a list:", heapq.nlargest(3, [5, 1, 9, 7, 3]))

for x in [5, 1, 8, 3]:

blocks.why: Children of i are at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.

blocks.html: Python only has a min-heap. For a max-heap, push -x and negate what comes out. For records, push tuples: (priority, tie_breaker, item) sorts by priority first.

sections.title: Top-k: a small heap is enough

blocks.html: To keep the k largest of a stream, keep a min-heap of size k. Its root is the smallest of your top k, the one to beat. A new item bigger than the root replaces it. Cost O(n log k), memory O(k), and it works on a stream you can't store.

blocks.title: kth_largest
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 215, one of the most-asked questions at Meta and Amazon. Return the k-th largest number. Keep a min-heap of the k biggest so far: push each number, and pop whenever the heap grows past k. The answer is the root.
blocks.tests:

assert kth_largest([3, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6], 4) == 4
assert kth_largest([7], 1) == 7
random.seed(1)
big = [random.randint(0, 10**9) for _ in range(10000)]
r, secs = timed(kth_largest, big, 5000)
assert r == sorted(big)[-5000] and secs < 0.05, f"{secs:.2f}s: re-sorting the top k for every number is too slow"
hints: heappush, then if len(h) > k: heappop(h). The smallest of the k biggest is the k-th biggest.
blocks.starter:
def kth_largest(a, k):
    best = []
    for x in a:
        best.append(x)
        best.sort(reverse=True)
        best = best[:k]
    return best[-1]

def k_closest(points, k):
    return heapq.nsmallest(k, points, key=lambda p: (p[0] ** 2 + p[1] ** 2, p))

blocks.html: Put the front of each sorted list in a heap. Pop the smallest, then push the next item from the same list. With k lists and n items in total that's O(n log k).

lines: h = [(lst[0], i, 0) for i, lst in enumerate(lists) if lst]

blocks.title: smallest_range
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 632, a hard one asked at Google. Each of k sorted lists must have at least one number inside the range [lo, hi]. Return the smallest such range (smallest hi - lo, then smallest lo). Keep one pointer per list in a heap, plus the current maximum; the range is [heap min, current max]. Pop the min, advance that list, and stop when any list runs out.
hints: It's merge-k with one extra variable: the biggest value currently in the heap. Check the range every time before you pop-and-advance.
blocks.starter:
def smallest_range(lists):
    lo = min(l[0] for l in lists)
    hi = max(l[-1] for l in lists)
    return [lo, hi]
blocks.solution:
def smallest_range(lists):
    h = [(l[0], i, 0) for i, l in enumerate(lists)]
    heapq.heapify(h)
    hi = max(l[0] for l in lists)
    best = [h[0][0], hi]
    while True:
        lo, i, j = heapq.heappop(h)
        if hi - lo < best[1] - best[0]:
            best = [lo, hi]
        if j + 1 == len(lists[i]):
            return best
        nxt = lists[i][j + 1]
        hi = max(hi, nxt)
        heapq.heappush(h, (nxt, i, j + 1))

sections.title: Heaps for scheduling and greedy choices

blocks.title: connect_ropes
blocks.prompt: Amazon's classic. Joining two ropes of lengths a and b costs a + b. Return the least total cost to join all ropes into one. Greedy with a heap: always join the two shortest (the same idea as Huffman coding).
blocks.tests:
assert connect_ropes([4, 3, 2, 6]) == 29
assert connect_ropes([1, 2, 3, 4, 5]) == 33
assert connect_ropes([7]) == 0
assert connect_ropes([]) == 0
hints: Pop two, add their sum to the total, push the sum back. Repeat until one rope is left.
blocks.solution:
def connect_ropes(r):
    h = list(r)
    heapq.heapify(h)
    total = 0
    while len(h) > 1:
        s = heapq.heappop(h) + heapq.heappop(h)
        total += s
        heapq.heappush(h, s)
    return total

blocks.title: reorganize_string
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 767, asked at Amazon and Google. Rearrange the letters so no two neighbours are equal; return any valid arrangement or "" if impossible. Greedy: always place the most common letter that isn't the one you just placed. Use a max-heap of (-count, letter) and hold the previous letter back for one turn.
hints: After placing a letter, push the previous one back (it's allowed again) and keep the current one aside. If the heap empties while a letter is still held back, it's impossible.
blocks.starter:
def reorganize(s):
    return "".join(sorted(s))
blocks.solution:
from collections import Counter

def reorganize(s):
    h = [(-c, ch) for ch, c in Counter(s).items()]
    heapq.heapify(h)
    out, prev = [], None
    while h:
        c, ch = heapq.heappop(h)
        out.append(ch)
        if prev:
            heapq.heappush(h, prev)
        prev = (c + 1, ch) if c + 1 < 0 else None
    return "".join(out) if len(out) == len(s) else ""

blocks.title: heap_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: kth_largest(a, k) with a size-k min-heap, and merge_k(lists) with a heap of list fronts.
hints: Top-k: push, pop when too big, answer at the root. Merge: heap of (value, list, index); pop, record, push the next from that list.

blocks.q: Explain how a binary heap works and the main heap patterns: top-k, merging k sorted lists, two heaps for a median, and greedy choices.
blocks.a: A binary min-heap is a tree where each parent is ≤ its children, stored in a list with the children of i at 2i+1 and 2i+2, so the minimum is at index 0. Push appends and sifts up; pop moves the last item to the root and sifts down with the smaller child; both follow one path, O(log n), and heapify builds a heap in O(n). Python's heapq is a min-heap, so push negated values for a max-heap and use tuples like (priority, counter, item) for records and fair ties. For the k largest of a stream keep a min-heap of size k and pop when it grows past k: O(n log k) time, O(k) memory, and the root is the k-th largest. To merge k sorted lists, heap the fronts, pop the smallest and push its successor: O(n log k). A running median keeps the lower half in a max-heap and the upper half in a min-heap, balanced, with the median on top. Greedy algorithms that repeatedly need the cheapest or most common item, like joining the two shortest ropes, rearranging letters, scheduling by priority or Dijkstra, use a heap for that choice.

chapters.title: Greedy and the exchange argument
chapters.tagline: Make the locally best choice, and know how to prove it's also the globally best
goals: Recognise when a greedy choice is safe and when it isn't
Prove a greedy rule with an exchange argument, or break it with a counterexample
Solve reach, scheduling and assignment problems greedily
Combine greedy choices with sorting and heaps
chapters.prelude:
import time
import random
import heapq

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
A greedy algorithm builds an answer one choice at a time, always taking what looks best right now, and never undoes a choice. When it works it's usually the simplest and fastest solution there is: often just a sort and one pass.

The catch: "looks best right now" has to be the right rule, and plausible rules are often wrong.

blocks.name: ds-greedy
blocks.title: See the most talks: three greedy rules, one winner
blocks.goal: Run all three rules to the end and compare how many talks each keeps.
blocks.intro: Each rule sorts the talks its own way and then keeps every talk that still fits.

blocks.html:
To prove a greedy rule, show that any optimal answer can be changed, one swap at a time, into the greedy answer without getting worse.

For the talks: let g be the talk that ends first, and take any best schedule. Its first talk ends no earlier than g, so swap it for g. Nothing after it clashes (g ends even sooner), and the count is the same. Repeat on the rest of the day.

To disprove a rule, one counterexample is enough. Always try to break your greedy idea with a small case before you code it.

blocks.title: Greedy coins: right for real currencies, wrong in general

blocks.code:
coins = [1, 5, 6, 9]
amount, used = 11, 0
for c in sorted(coins, reverse=True):
    used += amount // c
    amount %= c
print(used)

assert can_jump([0])

assert can_jump([2, 5, 0, 0, 0, 0, 1])

blocks.title: gas_station
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 134. Stations on a circular road: gas[i] fuel at station i, cost[i] fuel to drive to the next one. Return the start index that lets you go all the way round (it's unique if it exists), or -1. In one pass: if the total gas < total cost, it's -1. Otherwise, whenever your tank goes negative, no station from the current start up to here can work, so start again from the next station.
blocks.tests:
assert start_station([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [3, 4, 5, 1, 2]) == 3
assert start_station([2, 3, 4], [3, 4, 3]) == -1

blocks.title: assign_cookies
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 455. Child i is happy with a cookie of size at least greed[i]; each child gets at most one cookie. Return the most happy children. Sort both; give each cookie, smallest first, to the least greedy child it can satisfy (two pointers).

assert content_children([10, 9], [5, 6]) == 0

def content_children(greed, cookies):
    return min(len(greed), len(cookies))

sections.title: Greedy plus a heap: regret later

blocks.html: Some greedy algorithms take a choice now and swap it out later if something better turns up. A heap remembers the worst choice made so far.

blocks.title: course_schedule_iii
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 630, a hard one. Each course is (duration, deadline); courses run back to back from day 0 and must finish by their deadline. Return the most courses you can take. Sort by deadline. Take each course; if the total time now passes its deadline, drop the longest course taken so far (a max-heap of durations). Swapping a long course for a shorter one never hurts later ones: an exchange argument.
blocks.tests:
assert schedule_courses([(100, 200), (200, 1300), (1000, 1250), (2000, 3200)]) == 3
assert schedule_courses([(1, 2)]) == 1
assert schedule_courses([(3, 2), (4, 3)]) == 0
assert schedule_courses([(5, 5), (4, 6), (2, 6)]) == 2
hints: Push -d so the heap's top is the longest course. t += heappop(h) subtracts that duration (it's negative).

blocks.q: To see the most non-overlapping talks, the greedy rule that's always right is…
blocks.why: Ending first leaves the most room. The other two have small counterexamples.

blocks.q: What does an exchange argument show?

opts.t: That any optimal answer can be swapped, step by step, into the greedy one without getting worse
That the problem needs dynamic programming
That sorting is O(n log n)

blocks.why: If every best answer can be turned into yours, yours is a best answer.

blocks.q: You think of a greedy rule. What should you do before coding it?

opts.t: Try to break it with small hand-made cases (or a brute-force checker)

blocks.why: A single counterexample saves you a wrong submission. Chapter 60 automates this.

blocks.q: Jump game: why is tracking the farthest reachable index enough?

opts.t: Every index up to the farthest one is also reachable, so only the farthest matters

blocks.why: Reachable positions form a prefix of the array, so one number describes them all.

blocks.q: "Minimum number of coins for an amount, with arbitrary coin values." Greedy or not?

opts.t: Greedy: always take the biggest coin
Not greedy: it needs dynamic programming

blocks.why: With coins 1, 3, 4 and amount 6, greedy gives 4 + 1 + 1, but 3 + 3 is better.

sections.title: Real-world project: a road-trip fuel planner

blocks.title: Fewest fuel stops on a long drive
blocks.client: A van-life couple driving remote highways where stations are hundreds of kilometres apart
blocks.brief: Build fuel.py. Given the tank size, the trip length and the stations along the way (position, litres available), first check whether the trip is even possible, then find the fewest stops. The trick: drive as far as you can, and only when you'd run dry, pretend you'd stopped at the best station you already passed (a max-heap of the fuel you skipped). Prove to yourself with an exchange argument why taking the biggest skipped station first is safe.
blocks.why: Route planners, delivery fleets and EV charging apps all solve "fewest stops" problems. This is LeetCode 871, asked at Google.
milestones: The fewest stops with a heap
The list of stations to stop at
A brute-force checker on small random trips
stretch: Fuel prices: the cheapest trip instead of the fewest stops
A tank that can't be filled past its size

blocks.title: reachable
blocks.prompt: Start with fuel litres (1 litre = 1 km). stations is a list of (position, litres) sorted by position; at each you may take all its fuel (the tank has no limit). Can you reach target? Greedy: take every station's fuel as you pass it.
blocks.tests:
assert reachable(100, 10, [(10, 60), (20, 30), (30, 30), (60, 40)])
assert not reachable(100, 1, [(10, 100)])
assert reachable(1, 1, [])
assert not reachable(100, 50, [(60, 100)])
hints: fuel is also how far you can get. If the next station is beyond that, you're stuck, however much fuel it has.
blocks.starter:
def reachable(target, fuel, stations):
    return fuel + sum(l for _, l in stations) >= target

blocks.title: min_refuel_stops
blocks.prompt: Same setup: return the fewest stops to reach target, or -1. Drive forward; push every station you can reach onto a max-heap of litres. Whenever the next station (or the target) is out of reach, refuel from the biggest station passed so far and count a stop.
hints: The starter stops at every station it passes. Instead, keep the passed stations in a heap and only "stop" (pop the biggest) when you must.

blocks.title: greedy_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: max_talks(talks) (the most non-overlapping half-open intervals, greedy by end) and can_jump(a).
hints: Talks: sort by end, keep any that start at or after the last kept end. Jumps: track the farthest reachable index.

blocks.q: Explain what a greedy algorithm is, how you prove one with an exchange argument, and give examples where greedy works and where it fails.
blocks.a: A greedy algorithm builds the answer by repeatedly making the choice that looks best now and never undoing it, usually after sorting, so it is often O(n log n) and very short. It is only correct with the right rule. To prove a rule, use an exchange argument: take any optimal solution and show you can swap its choices one at a time for the greedy ones without making it worse, so the greedy answer is optimal too. For the most non-overlapping intervals, ending earliest is provably right while earliest start and shortest first have counterexamples. Greedy also works for reachability (track the farthest index in jump game), the gas station (restart after the tank goes negative), matching sorted items (cookies, boxers, queue order), partition labels, and with a heap of past choices for regret (drop the longest course, refuel from the biggest station passed). It fails for minimum coins with arbitrary values (1, 3, 4 for 6) and other problems that need dynamic programming, so always try small counterexamples or a brute-force check before trusting a greedy idea.

chapters.title: Tree traversals
chapters.tagline: Pre, in, post and level order, and letting recursion answer for each subtree
goals: Walk a binary tree in preorder, inorder, postorder and level order
Solve tree questions by asking "what does each subtree return?"
Use breadth-first search with a queue for levels and nearest answers
Carry extra information up (heights, best-so-far) for diameter and path sums

blocks.html:
A binary tree is nodes with up to two children, left and right. The top node is the root; nodes with no children are leaves. The depth of a node counts the nodes from the root down to it.

In every lesson here, build_tree([3, 9, 20, None, None, 15, 7]) builds a tree from its level order (row by row, left to right, None for a missing child):

`` 3 / \ 9 20 / \ 15 7 ``

Recursion visits a node and both its subtrees. The only question is when you handle the node itself:

OrderNode handledTypical use
preorderbefore its childrencopying a tree, writing it out
inorderbetween left and righta search tree in sorted order (chapter 18)
postorderafter its childrenanything that needs the children's answers first: heights, sizes, deleting

blocks.code:
root = build_tree([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, None, 6])
def pre(n):  return [n.val] + pre(n.left) + pre(n.right) if n else []
def ino(n):  return ino(n.left) + [n.val] + ino(n.right) if n else []
def post(n): return post(n.left) + post(n.right) + [n.val] if n else []
print("preorder: ", pre(root))
print("inorder:  ", ino(root))
print("postorder:", post(root))
blocks.title: The three depth-first orders

blocks.code:
root = build_tree([4, 2, 6, 1, 3])
def walk(n):
    return walk(n.left) + walk(n.right) + [n.val] if n else []
print(walk(root))

blocks.q: To compute every node's subtree size, which order do you need?

opts.t: Postorder: a node's size needs its children's sizes first

blocks.why: size(node) = 1 + size(left) + size(right). The children have to be done first.

blocks.html: Most tree questions have a three-line recursive answer if you ask: if I knew the answer for my left and right subtrees, what's mine? And what's the answer for None?

blocks.title: max_depth
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 104. Return the tree's depth: the number of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path. None has depth 0.
blocks.tests:
assert max_depth(build_tree([3, 9, 20, None, None, 15, 7])) == 3
assert max_depth(build_tree([1, None, 2])) == 2
assert max_depth(None) == 0
hints: My depth is 1 plus the deeper of my two subtrees.

blocks.title: invert_tree
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 226 (famously the question a well-known engineer failed at a Google interview). Mirror the tree: swap every node's left and right children. Return the root.
hints: Swap the children and invert each of them. The starter only swaps at the root.

blocks.title: symmetric
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 101. Is the tree a mirror image of itself? Write a helper mirror(a, b): two subtrees mirror each other if both are empty, or their values match and a.left mirrors b.right and a.right mirrors b.left.
blocks.tests:
assert is_symmetric(build_tree([1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 3]))
assert not is_symmetric(build_tree([1, 2, 2, None, 3, None, 3]))
assert not is_symmetric(build_tree([1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 3, 4]))
assert is_symmetric(None)
hints: Outside pairs with outside, inside with inside: (a.left, b.right) and (a.right, b.left).

blocks.title: path_sum
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 112. Is there a root-to-leaf path whose values add up to target? Pass the remaining amount down: at a leaf, check whether it's exactly the leaf's value.
blocks.tests:
t = build_tree([5, 4, 8, 11, None, 13, 4, 7, 2, None, None, None, 1])
assert has_path_sum(t, 22)
assert not has_path_sum(t, 5)
assert not has_path_sum(build_tree([1, 2]), 1)
assert not has_path_sum(None, 0)
hints: [1, 2] with target 1 is False: the root isn't a leaf, so the path must go on to 2.

blocks.html: Sometimes a subtree must report one thing to its parent (its height) while you track a different thing globally (the best path seen anywhere).

blocks.title: diameter
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 543, asked at Meta and Google. The diameter is the number of edges on the longest path between any two nodes (it needn't pass through the root). A postorder helper returns each subtree's height; at each node, the longest path bending there is left height + right height.
blocks.tests:
assert diameter(build_tree([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])) == 3
assert diameter(build_tree([1, 2])) == 1
assert diameter(build_tree([1, 2, None, 3, 4, 5, None, None, 6, 7, None, None, 8])) == 6
assert diameter(None) == 0
hints: The starter only bends at the root. Track best with nonlocal and update it at every node, while still returning the height.

blocks.title: balanced_bug
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 110. A tree is balanced if at every node the subtrees' heights differ by at most 1. This check only looks at the root, so it calls [1, 2, 2, 3, None, None, 3, 4, None, None, 4] balanced. Fix it in one pass: return -1 from the helper as soon as any subtree is unbalanced.
blocks.tests:
assert not is_balanced(build_tree([1, 2, 2, 3, None, None, 3, 4, None, None, 4]))
assert is_balanced(build_tree([3, 9, 20, None, None, 15, 7]))
assert not is_balanced(build_tree([1, 2, 2, 3, 3, None, None, 4, 4]))
assert is_balanced(None)
hints: Let the helper return the height, or -1 meaning "unbalanced somewhere below". Pass the -1 straight up.

blocks.title: max_path_sum
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 124, a hard one asked at Meta, Google and Amazon. Values can be negative. A path goes between any two nodes (at least one node). Return the largest path sum. Same shape as diameter: the helper returns the best path going down from a node (dropping a negative branch, i.e. max(0, ...)), and at each node you check node.val + left + right.
blocks.tests:
assert max_path_sum(build_tree([1, 2, 3])) == 6
assert max_path_sum(build_tree([-10, 9, 20, None, None, 15, 7])) == 42
assert max_path_sum(build_tree([-3])) == -3
assert max_path_sum(build_tree([2, -1])) == 2
hints: A branch that adds up to less than 0 is better left out: max(0, down(child)). The answer can bend at any node.

blocks.html: Put the root in a queue (chapter 12). Repeatedly take from the front and add its children to the back: nodes come out in order of depth. Taking len(q) nodes at a time gives you exactly one level per round.

blocks.name: ds-tree
blocks.title: The shallowest leaf: depth-first against breadth-first
blocks.goal: Run depth-first to the end, then run breadth-first and compare how many nodes each visits.
blocks.intro: The only difference between the two is a stack (take the newest) or a queue (take the oldest).

blocks.title: Level order, one list per level (LeetCode 102)
blocks.tests:
assert level_order(build_tree([3, 9, 20, None, None, 15, 7])) == [[3], [9, 20], [15, 7]]
assert level_order(None) == []
lines: out, q = [], deque([root] if root else [])

blocks.title: min_depth
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 111. Return the depth of the shallowest leaf. Use breadth-first search and stop at the first leaf (the simulation's lesson). Watch out: a node with only one child is not a leaf.
blocks.tests:
assert min_depth(build_tree([3, 9, 20, None, None, 15, 7])) == 2
assert min_depth(build_tree([2, None, 3, None, 4, None, 5, None, 6])) == 5
assert min_depth(None) == 0

blocks.title: right_side_view
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 199, asked at Meta. Standing to the right of the tree, return the values you can see from top to bottom: the last node of each level.
blocks.tests:
