assert right_view(build_tree([1, 2, 3, 4])) == [1, 3, 4]
assert right_view(None) == []
hints: Level by level; after the inner loop, n is the last node of that level.

blocks.title: lowest_common_ancestor
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 236, one of Meta's most-asked. Given two values p and q that are both in the tree (values are distinct), return the value of their lowest common ancestor: the deepest node that has both in its subtree (a node counts as its own descendant). Recursively: if this node is p or q, return it; otherwise ask both sides. If both sides found something, this node is the answer; otherwise pass up whichever side found something.
blocks.tests:
t = build_tree([3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 0, 8, None, None, 7, 4])
assert lca(t, 5, 1) == 3
assert lca(t, 5, 4) == 5
assert lca(t, 7, 4) == 2
assert lca(t, 6, 4) == 5
hints: go(n) returns a node that is p, q or their meeting point, or None. The first node where both sides return something is the answer.
blocks.starter:
def lca(root, p, q):
    return root.val

blocks.title: party_groups
blocks.prompt: Codeforces 115A "Party". Employee i's direct manager is boss[i] (or -1 for none). Split everyone into groups so that nobody is in the same group as anyone above them in the chain of command. Return the fewest groups. It's the depth of the deepest chain: build each manager's list of reports and run BFS from every top boss, counting levels.
blocks.tests:
assert groups([-1, 0, 1, -1, 3]) == 3
assert groups([-1, -1, -1]) == 1
assert groups([-1, 0, 0, 0]) == 2
assert groups([1, 2, 3, -1]) == 4
hints: Start the queue with every employee whose boss is -1. Each round of len(q) pops is one level.
blocks.starter:
def groups(boss):
    return 1 + sum(1 for b in boss if b != -1 and boss[b] != -1)

blocks.q: "Return the values level by level." Which traversal?
blocks.why: Taking len(q) items at a time gives exactly one level per round.

blocks.q: What's the base case for almost every recursive tree function?
blocks.why: Decide what None returns (0, True, an empty list…), and the leaves look after themselves.

blocks.q: In the diameter solution, why does the helper return the height but the answer is tracked separately?

opts.t: A path can bend at a node, but a parent can only extend one straight branch of it

blocks.why: What the parent needs (one branch) differs from the best answer at this node (both branches).

blocks.q: A tree with n nodes is just a long chain (every node has one child). What happens to recursive depth-first search?

opts.t: It recurses n deep, and Python's default limit (about 1000) can crash it

blocks.why: For deep trees, use an explicit stack or raise the recursion limit.

blocks.q: What does BFS guarantee that DFS doesn't?

opts.t: Nodes come out in order of depth, so the first match is the shallowest

blocks.why: That's why "nearest" and "fewest steps" questions use BFS.

blocks.title: An org-chart explorer for a growing startup

blocks.tests:
t = build_tree([1, 2, 3, 4, 5])

hints: Levels: a queue, len(q) at a time. Diameter: return height, track l + r.

blocks.q: Explain the ways to traverse a binary tree and how to design recursive tree solutions.
blocks.a: Depth-first traversal recurses into both subtrees and handles the node before them (preorder), between them (inorder, sorted order for a search tree) or after them (postorder, needed whenever a node's answer depends on its children's, like heights and sizes). Most tree problems are solved by asking what each subtree should return and what the empty tree returns: depth is 1 + max of the children, inverting swaps inverted children, symmetry compares outside with outside and inside with inside, and path sums pass the remaining target down. When the best answer can bend at a node, the helper returns one thing to its parent (a height or best downward path, dropping negative branches) while a nonlocal variable tracks the global best (diameter, maximum path sum); returning -1 can signal failure up the tree (balanced check). Breadth-first traversal uses a queue, takes len(q) nodes per round to get one level at a time, and finds the shallowest leaf or right-side view; the first match is the nearest. The lowest common ancestor is the first node where p and q come back from different sides, or with parent pointers the first shared node walking up. Deep chains can exceed Python's recursion limit.

blocks.html:
A binary search tree (BST) is a binary tree where, for every node, everything in its left subtree is smaller and everything in its right subtree is bigger. A search is binary search on a tree: compare, go left or right, repeat.

`` 8 / \ 4 12 / \ / \ 2 6 10 14 ``

Search, insert and delete each walk one path, so they cost O(height). Read the keys inorder and they come out sorted.

The largest key in the tree

blocks.q: Explain binary search trees: the ordering rule, search, insert and delete, validation, and why balance matters.
blocks.a: A binary search tree keeps, for every node, all smaller keys in its left subtree and all bigger keys in its right subtree, so inorder traversal lists the keys in sorted order and a search walks one path, going left or right after each comparison. Insert walks the same path and attaches a new leaf; delete replaces a node with one child by that child, and a node with two children takes its inorder successor's key (the leftmost node of its right subtree), which is then deleted from there. Validation must pass bounds down (lo, hi), because comparing only with children misses violations against higher ancestors. An iterative inorder walk with a stack gives the k-th smallest and an iterator; the LCA is the first node whose key lies between p and q; floor, ceiling and range sums prune whole subtrees. Every operation costs O(height): about log₂ n for a balanced tree but n for a chain, which is what sorted insertions produce. Building from a sorted list by taking the middle as the root gives a balanced tree, and self-balancing trees (AVL, red-black, B-trees) keep the height O(log n) under any sequence of operations.

blocks.q: Why does BFS find the fewest moves but DFS doesn't?

opts.t: BFS visits cells in order of distance, so its first arrival is shortest; DFS follows one path deep and stops at the first arrival

blocks.why: BFS never tries every path: each cell is visited once. The order is what makes it shortest.

blocks.title: nearest_zero
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 542. For a 0/1 matrix, return a matrix where each cell holds the distance to its nearest 0. One BFS from all the zeros, in O(rows × cols), instead of one BFS per cell.
blocks.tests:

big[99][99] = 0
for r in range(100):
    big[r][25] = big[r][75] = 0
r, secs = timed(nearest_zero, big)
assert r[0][15] == 10 and r[0][50] == 25 and r[99][98] == 1 and secs < 0.08, f"{secs:.2f}s: one BFS from every zero at once"

blocks.starter:
def nearest_zero(m):
    R, C = len(m), len(m[0])
    zeros = [(r, c) for r in range(R) for c in range(C) if m[r][c] == 0]
    return [[min(abs(r - a) + abs(c - b) for a, b in zeros) for c in range(C)] for r in range(R)]

blocks.q: Explain breadth-first search on grids and graphs and why it finds the fewest steps.
blocks.a: Breadth-first search starts from the source in a queue, repeatedly takes the oldest item and adds its unvisited neighbours (marking them visited when added, with distance one more). Because the queue releases nodes in order of distance, the first time a node is reached is by a shortest route, provided every move costs the same; depth-first search instead follows one path deep and returns whatever it finds first, which can be much longer. On a grid each open cell is a node with up to four (or eight) neighbours, so BFS costs O(rows × cols). To find the distance to the nearest of many sources (rotting oranges, nearest zero, nearest robot), put all sources in the queue at distance 0 and run once. Nodes can be abstract states generated on the fly: lock combinations, numbers reached by buttons, words differing by one letter. Storing each node's parent lets you rebuild the route. When moves cost 0 or 1, 0-1 BFS uses a deque, pushing free moves to the front; for general costs you need Dijkstra.

blocks.html: Depth-first search goes as deep as it can along one route before backing up. It visits everything reachable from the start in O(V + E). Recursion is the shortest way to write it, but Python's recursion limit makes an explicit stack safer for big inputs.

blocks.html: A connected component is a group of nodes that can all reach each other. To count them: loop over every node, and each time you find one that isn't visited, that's a new component. Search from it to mark the whole piece.

blocks.title: num_islands
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 200, the most-asked graph question at Amazon. In a grid of "1" (land) and "0" (water), count the islands (land connected up, down, left, right). Every time you meet unvisited land, count one and flood-fill the whole island.
hints: Outer loops find a new island; an inner stack (or recursion) marks all of its land so it isn't counted again.

def num_islands(grid):

blocks.html:
Undirected: during DFS, a neighbour that's already visited and isn't the node you just came from (your parent) closes a loop.

Directed: that test gives false alarms, because two routes can reach the same node without any loop. Use three colours: white (unseen), grey (on the current path), black (finished). Only an edge into a grey node is a cycle.

blocks.html: A graph is bipartite if you can colour every node red or blue so that every edge joins different colours (two teams, no rivals on the same team). Colour the start red, its neighbours blue, theirs red… If an edge ever joins two nodes of the same colour, it's impossible: that happens exactly when there's an odd-length cycle.

blocks.title: is_bipartite
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 785, asked at Meta. g[i] lists node i's neighbours (undirected; the graph may be disconnected). Return whether it's bipartite. BFS or DFS from every uncoloured node, giving each neighbour the opposite colour.
blocks.tests:

assert is_bipartite([[1, 3], [0, 2], [1, 3], [0, 2]])
assert not is_bipartite([[1, 2], [0, 2], [0, 1]])
assert is_bipartite([[], [2], [1]])
hints: color[w] = 1 - color[v]. A neighbour already holding the same colour proves it's impossible.
blocks.starter:
def is_bipartite(g):
    return all(len(nb) <= 2 for nb in g)

blocks.prompt: Codeforces 862B "Mahmoud and Ehab and the bipartiteness". A tree with n nodes is given as an edge list. Return how many more edges you can add (no repeats, no self-loops) while keeping the graph bipartite. hints: Nodes are numbered from 1. Count the reds; the blues are n - reds.
blocks.starter:
def more_edges(n, edges):

blocks.q: Explain depth-first search on graphs and how it counts components, fills regions and detects cycles in undirected and directed graphs.
blocks.a: Store a graph as an adjacency list (O(V + E)) and explore it with depth-first search, which follows one route as deep as possible before backing up, visiting everything reachable in O(V + E); in Python an explicit stack avoids the recursion limit. Looping over all nodes and starting a new search from each unvisited one counts connected components (islands, friend groups) and finds each region's size; flood fill on a grid treats cells as nodes, and starting from the border marks regions that escape (surrounded regions). In an undirected graph, a visited neighbour that isn't the parent means a cycle. In a directed graph that test gives false alarms, because two paths can reach the same node, so use three colours: white unseen, grey on the current path, black finished; only an edge to a grey node closes a cycle (course schedule). Two-colouring with BFS or DFS tests whether a graph is bipartite, which fails exactly when there is an odd cycle.

chapters.title: Topological sort
chapters.tagline: Put tasks in an order that respects every "must come before"
goals: Find a topological order with Kahn's algorithm (in-degrees and a queue)
Find one with DFS by reversing the finishing order
Detect when no order exists because of a cycle
Run dynamic programming along a topological order (longest path, fewest semesters)
chapters.prelude:
import time
import heapq
from collections import defaultdict, deque

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html: A directed acyclic graph (DAG) is a directed graph with no cycles: build steps, course prerequisites, spreadsheet formulas, package dependencies. A topological order lists its nodes so every arrow goes from earlier to later. One exists exactly when there's no cycle, and there are often several.

blocks.name: ds-topo
blocks.title: A build order: rescanning against Kahn's algorithm
blocks.goal: Run rescan for a ready step to the end, then run Kahn's algorithm and compare the steps.
blocks.intro: Each box shows how many prerequisites it is still waiting on in Kahn mode.

blocks.html:
Kahn's algorithm:

  1. Count each node's incoming arrows (its in-degree).
  2. Queue every node with in-degree 0: nothing is blocking them.
  3. Pop one, append it to the order, and decrement each node it points to; any that reach 0 join the queue.
  4. If the order ends up shorter than the number of nodes, the rest are stuck in a cycle.

blocks.title: Kahn's algorithm on a tiny morning routine

blocks.q: Kahn's algorithm finishes with 7 nodes in the order, but the graph has 10. What does that mean?

opts.t: The other 3 are in or behind a cycle, so no topological order exists

blocks.why: Nodes in a cycle wait on each other forever, so their in-degree never reaches 0.

blocks.title: course_order
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 210, asked at Amazon, Google and Meta. n courses, prereqs pairs (a, b) meaning b before a. Return an order to take them all, or [] if impossible. When several are ready, take the smallest number first (use a heap instead of a queue) so the answer is unique.
blocks.tests:
assert course_order(2, [(1, 0)]) == [0, 1]
assert course_order(4, [(1, 0), (2, 0), (3, 1), (3, 2)]) == [0, 1, 2, 3]
assert course_order(3, [(0, 2), (1, 0)]) == [2, 0, 1]
assert course_order(2, [(1, 0), (0, 1)]) == []
assert course_order(1, []) == [0]
hints: Edge b → a, so indeg[a] += 1. Pop the smallest ready course with heappop.
blocks.starter:
def course_order(n, prereqs):
    return list(range(n))
blocks.solution:
def course_order(n, prereqs):
    out = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    indeg = [0] * n
    for a, b in prereqs:
        out[b].append(a)
        indeg[a] += 1
    h = [v for v in range(n) if indeg[v] == 0]
    heapq.heapify(h)
    order = []
    while h:
        v = heapq.heappop(h)
        order.append(v)
        for w in out[v]:
            indeg[w] -= 1
            if indeg[w] == 0:
                heapq.heappush(h, w)
    return order if len(order) == n else []

blocks.title: fewest_semesters
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 1136. Courses 1..n; relations are (before, after). Each semester you can take any number of courses whose prerequisites are all done. Return the fewest semesters, or -1 if there's a cycle. Kahn's algorithm level by level: each round of len(q) pops is one semester.

blocks.title: A make-style build tool for a static website

Compute a valid build order with Kahn's algorithm and report a clear error naming the stuck targets if there's a cycle. Then the real win: when one file changes, rebuild only the targets that depend on it, directly or indirectly, in a valid order.

blocks.prompt: rules maps each target to the list of things it needs (needs must be built first; a need that isn't a target is a plain source file). Return a sorted list of the targets that can never be built because they're in a cycle or depend on one. Run Kahn's over the targets; whatever is left over is stuck.

rules = {"site": ["index", "about"], "index": ["header", "posts.json"], "about": ["header"], "header": ["logo.png"]}
assert stuck(rules) == []

blocks.title: downstream
blocks.prompt: When the file changed is edited, which targets must be rebuilt? Every target that needs it, directly or through other targets. Return them in a valid build order (ties: alphabetical). Find everything reachable along "is needed by" arrows, then topologically sort just those.

assert downstream(rules, "logo.png") == ["header", "about", "index", "site"]
assert downstream(rules, "posts.json") == ["blog", "index", "site"]
assert downstream(rules, "nothing.txt") == []

blocks.starter:
def downstream(rules, changed):
    return sorted(t for t, needs in rules.items() if changed in needs)

blocks.title: topo_rebuild
blocks.prompt: From memory: topo(n, edges) with Kahn's algorithm (edges (a, b) mean a before b, smallest-first when tied); return [] if there's a cycle.
hints: In-degrees, a heap of the zeros, pop and decrement, and check the length at the end.
blocks.starter:
def topo(n, edges):
    pass
blocks.solution:
def topo(n, edges):
    out = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    indeg = [0] * n
    for a, b in edges:
        out[a].append(b)
        indeg[b] += 1
    h = [v for v in range(n) if indeg[v] == 0]
    heapq.heapify(h)
    order = []
    while h:
        v = heapq.heappop(h)
        order.append(v)
        for w in out[v]:
            indeg[w] -= 1
            if indeg[w] == 0:
                heapq.heappush(h, w)
    return order if len(order) == n else []

blocks.q: Explain topological sorting: what it is, Kahn's algorithm, the DFS method, cycle detection and DP on a DAG.
blocks.a: A topological order lists the nodes of a directed graph so every edge goes from earlier to later; it exists exactly when the graph has no cycle (a DAG). Kahn's algorithm counts each node's in-degree (incoming edges), queues the nodes with in-degree zero, and repeatedly removes one, appends it to the order and decrements its successors, queueing any that reach zero; it runs in O(V + E), a heap gives the smallest order when ties must be broken, and processing the queue in rounds gives levels such as the fewest semesters. If the order ends shorter than the number of nodes, the leftovers are in or behind a cycle. Alternatively, depth-first search appends each node when it finishes, and the reverse of that finishing order is topological. Processing nodes in topological order lets you do dynamic programming on a DAG, such as the longest path, because every predecessor is final before a node is used. Real uses include build systems, course plans, recipe dependencies, alien alphabets and spreadsheet recalculation.

chapters.title: Union-find
chapters.tagline: Merge groups and ask "same group?" in almost constant time
goals: Build a disjoint set union with parent pointers, union by size and path compression
Count connected components as edges arrive, without rebuilding anything
Detect the edge that closes a cycle in an undirected graph
Spot union-find problems: equivalences, merging accounts, swappable positions
chapters.prelude:
import time
import random

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html: Lots of problems look like this: things get joined one at a time (friendships, cables, equal variables, accounts sharing an email), and you keep asking "are these two in the same group?" and "how many groups are there?". BFS would answer, but rerunning it after every join is far too slow. Union-find (also called a disjoint set union, DSU) answers both, as the joins arrive, in almost constant time each.

blocks.name: ds-dsu
blocks.title: Friend groups: relabelling everyone against union-find
blocks.goal: Run relabel everyone to the end, then run union-find and compare the steps.
blocks.intro: Click a person to see who they point at.

blocks.html:
The idea:

  • Every item has a parent. A root is its own parent, and the root names the group.
  • find(x) follows parents up to the root.
  • union(a, b) finds both roots and points one at the other.

Two tricks keep the trees flat:

  • Union by size: hang the smaller tree under the bigger one, so depth grows only when a group at least doubles: O(log n) at worst.
  • Path compression: after a find, point every node you passed straight at the root.

With both, each operation costs about α(n), the inverse Ackermann function, which is at most 4 for any input that fits in the universe.

blocks.title: A complete union-find in 15 lines

blocks.q: What does union(a, b) return False for in the code above?

opts.t: When a and b are equal numbers
When a and b are already in the same group, so the new link closes a cycle
When the groups have equal size

blocks.why: Same root before the union means they were already connected.

blocks.title: count_components
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 323, asked at Google, Meta and LinkedIn. n nodes 0..n-1 and an undirected edges list. Return the number of connected components. Use union-find: start with n groups and subtract one for every union that actually merges.

blocks.q: Explain union-find: how it is stored, its two optimisations, its cost and the kinds of problems it solves.
blocks.a: Union-find, or disjoint set union, tracks groups that only ever merge. Each item stores a parent pointer; a group is a tree and its root, the one item that is its own parent, names the group. find follows parents to the root, and union finds both roots and points one at the other, returning false if they were already the same, which in a graph means the new edge closes a cycle. Union by size (or rank) hangs the smaller tree under the larger, so depth is at most O(log n); path compression, or path halving, re-points the nodes on a find path toward the root. Together they make each operation run in amortised inverse-Ackermann time, effectively constant. It answers connectivity and group counts as edges arrive, so it is used for counting components, finding the redundant edge, checking equality constraints, grouping swappable positions, online island counting, merging accounts by shared details, and Kruskal's minimum spanning tree. It cannot delete edges directly.

blocks.html: BFS (chapter 19) finds the path with the fewest edges. Once each edge has a weight (minutes, kilometres, money), the fewest edges can be far from the cheapest route.

blocks.name: ds-dijkstra
blocks.title: A road map: fewest roads against least time

blocks.intro: Click a place to see its roads and its best time so far.

blocks.html:
Dijkstra's algorithm (for weights that are never negative):

  1. dist[start] = 0, everything else infinity. Push (0, start) on a min-heap.
  2. Pop the smallest (d, v). If d > dist[v], it's a stale entry: skip it (lazy deletion).
  3. Otherwise v is settled: d is final. For each edge v → w with weight t, if d + t < dist[w], improve dist[w] and push (d + t, w).

Why is a popped distance final? Any other route to v must leave the settled region through some place whose distance is already at least d, and weights can't go negative, so it can't arrive with less than d. That argument is exactly why Dijkstra breaks with negative weights (chapter 24).

blocks.title: Dijkstra with a heap, plus the route

blocks.q: Why does Dijkstra skip a popped entry when d > dist[v]?

opts.t: A better distance for v was found after this entry was pushed, so this entry is out of date

blocks.why: Python's heapq can't lower a key in place, so we push duplicates and ignore the stale ones.

blocks.q: Explain Dijkstra's algorithm: what it solves, how it works with a heap, why it is correct, its cost, its limits and its common variations.
blocks.a: Dijkstra finds shortest paths from a source in a graph whose edge weights are never negative, where BFS's fewest-edges answer is no longer the cheapest. It keeps a tentative distance for each node and a min-heap of (distance, node); it repeatedly pops the smallest, skips it if stale (larger than the recorded distance), otherwise treats it as settled and relaxes each outgoing edge, pushing any neighbour whose distance improves. A popped distance is final because any other route must leave the settled set through a node at least as far away and weights cannot be negative, which is also why negative edges break it. With a binary heap it costs O((V + E) log V). A parent map recovers the path. Variations keep the same loop: different path costs such as maximum step or multiplied probabilities, extra state such as (node, coupon used), many sources started at distance zero together, and 0-1 BFS with a deque when weights are only 0 or 1. It powers maps, delivery quotes and network routing.

goals: Explain why Dijkstra breaks on negative edges
Write Bellman-Ford, stop it early, and detect negative cycles
Limit the number of edges on a path with round-by-round Bellman-Ford
Compute all-pairs shortest paths with Floyd-Warshall

sections.title: When an edge pays you back

blocks.html: Sometimes an edge has a negative weight: a rebate, an energy gain, a currency trade that leaves you richer. Dijkstra's "the closest unsettled node is final" argument needs weights that are never negative, so it can settle a node too early.

blocks.name: ds-bellman
blocks.title: A rebate road: Dijkstra against Bellman-Ford
blocks.goal: Run Dijkstra to the end, then run Bellman-Ford and compare the cost of reaching T.
blocks.intro: The red road pays you 5.

blocks.html:
Bellman-Ford does something dumber and safer:

  • Set dist[s] = 0 and everything else to infinity.
  • Repeat V − 1 times: for every edge (u, v, w), if dist[u] + w < dist[v], lower dist[v].
  • After round i, every shortest path that uses at most i edges is correct. A shortest path never needs more than V − 1 edges, so that's enough. O(V · E).
  • Stop early if a whole round changes nothing.
  • Negative cycle: if a V-th round still improves something, some loop has negative total cost, and you could go round it forever.

blocks.title: Bellman-Ford on the rebate road map

blocks.q: Why are V − 1 rounds of Bellman-Ford enough (with no negative cycle)?

opts.t: A shortest path has at most V − 1 edges, and round i fixes every path of up to i edges
Because the graph is a tree
It's a guess that usually works

blocks.why: A shortest path never repeats a node, so it has at most V − 1 edges.

blocks.title: bellman_ford

blocks.html:
To get the shortest distance between every pair, Floyd-Warshall builds an n × n table. It asks, for each node k in turn: "does going through k improve the route from i to j?"

  • d[i][j] = min(d[i][j], d[i][k] + d[k][j])
  • k must be the outer loop. After pass k, d[i][j] is the best route whose middle stops all come from nodes 0..k.
  • O(n³): great up to a few hundred nodes, and negative edges are fine. A negative d[i][i] at the end means a negative cycle.

blocks.q: Explain Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall: when Dijkstra fails, how each works, their costs, negative cycles and the hop-limited variant.
blocks.a: Dijkstra assumes non-negative weights, so a negative edge can lower a node it already declared final. Bellman-Ford instead relaxes every edge in rounds; after round i, all shortest paths of at most i edges are correct, so V − 1 rounds suffice, giving O(V·E), and it can stop early when a round changes nothing. If a further round still improves a distance, a negative cycle is reachable and shortest paths are undefined. Running exactly k + 1 rounds while reading from a copy of the previous round gives the cheapest path with at most k + 1 edges, as in cheapest flights within k stops. Floyd-Warshall computes all pairs in O(n³) with a table: for each middle node k (the outer loop), it sets d[i][j] to the minimum of d[i][j] and d[i][k] + d[k][j]; a negative diagonal entry means a negative cycle. The same triple loop with booleans gives transitive closure, and with max and multiplication gives best exchange rates; using minus log rates turns arbitrage into negative cycle detection.

chapters.title: Minimum spanning trees
chapters.tagline: Connect everything for the least total cost
goals: Say what a spanning tree is and why the cheapest one has n − 1 edges
Build one with Kruskal's algorithm (sort + union-find)
Build one with Prim's algorithm (a heap growing from one node)
Use the tricks: a virtual node, pre-joined edges, stopping early to cluster

sections.title: The cheapest way to connect everything

blocks.html: You have places and possible links between them, each with a cost: cables, roads, pipes. You want every place connected (directly or through others) for the least total cost. Any extra link would close a loop, and you could drop the dearest link in that loop and stay connected. So the answer has no cycles: it's a tree that touches every node, with exactly n − 1 edges. That's a minimum spanning tree (MST).

blocks.name: ds-mst
blocks.title: Fibre for eight villages: cheapest first against Kruskal
blocks.goal: Run cheapest first, no check to the end, then run Kruskal + union-find and compare the cost.
blocks.intro: Click a village to see the cables it could have.

blocks.html:
Kruskal's algorithm:

  1. Sort the edges by cost.
  2. Go through them in order. If the two ends are in different groups (union-find from chapter 22), take the edge and merge the groups; otherwise skip it.
  3. Stop after n − 1 edges.

O(E log E), and the sort is most of it.

Why is greedy safe here? The cut property: split the nodes into any two sides; the cheapest edge crossing between them belongs to some MST. Every edge Kruskal takes is the cheapest one joining its group to the rest.

blocks.q: A connected graph has 50 nodes. How many edges does any spanning tree of it have?
blocks.why: A tree on n nodes always has n − 1 edges.

blocks.title: kruskal
blocks.prompt: Return the total cost of a minimum spanning tree of n nodes 0..n-1 with undirected edges (a, b, w), or -1 if the graph isn't connected. Use the DSU from the prelude.
blocks.tests:
assert mst_cost(4, [(0, 1, 1), (1, 2, 2), (0, 2, 2), (2, 3, 3)]) == 6
assert mst_cost(3, [(0, 1, 1), (0, 1, 2), (1, 0, 3)]) == -1
assert mst_cost(4, [(0, 1, 1), (1, 2, 1), (0, 2, 1), (2, 3, 5), (1, 3, 4)]) == 6
assert mst_cost(1, []) == 0
random.seed(5)
n = 3000
edges = [(i, i + 1, random.randint(1, 100)) for i in range(n - 1)] + [(random.randrange(n), random.randrange(n), random.randint(1, 100)) for _ in range(60000)]
out, t = timed(mst_cost, n, edges)
assert t < 1.5, f"too slow: {t:.2f}s"
hints: The starter just takes the n − 1 cheapest edges, even when some of them form a loop. Only take an edge when union says it merged two groups.
blocks.starter:
def mst_cost(n, edges):
    return sum(w for _, _, w in sorted(edges, key=lambda e: e[2])[:n - 1])

blocks.title: sort_key_bug

hints: key=lambda e: e[2], or store edges as (w, a, b) from the start.

blocks.html: Prim grows one tree from a start node. A heap holds the edges leaving the tree; pop the cheapest, and if it reaches a node not yet in the tree, add that node and push its edges. It's Dijkstra's loop with "edge weight" instead of "distance so far". With a heap it's O(E log V); on a dense graph (every pair connected) a simple O(n²) array version is faster still.

blocks.title: connect_points
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 1584, asked at Amazon and Microsoft. Points on a plane; connecting two costs their Manhattan distance |x1 − x2| + |y1 − y2|. Return the minimum cost to connect them all. Every pair is a possible edge (a dense graph), so use the O(n²) Prim: keep best[v] = cheapest link from the tree to v, and each round add the closest outside point.
hints: No edge list at all: compute distances on the fly. n rounds, each scanning n points: O(n²).
blocks.solution:
def min_cost(points):
    n = len(points)
    best = [float("inf")] * n
    best[0] = 0
    inside = [False] * n
    total = 0
    for _ in range(n):
        v = min((i for i in range(n) if not inside[i]), key=lambda i: best[i])
        inside[v] = True
        total += best[v]
        x, y = points[v]
        for i in range(n):
            if not inside[i]:
                d = abs(points[i][0] - x) + abs(points[i][1] - y)
                if d < best[i]:
                    best[i] = d
    return total

blocks.prompt: A Codeforces and interview classic. Connect all n towns with roads chosen from edges (a, b, height_limit_cost). An MST also minimises the largest edge, so it's the last edge Kruskal takes.

blocks.q: Why does an MST never contain a cycle?

opts.t: Trees are required by definition, for no reason
In a cycle you could drop the most expensive edge and still be connected, for less

blocks.why: Every cycle has a removable edge.

blocks.q: What does Kruskal use union-find for?

opts.t: To check whether an edge's two ends are already connected

blocks.why: Same root means the edge would close a loop.

blocks.q: How is Prim's algorithm like Dijkstra's?

opts.t: Both grow from a start node with a heap; Prim keys on the single edge weight, Dijkstra on the total distance

blocks.why: Turning a node cost into an edge cost is a common trick.

blocks.q: Explain minimum spanning trees: what they are, Kruskal and Prim, why greedy is correct, their costs and the common tricks.
blocks.a: A spanning tree connects all n nodes of an undirected graph with n − 1 edges and no cycles; a minimum spanning tree has the smallest total weight, because any cycle would have a most expensive edge that could be dropped. Kruskal sorts edges by weight and takes each one whose ends are in different union-find groups, skipping edges that would close a loop, in O(E log E). Prim grows a tree from one node with a heap of edges leaving it, adding the cheapest edge to a new node, in O(E log V), or O(n²) with an array on dense graphs such as all pairs of points. Greedy works because of the cut property: the cheapest edge crossing any split of the nodes belongs to some MST. An MST also minimises the largest edge, giving bottleneck answers. Tricks include a virtual source node so node costs become edges (wells), pre-joining free existing links, and stopping Kruskal at k groups for single-linkage clustering with maximum spacing.

chapters.title: Tries
chapters.tagline: A tree of letters for prefixes, autocomplete and XOR tricks
goals: Build a trie with insert, search and starts_with
Answer prefix questions without scanning the whole dictionary
Search a trie with wildcards and from a grid
Use a binary trie to find the maximum XOR pair
chapters.prelude:
import time
import random

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html: A trie (said "try", from re*trie*val) stores strings letter by letter. Each node is a dictionary from a letter to a child node, plus a flag saying "a word ends here". Words that share a beginning share the path for it: "car", "card", "care" and "careful" all walk through c → a → r.

blocks.name: ds-trie
blocks.title: Autocomplete: scanning every word against walking a trie
blocks.goal: Run scan every word to the end, then run walk the trie and compare the steps.
blocks.intro: Click a trie node to see the prefix it spells.

blocks.html:
• Insert or search a word of length L: O(L), no matter how many words are stored.
  • All words with a prefix: walk the prefix (O(|prefix|)), then collect everything below.
  • Memory is the cost: one small dictionary per node. Sharing prefixes helps.

blocks.title: A trie made of nested dictionaries

blocks.q: How long does it take to check whether a word of length 8 is in a trie holding a million words?
blocks.why: The dictionary's size never enters into it.

blocks.title: trie_class
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 208, asked at Google, Amazon and Microsoft. Build a Trie with insert(word), search(word) (is this exact word stored?) and starts_with(prefix) (is any stored word starting with it?).
blocks.tests:
t = Trie()
t.insert("apple")
assert t.search("apple") and not t.search("app")
assert t.starts_with("app") and not t.starts_with("b")
t.insert("app")
assert t.search("app")
t2 = Trie()
for i in range(20000):
    t2.insert("word%05d" % i)
def many():

out, sec = timed(many)
assert out == 4000
assert sec < 0.4, f"too slow: {sec:.2f}s (scanning every word for every query?)"

assert not search("app")

insert(r, "hi")

blocks.prompt: LeetCode 1268, asked at Amazon. After each letter of typed, suggest up to 3 product names starting with what's typed so far, in alphabetical order. Return the list of suggestion lists. Build a trie where each node keeps the (up to) 3 smallest words passing through it, by inserting the words in sorted order.

prods = ["mobile", "mouse", "moneypot", "monitor", "mousepad"]
assert suggest(prods, "mouse") == [["mobile", "moneypot", "monitor"], ["mobile", "moneypot", "monitor"], ["mouse", "mousepad"], ["mouse", "mousepad"], ["mouse", "mousepad"]]
assert suggest(["havana"], "tatiana") == [[]] * 7
assert suggest(["bags", "baggage", "banner", "box", "cloths"], "bags") == [["baggage", "bags", "banner"], ["baggage", "bags", "banner"], ["baggage", "bags"], ["bags"]]

blocks.tests:

assert replace(["a", "b", "c"], "aadsfasf absbs bbab cadsfafs") == "a a b c"

Return all words (sorted) that can be spelled in the letter board by moving between neighbouring cells (up, down, left, right), using each cell at most once per word. Put the words in a trie and run one DFS from each cell, following the trie as you go, so all the words are searched together.

board = [list("oaan"), list("etae"), list("ihkr"), list("iflv")]
assert find_words(board, ["oath", "pea", "eat", "rain"]) == ["eat", "oath"]
assert find_words([list("ab"), list("cd")], ["abcb"]) == []
assert find_words([list("ab"), list("cd")], ["abdc", "acdb", "ad"]) == ["abdc", "acdb"]
hints: Mark a cell "#" while it's on the current path and restore it after: that's backtracking (chapter 27). If the next letter isn't a child of the current trie node, stop immediately.

blocks.title: max_xor_pair
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 421, and a Codeforces favourite. Return the largest a ^ b over all pairs in nums (values below 2³¹). Comparing every pair is O(n²). Instead, insert each number's bits (from bit 30 down to 0) into a binary trie; for each number, walk down choosing the opposite bit whenever that child exists, since a 1 in a high bit beats anything in the lower ones.
blocks.tests:
assert max_xor([3, 10, 5, 25, 2, 8]) == 28
assert max_xor([14, 70, 53, 83, 49, 91, 36, 80, 92, 51, 66, 70]) == 127
assert max_xor([7]) == 0
random.seed(8)
nums = random.sample(range(1, 2 ** 30), 8000)
out, sec = timed(max_xor, nums)
assert sec < 0.8, f"too slow: {sec:.2f}s"
hints: Greedy from the top bit works because 2^i is bigger than all the lower bits added together.
blocks.starter:
def max_xor(nums):
    return max((a ^ b for a in nums for b in nums), default=0)

blocks.q: What does a trie node store?

opts.t: Its children by letter, plus a flag for "a word ends here"

blocks.why: The path from the root spells the prefix; the node doesn't need to store it.

blocks.q: Why is the end-of-word flag needed?

opts.t: Without it, a prefix like "app" would look like a stored word just because "apple" is

blocks.why: Reaching a node proves a prefix exists, not a word.

blocks.q: Which question is a trie best at, compared with a hash set of words?

opts.t: Which stored words start with this prefix?

blocks.why: A hash set must scan everything for a prefix; a trie walks straight to it.

blocks.q: In the maximum XOR trie, why go from the highest bit down?

opts.t: A 1 in a higher bit is worth more than all lower bits together, so greedy from the top is optimal
Tries must be built that way

blocks.why: Bit i is worth 2^i, more than 2^(i−1) + … + 1.

blocks.q: Searching many words in a letter grid: why one trie instead of searching each word separately?

opts.t: One DFS follows all words at once and stops as soon as the path isn't a prefix of any of them

blocks.why: Shared prefixes are explored once, and dead paths die early.

blocks.q: Explain tries: their structure, operation costs, why they beat a hash set for prefixes, and the main problems they solve.
blocks.a: A trie stores strings letter by letter in a tree: each node maps letters to child nodes and has an end-of-word flag, so words that share a prefix share the path for it. Inserting or looking up a word of length L takes O(L) regardless of how many words are stored, and finding all words with a prefix walks the prefix and then collects the subtree, which a hash set can only do by scanning every word. The end flag distinguishes stored words from mere prefixes. Nodes can carry extra data such as counts of words passing through or the top suggestions below. Uses include autocomplete and search suggestions, replacing words by their shortest root, wildcard search by branching on every child, searching many words in a grid with a single trie-guided DFS, longest-prefix matching in routing, and a binary trie over bits from the highest down for the maximum XOR pair. The cost is memory, one small map per node.

chapters.title: Backtracking
chapters.tagline: Choose, explore, un-choose, and prune what can't work
goals: Write the choose / explore / un-choose template
Generate subsets, permutations and combinations without duplicates
Prune branches that can't lead to an answer
Solve constraint puzzles such as N-Queens and Sudoku
chapters.prelude:
import time

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html: Many problems ask for every arrangement, or any arrangement, that satisfies some rules: all subsets, all orderings, a valid Sudoku. There's no clever formula, so you search. Backtracking builds a candidate one choice at a time, and the moment a partial candidate breaks a rule, it gives up on it and undoes the last choice.

blocks.name: ds-queens
blocks.title: 6 queens: whole boards against one queen at a time
blocks.goal: Run brute force to the end, then run backtracking and compare the work.
blocks.intro: Each row gets exactly one queen.

blocks.html:
Every backtracking solution has the same skeleton:

`` def explore(state): if state is complete: record it return for each choice: if the choice is allowed: # pruning make the choice # choose explore(new state) # explore undo the choice # un-choose ``

The calls form a tree. The work is the number of nodes you visit, so pruning near the top is what saves you.

blocks.code:
def subsets(nums):
    out, path = [], []
    def go(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            out.append(path[:])
            return
        path.append(nums[i])     # choose: take nums[i]
        go(i + 1)
        path.pop()               # un-choose
        go(i + 1)                # choose: skip nums[i]
    go(0)
    return out
print(subsets([1, 2, 3]))
blocks.title: Every subset of [1, 2, 3], two ways to choose

opts.t: 2ⁿ: each item is either in or out

blocks.why: Two choices per item, independently.

def permute(nums):
    return [nums[i:] + nums[:i] for i in range(len(nums))]

assert len(subsets([1, 2, 3, 4])) == 16
assert [3] in subsets([1, 2, 3])

blocks.solution:
def subsets(nums):
    out, path = [], []
    def go(i):
        if i == len(nums):
            out.append(path[:])
            return
        path.append(nums[i])
        go(i + 1)
        path.pop()
        go(i + 1)
    go(0)
    return out

blocks.html:
Pruning means refusing to enter a branch that can't produce an answer. Good prunes:

  • Bound: the running total already exceeds the target (and numbers are positive).
  • Sorted input: once one candidate is too big, every later one is too.
  • Duplicates: after sorting, skip a value equal to the previous one at the same depth.
  • Constraints: a queen that's already attacked, a Sudoku digit already in the row.

blocks.title: combination_sum
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 39, asked at Airbnb, Amazon and Uber. Distinct positive candidates; return every combination (each sorted, list in sorted order) that sums to target, where a number may be used any number of times. Sort, and stop the loop as soon as a candidate is bigger than what's left.
hints: Recursing with i (not i + 1) lets the same number be reused; starting from i (not 0) stops [2, 3] and [3, 2] both appearing.
blocks.starter:
def combos(candidates, target):
    return [[c] for c in candidates if c == target]

blocks.q: Explain backtracking: the template, how it generates subsets, permutations and combinations, what pruning is, and how it solves constraint puzzles.
blocks.a: Backtracking searches a tree of choices by building a candidate one step at a time: choose an option, recurse to explore what follows, then un-choose it to restore the state before trying the next option, recording the candidate when it is complete. Subsets come from deciding in or out for each item (2ⁿ of them), permutations from picking any unused item for each position with a used array (n!), and combinations from only picking items after the last one chosen so order doesn't repeat. Record a copy of the path, not the shared list. The cost is the number of tree nodes visited, so pruning, refusing to enter branches that cannot succeed, is what makes it fast: break when a sorted candidate exceeds the remaining target, skip equal values at the same depth to avoid duplicates, and reject moves that break constraints, such as queens sharing a column or diagonal (tracked with sets of c, r − c and r + c) or Sudoku digits already in the row, column or box. Counting solutions can stop early at a limit, as when checking a puzzle is unique.

chapters.title: Dynamic programming in one dimension
chapters.tagline: Same recursion, but every answer is worked out once
goals: Spot overlapping subproblems in a recursion
Turn a recursion into a memo, then into a bottom-up table
Define a DP by its state, transition, base cases and order
Shrink a 1D table to a couple of variables
chapters.prelude:
import time
import bisect
from functools import lru_cache

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
Backtracking (chapter 27) explores every branch. Sometimes different branches lead to the same smaller question. How many ways are there to climb 10 stairs, 1 or 2 at a time? The last move was either 1 step (from stair 9) or 2 steps (from stair 8), so:

ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2), with ways(0) = ways(1) = 1.

Correct, but plain recursion asks for ways(8) from ways(10) and again from ways(9), and the repeats multiply.

blocks.name: ds-stairs
blocks.title: Ten stairs: plain recursion against a table
blocks.goal: Run plain recursion to the end, then run table, bottom up and compare the work.
blocks.intro: Bar height counts how many times each ways(i) was worked out.

blocks.html:
Dynamic programming (DP) = a recursion whose subproblems overlap, plus storing each answer the first time. Two ways to store:

  • Memoisation (top down): keep the recursion, add a dictionary (or @lru_cache). Return the saved answer if there is one.
  • Tabulation (bottom up): fill an array from the base cases upwards, so everything dp[i] needs is already there.

blocks.title: The same recurrence, three ways

blocks.q: What makes a problem a good fit for dynamic programming?

opts.t: Its recursion asks the same smaller questions many times, and each answer can be built from smaller answers

blocks.why: Overlapping subproblems plus optimal substructure.

blocks.html:
Every DP answers four questions. Write them down before coding:

  1. State: what does dp[i] mean, in words? ("the number of ways to reach stair i")
  2. Transition: how is dp[i] built from smaller states?
  3. Base cases: the smallest states, known directly.
  4. Order: fill so every state you read is already filled.

blocks.q: What's the difference between memoisation and tabulation?

opts.t: Memoisation keeps the recursion and caches answers (top down); tabulation fills an array from the base cases up

blocks.why: Same states and same transitions, different order of filling.

blocks.q: Plain recursion for ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2) takes roughly how long?
blocks.why: The call count grows like the Fibonacci numbers themselves.

blocks.q: House Robber's dp[i] reads only dp[i − 1] and dp[i − 2]. What does that let you do?

opts.t: Keep two variables instead of an array: O(1) extra space
Process the houses in any order

blocks.why: When a state only looks back k steps, keep a window of k values.

blocks.q: In word break, what does dp[i] mean?

opts.t: The number of words in s
Whether the first i characters can be split into dictionary words
The longest word ending at i

blocks.why: Writing the state in words is half the solution.

blocks.q: Why does max product subarray track the smallest product too?

opts.t: Multiplying by a negative number turns the smallest product into the largest

blocks.why: The state is a pair: (biggest, smallest) product ending here.

sections.title: Real-world project: a courier's shift planner

blocks.title: Pick the best set of delivery jobs
blocks.client: A courier app that offers drivers overlapping paid jobs during a shift and wants to suggest the most profitable plan
blocks.brief: Build planner.py. Each job is (start, end, pay); a driver can do jobs back to back (one may start when the last ends) but never two at once. Sort jobs by end time. dp[i] = best pay using the first i jobs: either skip job i, or take it plus the best from the jobs that end by its start (find that index with binary search). Then walk back through the table to list which jobs to take.
blocks.why: Ad slot scheduling, room and equipment booking, CPU job selection and broadcast scheduling are all weighted interval scheduling. Greedy (best-paid first) is fast but wrong; DP is fast and right.
milestones: Find the last compatible job with bisect
Walk back to recover the chosen jobs
stretch: Allow a travel gap between jobs
Let each driver work at most k jobs

blocks.title: max_pay
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 1235, a hard one asked at Google, DoorDash and Amazon. Return the most pay from non-overlapping jobs (start, end, pay). A job starting at time t can follow one ending at t. Sort by end; bisect_right(ends, start, 0, i) counts the earlier jobs ending by start.
hints: The starter is greedy by pay: one big job can block three smaller ones worth more.
blocks.solution:
def max_pay(jobs):
    jobs = sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[1])
    ends = [e for _, e, _ in jobs]
    dp = [0] * (len(jobs) + 1)
    for i, (s, e, p) in enumerate(jobs):
        k = bisect.bisect_right(ends, s, 0, i)
        dp[i + 1] = max(dp[i], dp[k] + p)
    return dp[-1]

blocks.title: chosen_jobs
blocks.prompt: Return the jobs in a best plan, sorted by end time. Fill the same table as max_pay, then walk back from i = n: if dp[i] == dp[i − 1] the job wasn't needed, so skip it; otherwise take job i − 1 and jump to its compatible index.
hints: Store each job's compatible index during the fill so the walk back is a simple loop.
blocks.starter:
def chosen_jobs(jobs):
    return sorted(jobs, key=lambda j: j[1])

blocks.q: Explain dynamic programming in one dimension: when it applies, memoisation versus tabulation, the four parts of a DP, and how to save space.
blocks.a: Dynamic programming applies when a recursion asks the same smaller questions repeatedly (overlapping subproblems) and each answer can be built from smaller answers (optimal substructure), like counting stair climbs with ways(n) = ways(n − 1) + ways(n − 2), which plain recursion solves in exponential time. Storing each answer the first time makes every subproblem cost O(1) after that. Memoisation keeps the recursion and caches results top down (a dict or lru_cache); tabulation fills an array from the base cases upwards with a loop, avoiding deep recursion. Design a DP by writing the state in words (what dp[i] means), the transition (how dp[i] is built from smaller states, e.g. skip or take for House Robber), the base cases, and an order that fills everything a state reads before it. If dp[i] only reads the last few states, keep just those values for O(1) space. Some states need more than one number, like the max and min product ending at i, and the choices can be recovered by walking back through the table.

chapters.title: Knapsack problems
chapters.tagline: Take it or leave it, for every capacity at once
goals: Fill the 0/1 knapsack table and walk back to find the items
Squash the table to one row, looping capacity the right way
Tell 0/1, unbounded and counting knapsacks apart
Recognise knapsacks in disguise: subset sums, target signs, two budgets
chapters.prelude:
import time

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html:
You have a bag that holds W kg and some items, each with a weight and a value. Take each item whole or not at all (that's the "0/1"). What's the most value that fits?

Trying every subset is 2ⁿ. Grabbing the best value per kilo first is fast, but watch what it does here:

blocks.name: ds-knap
blocks.title: A 10 kg bag: greedy against a DP table
blocks.goal: Run greedy to the end, then run DP table and compare the bags.
blocks.intro: Four items; each is in the bag or not.

blocks.html:
The DP state is two numbers: dp[i][c] = the best value using only the first i items with capacity c. For item i (weight w, value v):

  • skip it: dp[i − 1][c]
  • take it (if w ≤ c): dp[i − 1][c − w] + v

dp[i][c] is the larger. The answer is dp[n][W]. That's n × W cells, so O(n·W) time: fast when W is small, which is why it's called pseudo-polynomial.

blocks.title: The table, then the walk back

blocks.q: Why does the 0/1 knapsack take O(n · W) time?

opts.t: There are n × W table cells, and each is a max of two numbers
It's a binary search over W

blocks.why: One cell per (items so far, capacity).

blocks.html: Each row of the table only reads the row above it, so one row is enough, if you loop capacity downwards. Going down, dp[c − w] still holds the previous row's value when you read it.

blocks.q: In a one-row 0/1 knapsack, why must capacity loop downwards?

opts.t: So dp[c − w] still holds the previous item's row, and the current item isn't used twice

blocks.why: Upwards makes it the unbounded knapsack.

blocks.q: Coin change II counts combinations. Which loop goes outside?

opts.t: Either, the answer is the same

blocks.why: Amounts outside counts orderings (permutations) instead.

blocks.q: Why is O(n · W) called pseudo-polynomial?

opts.t: It's polynomial in the value W, but W can be exponential in the number of digits used to write it
It only works for small n

blocks.why: A capacity of 10¹⁸ makes the table impossible.

blocks.q: "Can nums be split into two equal-sum halves?" becomes which knapsack?

opts.t: 0/1 with true/false cells: can a subset reach sum / 2?

blocks.why: Equal halves means one half sums to exactly total / 2.

blocks.q: How do you recover which items the 0/1 knapsack took?

opts.t: Walk back from dp[n][W]: if dp[i][c] differs from dp[i − 1][c], item i was taken, so subtract its weight
Store the items in each cell

blocks.why: The full 2D table is needed for this walk; the one-row version loses it.

sections.title: Real-world project: a marketing budget planner

blocks.title: Spend the budget where it reaches the most people
blocks.client: A small marketing agency choosing which ad placements to buy for a client with a fixed budget
blocks.brief: Build budget.py. Each placement has a cost (in £100 units) and an estimated reach. Pick placements (each at most once) to maximise reach within budget, and report which ones. Then answer the reverse question the client always asks: "what's the least we can spend to reach at least N people?", which is a knapsack where the reach is the capacity.
blocks.why: Ad buying, cloud cost planning, picking features for a release, cargo loading and portfolio-style selection under a cap are knapsacks. Planners show the chosen set, not just the number.
milestones: Walk back for the chosen placements
Minimum cost to reach a target
stretch: Some placements require another one (bundles)
Two budgets at once: money and staff hours

blocks.title: plan_budget

hints: Swap the roles: reach is the "capacity", cost is what you minimise. Clamp at 0 so overshooting is allowed.

def min_spend(costs, reach, target):

blocks.q: Explain the knapsack family: the 0/1 table and its transition, the one-row trick and loop direction, how to recover the items, and the unbounded and counting variants.
blocks.a: In the 0/1 knapsack each item is taken whole or not, and greedy by value per weight can fail. The state dp[i][c] is the best value using the first i items with capacity c; it is the larger of skipping the item, dp[i − 1][c], and taking it if it fits, dp[i − 1][c − w] + v. There are n × W cells, so it is O(nW), pseudo-polynomial because W can be huge. Since each row only reads the row above, one row is enough if capacity loops downwards, so dp[c − w] still holds the previous row and no item is used twice; looping upwards instead gives the unbounded knapsack, where items repeat, as in fewest coins. Walking back from dp[n][W] in the full table recovers the items: if a cell differs from the one above, that item was taken. Counting versions replace max with +; for combinations of coins the coin loop goes outside the amount loop. Many problems are knapsacks in disguise: partitioning into equal halves is a true/false subset-sum knapsack to half the total, target sum counts ways per running sum, two budgets give a 2D capacity, and minimum cost for a target value swaps which quantity is the capacity.

chapters.tagline: Each square is built from its neighbours that come first
goals: Fill a grid DP row by row from the squares above and to the left
Handle walls, edges and starting squares cleanly
Choose the fill direction from what each square depends on
Use memoised DFS when the order isn't simply row by row

sections.title: A map, a start and a goal

blocks.html: Many DPs live on a 2D grid. The state is a square (r, c), and the transition reads neighbouring squares that were already filled. When moves only go right or down, a square can only be reached from above or from the left, so row-by-row order works.

blocks.name: ds-pathsum
blocks.title: A 5 × 6 map: greedy steps against grid DP
blocks.goal: Run greedy to the end, then run DP and compare the effort.
blocks.intro: Move only right or down; the number is the effort for each square.

blocks.html:
The cheapest route (LeetCode 64, minimum path sum):

  • State: dp[r][c] = the least effort to reach (r, c).
  • Transition: dp[r][c] = grid[r][c] + min(dp[r − 1][c], dp[r][c − 1]).
  • Base cases: the start square; along the top row and left column there's only one neighbour.
  • Order: row by row, left to right.

blocks.code:
R, C = 3, 4
row = [1] * C
print(row)
for r in range(1, R):
    for c in range(1, C):
        row[c] += row[c - 1]     # from above (old row[c]) + from the left (new row[c-1])
    print(row)
blocks.title: Counting routes on a 3 × 4 grid, one row at a time

g = [[1, 2], [3, 4]]
dp = [[0, 0], [0, 0]]
for r in range(2):

        best = 0 if r == c == 0 else min(dp[r - 1][c] if r else 99, dp[r][c - 1] if c else 99)

blocks.q: Moves go only right or down. Why is row-by-row, left-to-right a valid fill order?

opts.t: It's the order the grid is stored in
Each square only reads the square above (an earlier row) and the square to the left (earlier in this row), which are already filled
It isn't; you must go column by column

blocks.why: The order has to respect what each state depends on.

blocks.title: unique_paths
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 62, asked at Google, Amazon and Bloomberg. A robot on an m × n grid moves only right or down. How many routes go from the top-left to the bottom-right? Keep one row and update it in place.

assert unique_paths(3, 7) == 28
assert unique_paths(3, 2) == 3
assert unique_paths(1, 1) == 1
assert unique_paths(17, 17) == 601080390
hints: Routes into a square = routes into the square above + routes into the square on the left.
blocks.starter:
def unique_paths(m, n):
    return m * n

blocks.title: obstacle_edge_bug
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 63. 1 marks a rock. This solution sets the whole top row and left column to 1 route unless that exact square is a rock, but a rock earlier in the top row blocks every square after it too. Fix it.
hints: Don't special-case the edges with a constant. Use the same rule everywhere and treat squares outside the grid as 0 routes.

blocks.title: Minimum path sum in one row of memory

sections.title: Which way do the arrows point?

blocks.html:
The fill order follows the dependencies, and not every grid goes top-left to bottom-right:

  • Triangle (bottom-up): each number reads the two below it, so start at the last row.
  • Dungeon: the health you need now depends on what's ahead, so fill from the goal backwards.
  • Longest increasing path: you can move in all four directions, so there's no simple order. Use memoised DFS: each square's answer is cached the first time it's asked.

blocks.title: triangle
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 120, asked at Amazon and Apple. From the top of the triangle, move to one of the two numbers directly below each step. Return the smallest total from top to bottom. Work from the bottom row up.
hints: The starter is greedy and walks into the 9s. From the bottom, each number's best total is itself plus the smaller of its two children.

blocks.title: maximal_square
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 221, asked at Google, Amazon and Apple. matrix is a list of strings of "0"/"1". Return the area of the largest square of all 1s. dp[r][c] = side of the biggest square whose bottom-right corner is (r, c).
blocks.tests:
assert maximal_square(["10100", "10111", "11111", "10010"]) == 4
assert maximal_square(["01", "10"]) == 1
assert maximal_square(["0"]) == 0
assert maximal_square(["1111", "1111", "1110"]) == 9
hints: A square of side k ending at a corner needs squares of side k − 1 ending above, to the left, and diagonally. Take the smallest of the three, plus 1. The padded row and column of zeros remove edge checks.
blocks.starter:
def maximal_square(matrix):
    return max(row.count("1") for row in matrix) ** 2

blocks.title: dungeon_game
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 174, a hard one asked at Microsoft and Amazon. A knight starts top-left and must reach the princess bottom-right, moving right or down. Each square changes health by its number; health must stay at least 1 the whole way. Return the minimum starting health. Fill backwards from the goal: need[r][c] = max(1, min(need below, need right) − d[r][c]).
hints: Going forwards, the best route's total doesn't tell you its lowest point along the way. Going backwards, you know exactly how much the rest of the trip will cost.

blocks.title: longest_increasing_path
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 329, a hard one asked at Google, Meta and Amazon. Return the length of the longest strictly increasing path, moving up, down, left or right. Memoised DFS: go(r, c) = longest path starting at (r, c), cached with lru_cache.
blocks.tests:
assert longest_path([[9, 9, 4], [6, 6, 8], [2, 1, 1]]) == 4
assert longest_path([[3, 4, 5], [3, 2, 6], [2, 2, 1]]) == 4
assert longest_path([[1]]) == 1
big = [[r * 20 + (c if r % 2 == 0 else 19 - c) for c in range(20)] for r in range(20)]
out, t = timed(longest_path, big)
assert out == 400
assert t < 1.0, f"too slow: {t:.2f}s"
hints: "Strictly increasing" means a path can never loop, so caching each square's answer is safe. Each square is solved once: O(R·C).

blocks.q: In unique paths, what does each square hold?

opts.t: The number of routes from the start that end on that square

blocks.why: Routes in = routes from above + routes from the left.

blocks.q: Why does the dungeon DP fill from the goal backwards?

opts.t: Because the grid is upside down
The health needed at a square depends on the squares still ahead, which backwards order has already solved

blocks.why: Forwards you'd need to track both the total and the lowest point so far.

blocks.q: Maximal square: what is dp[r][c]?

opts.t: The side of the largest all-1 square whose bottom-right corner is (r, c)
The area of the largest square in the grid

blocks.why: It's 1 + the smallest of the three neighbours above, left and diagonal.

blocks.q: Longest increasing path allows moves in four directions. Why is memoised DFS safe?

opts.t: Strictly increasing paths can't revisit a square, so the dependencies have no cycles

blocks.why: No cycles means every square's answer is final once computed.

blocks.q: How much memory does unique paths need with the one-row trick?

opts.t: O(n): one row, updated left to right

blocks.why: The previous row's value sits in row[c] until you overwrite it.

blocks.q: Explain DP on grids: the state and transition for path counting and minimum path sum, how edges and walls are handled, how to choose the fill direction, and when to use memoised DFS.
blocks.a: In a grid DP the state is a square (r, c), and its value is built from neighbouring squares that are already solved. With moves only right or down, a square is reached from above or from the left, so unique paths adds the two counts and minimum path sum adds the square's cost to the smaller of the two, filling row by row; one row of memory is enough because row[c] still holds the value from above until it is overwritten. Edges and walls are handled by one uniform rule: squares outside the grid or blocked count as zero routes or minus infinity, rather than special constants that ignore an earlier wall. The fill order must follow the dependencies: triangle minimum works from the bottom row up, the dungeon fills backwards from the goal because the health needed depends on what lies ahead, and maximal square uses the three neighbours above, left and diagonal. When moves go in every direction but the dependencies cannot cycle, as in a strictly increasing path, memoised DFS caches each square's answer the first time it is asked. Pairing a count table with a best table counts the routes that tie for the best.

chapters.title: DP on strings and sequences
chapters.tagline: Every prefix against every prefix
goals: Fill the two-string table for LCS and edit distance
Walk back through the table to rebuild the alignment or diff
Find the longest increasing subsequence in O(n log n)
Recognise prefix-against-prefix states in matching problems
chapters.prelude:
import time
import bisect

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html: Spell checkers, git diff and DNA alignment all compare two sequences. The trick is to compare prefixes: dp[i][j] answers the question for the first i letters of a and the first j letters of b. Each cell looks at the last letters, a[i − 1] and b[j − 1], and reads three smaller cells.

blocks.name: ds-edit
blocks.title: Turning "sunday" into "saturday"
blocks.goal: Run letter by letter to the end, then run edit distance table and compare.
blocks.intro: Inserts, deletes and replacements each cost 1.

blocks.html:
Edit distance (LeetCode 72):

  • a[i − 1] == b[j − 1]: dp[i][j] = dp[i − 1][j − 1] (keep the letter, free)
  • otherwise, 1 + the cheapest of: dp[i − 1][j − 1] (replace), dp[i − 1][j] (delete from a), dp[i][j − 1] (insert into a)
  • base cases: dp[i][0] = i, dp[0][j] = j

Longest common subsequence (LeetCode 1143) is the same shape: if the last letters match, dp[i − 1][j − 1] + 1; otherwise max(dp[i − 1][j], dp[i][j − 1]).

blocks.title: Both tables side by side

blocks.q: In the edit distance table, moving from the cell above, dp[i − 1][j], means what?

opts.t: Delete a[i − 1]: the first i − 1 letters of a already became the first j letters of b

blocks.why: Above = delete, left = insert, diagonal = replace or match.

blocks.title: longest_common_subsequence
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 1143, asked at Google, Amazon and Microsoft. Return the length of the longest sequence of letters appearing in both strings in the same order (not necessarily next to each other).
blocks.tests:
assert lcs("abcde", "ace") == 3
assert lcs("abc", "abc") == 3
assert lcs("abc", "def") == 0
assert lcs("AGGTAB", "GXTXAYB") == 4
assert lcs("ab", "ba") == 1
hints: Sets ignore order. On a mismatch, one of the two last letters isn't in the answer: drop either and take the better.
blocks.starter:
def lcs(a, b):
    return len(set(a) & set(b))

blocks.title: mismatch_bug
blocks.prompt: On a mismatch this LCS drops both last letters (dp[i − 1][j − 1]), but one of them might still pair with something earlier in the other string. lcs("abcd", "bcda") should be 3 ("bcd"), and it returns 0. Fix it.
blocks.tests:
assert lcs("abcd", "bcda") == 3
assert lcs("abcde", "ace") == 3
assert lcs("sunday", "saturday") == 5
hints: Drop one letter at a time: max(dp[i − 1][j], dp[i][j − 1]).

blocks.title: Edit distance with two rows
blocks.tests:
assert edit_distance("horse", "ros") == 3
assert edit_distance("intention", "execution") == 5
assert edit_distance("", "abc") == 3
assert edit_distance("sunday", "saturday") == 3

blocks.html:
The longest increasing subsequence (LIS) has an O(n²) DP: dp[i] = longest increasing subsequence ending at i = 1 + the best dp[j] with j < i and nums[j] < nums[i]. There's a faster way. Keep tails[k] = the smallest possible last number of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1. tails is always sorted, so each new number finds its place by binary search:

  • bigger than every tail: it extends the longest subsequence (append)
  • otherwise: it replaces the first tail ≥ it (a smaller ending is easier to extend later)

The length of tails is the answer: O(n log n).

blocks.title: lis_fast
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 300, asked at Google, Microsoft and Amazon. Return the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence in O(n log n) with tails and bisect_left.
blocks.tests:
assert lis([10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]) == 4
assert lis([0, 1, 0, 3, 2, 3]) == 4
assert lis([7, 7, 7, 7]) == 1
assert lis([]) == 0
big = [(i * 7919) % 100003 for i in range(100000)]
out, t = timed(lis, big)
assert out == 306
assert t < 1.0, f"too slow: {t:.2f}s"
hints: bisect_left (not right) keeps it strictly increasing: an equal number replaces, it doesn't extend.
blocks.starter:
def lis(nums):
    return 1 + sum(1 for i in range(1, len(nums)) if nums[i] > nums[i - 1]) if nums else 0

blocks.title: longest_palindromic_subsequence
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 516, asked at Amazon and Uber. Return the length of the longest subsequence of s that reads the same backwards. A palindrome in s is a common subsequence of s and s reversed.
blocks.tests:
assert lps("bbbab") == 4
assert lps("cbbd") == 2
assert lps("a") == 1
assert lps("character") == 5
hints: The starter finds the longest palindromic substring (contiguous). A subsequence can skip letters: reuse LCS.

blocks.title: distinct_subsequences
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 115, a hard one asked at Google and Bloomberg. Count the ways t appears in s as a subsequence. Keep dp[j] = ways to form t[:j] so far; for each letter of s, update j from right to left.
blocks.tests:
assert num_distinct("rabbbit", "rabbit") == 3
assert num_distinct("babgbag", "bag") == 5
assert num_distinct("abc", "") == 1
assert num_distinct("a", "b") == 0
assert num_distinct("a" * 30, "a" * 10) == 30045015
hints: Each letter of s can either be used as t[j − 1] (adding dp[j − 1] ways) or skipped. Right to left so a letter isn't used twice, as in the 0/1 knapsack.
blocks.starter:
def num_distinct(s, t):
    return s.count(t)

blocks.title: interleaving_string
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 97, asked at Google and Microsoft. Is c made by interleaving a and b (keeping each one's letter order)? dp[i][j] = "the first i of a and the first j of b make the first i + j of c".
blocks.tests:
assert is_interleave("aabcc", "dbbca", "aadbbcbcac")
assert not is_interleave("aabcc", "dbbca", "aadbbbaccc")
assert is_interleave("", "", "")
assert is_interleave("ab", "cd", "acbd")
assert not is_interleave("ab", "cd", "abdc")
hints: The last letter of c[:i + j] came from a or from b. Check both.
blocks.starter:
def is_interleave(a, b, c):
    return sorted(a + b) == sorted(c)

blocks.title: wildcard_matching
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 44, a hard one asked at Google, Meta and Microsoft. ? matches any one character and matches any sequence (even empty). Does pattern p match all of s? For : either it matches nothing (dp[i][j − 1]) or it eats one more character (dp[i − 1][j]).
blocks.tests:
assert not is_match("aa", "a")
assert is_match("aa", "*")
assert not is_match("cb", "?a")
assert is_match("adceb", "*a*b")
assert not is_match("acdcb", "a*c?b")
assert is_match("", "***")
assert is_match("abc", "a*?*c")
hints: Row 0 is the empty string: only a run of *s matches it.
blocks.starter:
def is_match(s, p):
    return len(s) == len(p) and all(x == y or y == "?" for x, y in zip(s, p))

blocks.q: What does dp[i][j] mean in a two-string DP?

opts.t: The letters at positions i and j
The answer for the first i letters of a and the first j letters of b
The answer for a[i:] and b[j:]

blocks.why: Prefix against prefix. (Suffix against suffix also works, filled backwards.)

blocks.q: How long does edit distance take for strings of lengths n and m?
blocks.why: One O(1) cell per pair of prefixes.

blocks.q: In the fast LIS, what is tails[k]?

opts.t: The k-th number of the answer
The smallest last number of any increasing subsequence of length k + 1 seen so far
The number of subsequences of length k

blocks.why: Smaller tails are easier to extend; tails stays sorted, so binary search works.

blocks.q: Why does lcs(s, reversed(s)) give the longest palindromic subsequence?

opts.t: A palindrome reads the same both ways, so it's a subsequence of s and of s reversed
It only works for even lengths
It doesn't; it gives the longest substring

blocks.why: Any common subsequence of s and its reverse can be arranged as a palindrome of that length.

blocks.q: How do you get the actual diff, not just the number?

opts.t: Walk back through the full table from the corner, following whichever move produced each cell

blocks.why: Same walk-back as the knapsack, choosing between diagonal, up and left.

sections.title: Real-world project: a tiny diff and spell checker

blocks.title: Build `mydiff` and a "did you mean?" helper
blocks.client: A team writing a plain-text notes app that wants change tracking between saved versions and spelling suggestions, without pulling in big libraries
blocks.brief: Build mydiff.py. Given the old and new versions of a file as lists of lines, compute the LCS table over lines and walk it to print a diff: " " for an unchanged line, "- " for a removed one and "+ " for an added one. Then add suggest(word, dictionary, k): the k dictionary words with the smallest edit distance to word, ties broken alphabetically.
blocks.why: git diff, code review tools, document version history, DNA alignment (with scores instead of 1s) and spell checkers run these exact tables.
milestones: Walk it into a list of diff lines
stretch: Group changes into hunks with 3 lines of context, like diff -u
Speed up suggestions by skipping words whose length differs by more than the current kth best distance

blocks.title: diff_lines
blocks.prompt: Return the diff as a list of strings. Fill the LCS table on suffixes (dp[i][j] = LCS of a[i:] and b[j:], filled from the end) so you can walk forwards: if the lines match, keep (" "); else if dp[i + 1][j] >= dp[i][j + 1], remove a[i] ("- "); else add b[j] ("+ "). Leftovers are removals then additions.
blocks.tests:
assert diff(["a", "b", "c", "d"], ["a", "c", "d", "e"]) == ["  a", "- b", "  c", "  d", "+ e"]
assert diff(["x", "y"], ["y", "x"]) == ["- x", "  y", "+ x"]
assert diff([], ["new"]) == ["+ new"]
old = ["import os", "def f():", "    return 1", "print(f())"]
new = ["import os", "import sys", "def f():", "    return 2", "print(f())"]
assert diff(old, new) == ["  import os", "+ import sys", "  def f():", "-     return 1", "+     return 2", "  print(f())"]
hints: The starter loses the order, and it can't show a line that moved. The LCS is the set of lines that stay put.
blocks.starter:
def diff(a, b):
    return ["- " + x for x in a if x not in b] + ["+ " + x for x in b if x not in a]

blocks.title: suggest_words
blocks.prompt: Return the k words from words closest to word by edit distance, ties broken alphabetically. Write a two-row edit distance and sort by (distance, word).
blocks.tests:
D = ["apple", "apply", "ape", "maple", "applet", "angle", "ample", "pale"]
assert suggest("appel", D) == ["ape", "apple", "applet"]
assert suggest("aple", D, 2) == ["ample", "ape"]
assert suggest("zzz", ["a"], 3) == ["a"]

blocks.starter:
def suggest(word, words, k=3):
    return sorted(words, key=lambda w: abs(len(w) - len(word)))[:k]

blocks.prompt: From memory: LeetCode 712. Return the smallest total of character codes (ord) you must delete from a and b to make them equal. It's LCS-shaped, but a mismatch costs the deleted letter's code.
blocks.tests:
assert min_delete_sum("sea", "eat") == 231
assert min_delete_sum("delete", "leet") == 403
assert min_delete_sum("a", "a") == 0
assert min_delete_sum("", "ab") == 195
hints: Base cases: against an empty string you delete everything. Matching last letters are free.

blocks.q: Explain DP on strings: the prefix-against-prefix state, the edit distance and LCS transitions, how to rebuild the alignment, and the fast longest increasing subsequence.
blocks.a: Comparing two sequences uses dp[i][j] for the first i items of one and the first j of the other, deciding by the last items and reading three smaller cells, so it costs O(n·m). Edit distance keeps a matching letter for free from the diagonal; otherwise it is one plus the cheapest of replace (diagonal), delete (above) and insert (left), with base cases i and j against the empty string. Longest common subsequence adds one on the diagonal for a match and otherwise takes the better of dropping either last letter; dropping both is a bug. Only two rows are needed for the number, but the full table lets you walk back from the corner (or forward on a suffix table) to rebuild the alignment, which is how a line diff prints kept, removed and added lines. The same state solves palindromic subsequences (LCS with the reverse), counting subsequences, interleaving and wildcard matching, where a star either matches nothing or eats one more character. The longest increasing subsequence can be found in O(n log n) by keeping tails, the smallest ending value for each length, which stays sorted so each number is placed with bisect_left.

chapters.title: Interval DP
chapters.tagline: Solve every stretch, shortest first
goals: Recognise problems whose state is a stretch i..j
Try every split point and combine the two sides
Fill by interval length so the smaller stretches are ready
Use the "last action" trick for burst balloons and cutting problems
chapters.prelude:
import time

def timed(fn, *args):
