sections.title: When the answer depends on a stretch

blocks.html:
Some problems keep combining neighbours: merging files, multiplying a chain of matrices, bursting balloons, cutting a stick. Whatever you do, the final step joins a left part and a right part. So the state is a stretch i..j:

dp[i][j] = best over k of ( dp[i][k] + dp[k + 1][j] + cost of joining them )

blocks.name: ds-piles
blocks.title: Merging six files: greedy against interval DP
blocks.goal: Run greedy to the end, then run interval DP and compare the total cost.
blocks.intro: Merging two neighbouring files costs their combined size.

blocks.html: Order matters. dp[i][j] reads shorter stretches inside it, so fill by length: all stretches of length 2, then 3, and so on. (Going i from high to low and j from low to high also works.) There are O(n²) stretches and O(n) splits each: O(n³), fine for n up to a few hundred.

blocks.title: Merge cost, filled by length

blocks.code:
s = "abba"
n = len(s)
pal = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]
for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1):
    for j in range(i, n):
        pal[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] and (j - i < 2 or pal[i + 1][j - 1])
print(sum(map(sum, pal)))

blocks.q: Why fill interval DP by length?

opts.t: Every stretch is built from strictly shorter stretches inside it, so those must be filled first

blocks.why: Row-by-row (i increasing) would read dp[k + 1][j] before it exists.

blocks.title: merge_cost
blocks.prompt: Merging two neighbouring piles costs their combined size; keep merging until one pile is left. Return the cheapest total. Use prefix sums for the size of a stretch and fill dp by length.
blocks.tests:
assert merge_cost([7, 3, 7, 2, 9, 9]) == 93
assert merge_cost([3, 2, 4, 1]) == 20
assert merge_cost([5]) == 0
assert merge_cost([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]) == 102
hints: The starter is the sim's greedy. In the DP the last merge joins i..k with k + 1..j, and it costs the size of the whole stretch whatever k is.
blocks.starter:
def merge_cost(piles):
    piles, cost = piles[:], 0
    while len(piles) > 1:
        k = min(range(len(piles) - 1), key=lambda k: piles[k] + piles[k + 1])
        s = piles[k] + piles[k + 1]
        cost += s
        piles[k:k + 2] = [s]
    return cost

lines: pal[i][j] = s[i] == s[j] and (j - i < 2 or pal[i + 1][j - 1])

blocks.html:
Two ways to think about k:

  • First split: the stretch is cut into i..k and k + 1..j (merging files, matrix chains).
  • Last action: k is the last thing done inside i..j. For balloons, if k bursts last, its neighbours at that moment are the edges i and j, and the two sides never interact. Thinking "first" here fails because bursting changes who is next to whom.

blocks.title: matrix_chain
blocks.prompt: The classic interview DP. Matrix t has shape dims[t] × dims[t + 1]. Multiplying a p × q by a q × r matrix costs p·q·r. Return the fewest scalar multiplications to multiply the whole chain.
blocks.tests:
assert matrix_chain([10, 30, 5, 60]) == 4500
assert matrix_chain([40, 20, 30, 10, 30]) == 26000
assert matrix_chain([10, 20]) == 0
assert matrix_chain([1, 2, 3, 4, 3]) == 30
hints: The product of matrices i..k has shape dims[i] × dims[k + 1], and k + 1..j has shape dims[k + 1] × dims[j + 1].

blocks.title: burst_balloons
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 312, a hard one asked at Google and Amazon. Bursting balloon k earns left × nums[k] × right, using its current neighbours (1 past either end). Return the most coins. Pad with 1s; dp[i][j] = best for the balloons strictly between i and j, choosing which one k bursts last.
blocks.tests:
assert max_coins([3, 1, 5, 8]) == 167
assert max_coins([1, 5]) == 10
assert max_coins([7]) == 7
assert max_coins([9, 76, 64, 21, 97, 60]) == 1086136
hints: If k is the last balloon between i and j, everything between i and k is already gone, so its neighbours are exactly a[i] and a[j].
blocks.starter:
def max_coins(nums):
    a, total = [1] + nums + [1], 0
    while len(a) > 2:
        k = min(range(1, len(a) - 1), key=lambda k: a[k])
        total += a[k - 1] * a[k] * a[k + 1]
        a.pop(k)
    return total

blocks.prompt: LeetCode 1547, a hard one asked at Google. A stick of length n must be cut at every position in cuts; each cut costs the length of the piece being cut. Return the cheapest total. Sort the cuts, add 0 and n as edges, and choose which cut happens first inside each piece.

assert min_cut_cost(9, [5, 6, 1, 4, 2]) == 22
assert min_cut_cost(5, []) == 0
assert min_cut_cost(10, [5]) == 10

blocks.starter:
def min_cut_cost(n, cuts):
    return n * len(cuts)

blocks.title: predict_the_winner
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 486, asked at Google and Amazon. Two players take turns taking a number from either end of nums; both play perfectly. Return how many points the first player wins by (first minus second; may be negative). dp[i][j] = best margin for whoever moves on nums[i..j].

blocks.title: triangulate_polygon
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 1039, asked at Uber. A convex polygon's corners have values v in order. Split it into triangles; each triangle scores the product of its three corners. Return the smallest total. The edge i–j belongs to exactly one triangle (i, k, j).

def min_score(v):

blocks.q: What's the usual running time of interval DP?

opts.t: O(n³): O(n²) stretches, each trying O(n) split points

blocks.why: Fine for n in the hundreds; too slow for 10⁵.

blocks.q: In burst balloons, why choose the balloon burst last in i..j?

opts.t: Its neighbours at that moment are fixed (i and j), so the two sides are independent

blocks.why: Choosing the first one burst would change who is next to whom.

blocks.q: In matrix chain, what does the cost dims[i] · dims[k + 1] · dims[j + 1] pay for?

opts.t: Multiplying the product of matrices i..k by the product of k + 1..j

blocks.why: Shapes (dims[i] × dims[k+1]) times (dims[k+1] × dims[j+1]).

blocks.q: In "predict the winner", why is it nums[i] − dp[i + 1][j]?

opts.t: After you take nums[i], the opponent plays the rest perfectly and their margin counts against you

blocks.why: One table works for both players because it stores the margin of whoever is to move.

blocks.q: Which of these is not usually interval DP?

opts.t: Shortest path in a graph with non-negative weights

blocks.why: That's Dijkstra (chapter 23).

sections.title: Real-world project: a keyword lookup tree

blocks.title: The fastest lookup tree for a compiler's keywords
blocks.client: A language tool team whose tokenizer checks every word against a fixed list of keywords, millions of times a day, with very uneven frequencies
blocks.brief: Build obst.py. Given sorted keywords and how often each is looked up, build the binary search tree with the smallest expected cost, where a lookup costs the depth of its key (root = 1). For each stretch of keys i..j − 1, try every key r as the root: the cost is the two subtrees plus the total frequency of the stretch (everything gets one level deeper). Store the best root so you can rebuild the tree.
blocks.why: Compilers, static dictionaries and database indexes built once and read constantly benefit from this. It's also the classic interval DP that Knuth sped up to O(n²).
skills: rebuilding the tree from root choices
milestones: Record the best root per stretch
stretch: Knuth's speed-up: the best root lies between the roots of the two neighbouring stretches
Include the cost of unsuccessful searches

blocks.title: obst_cost
blocks.prompt: Return the smallest total Σ freq × depth for a BST over the keys (in the given order) with frequencies freq. Use half-open stretches: dp[i][j] for keys i..j − 1, with dp[i][i] = 0.
blocks.tests:

assert obst_cost([10, 12]) == 32
assert obst_cost([5]) == 5
assert obst_cost([4, 2, 6, 3]) == 26
hints: Making r the root pushes every other key in the stretch one level down, which adds the stretch's total frequency once.

blocks.title: obst_preorder

blocks.tests:
assert obst_preorder(["do", "if", "int"], [34, 8, 50]) == ["int", "do", "if"]
assert obst_preorder(["a", "b", "c", "d"], [4, 2, 6, 3]) == ["c", "a", "b", "d"]
assert obst_preorder(["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"], [1, 1, 1, 1, 1]) == ["b", "a", "d", "c", "e"]

blocks.starter:
def obst_preorder(keys, freq):
    return [k for _, k in sorted(zip(freq, keys), reverse=True)]

blocks.q: Explain interval DP: what the state is, the split-point transition, the fill order, its running time, and the "last action" idea.
blocks.a: Interval DP solves problems where neighbours keep being combined, so the final step always joins a left part and a right part; the state dp[i][j] is the best answer for the stretch i..j. The transition tries every split point k and combines dp[i][k] and dp[k + 1][j] with the cost of joining them, such as the size of the stretch when merging files or dims[i]·dims[k + 1]·dims[j + 1] for a matrix chain. Each stretch reads strictly shorter stretches, so it is filled by length (or i decreasing with j increasing); filling rows with i increasing reads cells that are not yet computed. There are O(n²) stretches with O(n) splits each, so O(n³). When an action changes the neighbours, as in burst balloons, choose k as the last action in the stretch so its neighbours are the fixed edges and the two sides stay independent; cutting a stick chooses the first cut instead. Two-player games taking from the ends store the margin for whoever moves, nums[i] − dp[i + 1][j]. Recording the best split per stretch rebuilds the structure, such as an optimal binary search tree.

chapters.title: Bitmask DP
chapters.tagline: When the state is "which ones are used", store it in the bits of an integer
goals: Store a set of up to ~20 items as the bits of one integer
Test, add and remove items with &, | and ^
Solve assignment and tour problems over subsets in O(2ⁿ · n) or O(2ⁿ · n²)
Search (node, set) states with BFS
chapters.prelude:
import time
from collections import deque

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

sections.title: Remember the set, not the order

blocks.html: Some problems ask for the best order or matching of a few items: visit every shop, give each worker one job, split numbers into equal groups. Backtracking tries all n! orders. But often the future only depends on which items are already used (and maybe where you are now), not on the order you used them in. There are only 2ⁿ sets, far fewer than n!.

blocks.name: ds-tsp
blocks.title: A van, a depot and nine shops
blocks.goal: Run brute force to the end, then run Held-Karp and compare the work.
blocks.intro: Find the shortest round trip from the depot through every shop.

blocks.html:
A set of items 0..n − 1 fits in one integer: bit j is 1 if item j is in the set.

OperationCode
is j in m?m >> j & 1 (or m & (1 << j))
add j`m(1 << j)`
remove jm & ~(1 << j), or m ^ (1 << j) if it's in
size of the setbin(m).count("1")
all n items(1 << n) − 1

Held-Karp (the travelling salesperson): dp[m][last] = the shortest path that starts at the depot, visits exactly the shops in m, and ends at last. Extend it to any shop nxt not in m. Answer: min over last of dp[full][last] + d[last][depot]. That's O(2ⁿ · n²): n = 20 is about 400 million simple steps in C++, and n! for n = 20 is 2.4 × 10¹⁸.

blocks.code:
m = 0
for j in [0, 3, 4]:
    m |= 1 << j
print(bin(m), m)
print([j for j in range(6) if m >> j & 1])
print("has 3:", m >> 3 & 1, " has 2:", m >> 2 & 1)
m ^= 1 << 3
print("removed 3:", bin(m), "size", bin(m).count("1"))
print("all of 0..5:", bin((1 << 6) - 1))
blocks.title: Sets as integers

blocks.code:
m = 0b1011
subs = []
s = m
while s:
    subs.append(bin(s))
    s = (s - 1) & m
print(subs)

blocks.q: Why is (set visited, current shop) enough state for the shortest tour?

opts.t: What's left to do depends only on which shops remain and where you are, not on the order you came
Because the graph is a tree
It isn't; you need the whole path

blocks.why: Two partial routes with the same set and the same end are interchangeable, so keep the shorter.

blocks.title: assign_jobs
blocks.prompt: The assignment problem. cost[w][j] is what worker w charges for job j. Give each worker exactly one job (all different). Return the cheapest total. dp[m] = cheapest way to give jobs m to the first popcount(m) workers.
hints: The next worker to assign is the one numbered popcount(m), so the worker isn't part of the state. Greedy lets the first worker grab a job someone else needed more.
blocks.starter:
def assign(cost):
    used, total = set(), 0
    for row in cost:
        j = min((j for j in range(len(row)) if j not in used), key=lambda j: row[j])
        used.add(j)
        total += row[j]
    return total

blocks.title: membership_bug
blocks.prompt: This assignment DP tests "is job j used?" with m & j, which compares the numbers m and j bit by bit instead of looking at bit j. Job 0 always looks free, so it gets handed out again and again. Fix the test.
hints: 1 << j is the number with only bit j set. Test against that.

blocks.title: Every non-empty submask of a mask
blocks.tests:

assert submasks(0b100) == [4]
assert submasks(0) == []

blocks.html: Iterating every submask of every mask costs O(3ⁿ) in total (each item is out, in the mask only, or in both), which is fine for n ≤ 15 or so.

blocks.title: shortest_tour
blocks.prompt: Held-Karp. d is an n × n distance matrix; start and end at city 0 and visit every other city once. Return the length of the shortest tour. Use dp[m][last] over the cities 1..n − 1.
hints: The starter always drives to the nearest unvisited city: fast, often wrong (456 here). Push forward from each state: try every city not yet in m.
blocks.starter:
def tour(d):
    n, cur, seen, total = len(d), 0, {0}, 0
    while len(seen) < n:
        j = min((j for j in range(n) if j not in seen), key=lambda j: d[cur][j])
        total += d[cur][j]
        seen.add(j)
        cur = j
    return total + d[cur][0]

blocks.title: partition_k_subsets
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 698, asked at LinkedIn and Amazon. Can nums be split into k groups with equal sums? Let t = sum / k. dp[m] = the sum in the current, unfinished group after using the numbers in m (that's the total mod t), or -1 if m can't be reached. Add a number only if it fits in the current group.
blocks.tests:

assert not can_partition_k([1, 2, 3, 4], 3)
assert not can_partition_k([2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5], 4)
assert can_partition_k([1, 1, 1, 1], 2)
assert can_partition_k([10, 10, 10, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 7, 6, 6, 6], 3)

blocks.starter:
def can_partition_k(nums, k):
    return sum(nums) % k == 0

blocks.q: What does m >> j & 1 tell you?

opts.t: The number m divided by j
Whether bit j of m is set, i.e. whether item j is in the set

blocks.why: Shift bit j down to position 0, then keep just that bit.

blocks.q: Roughly how big can n be for an O(2ⁿ · n²) bitmask DP?
blocks.why: 2²⁰ ≈ 10⁶, times n² = 400 makes 4 × 10⁸.

blocks.q: In the assignment problem, why isn't the worker part of the state?

opts.t: The next worker is always number popcount(m), because workers are assigned in order
The worker is the highest bit of m

blocks.why: Fixing the order of workers removes one dimension.

blocks.q: s = (s - 1) & m repeated from s = m lists what?

opts.t: Every submask of m, from largest to smallest

blocks.why: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and everything below it; & m keeps only bits of m.

blocks.q: Why does "shortest path visiting all nodes" BFS over (node, mask) instead of nodes?

opts.t: You may revisit nodes, so the same node with a different visited set is a different state

blocks.why: The mask records progress; the node records where you are.

sections.title: Real-world project: a field technician's day

blocks.title: Plan the technician's route
blocks.client: A home-appliance repair company whose technicians visit up to a dozen customers a day from the depot

Then answer the dispatcher's other question: if the day only allows a total driving distance budget, what's the most customers that can be visited (returning to the depot)?

Two technicians splitting the customers

blocks.q: Explain bitmask DP: when the set of used items can replace the order, how sets are stored and manipulated as integers, Held-Karp and the assignment problem, and the cost and limits.
blocks.a: When the rest of a problem depends only on which items have been used (and perhaps where you are), not on the order they were used in, the state can be a set instead of a sequence: 2ⁿ sets instead of n! orders. A set of up to about 20 items is stored as an integer whose bit j says whether item j is in it: m >> j & 1 tests membership, m | 1 << j adds, m ^ 1 << j removes a member, popcount gives the size, and (1 << n) − 1 is everything. Comparing m & j instead of m & (1 << j) is a common bug. The assignment problem uses dp[m] with the next worker fixed as popcount(m), O(2ⁿ · n). Held-Karp for the shortest tour uses dp[m][last], the shortest path from the start through exactly the cities in m ending at last, extended to every city not in m, then closed back to the start: O(2ⁿ · n²), with parent pointers to rebuild the route. Partitioning into equal groups tracks the fill of the current group, (s − 1) & m enumerates submasks (O(3ⁿ) over all masks), and BFS over (node, mask) handles shortest walks that must visit every node. The limit is about n = 20.

chapters.title: DP on trees
chapters.tagline: Each node combines answers from its children
goals: Solve a tree bottom-up, one small tuple of answers per node
Choose node states such as (taken, not taken) or (covered, camera, needs cover)
Track a global best through each node for paths and diameters
Re-root a tree to get an answer for every node in O(n)

blocks.html: A tree has no cycles, so every node's subtree is its own little problem, and the subtrees of different children don't overlap. Solve the children first (post-order), then combine. The question is what each node should report to its parent: often a small tuple, one number per "situation" the parent might need.

blocks.name: ds-party
blocks.title: The company party: never invite someone with their direct boss
blocks.goal: Run greedy to the end, then run tree DP and compare the fun.
blocks.intro: Each box is a person; the number is how much fun they bring.

blocks.html:
For the party (maximum independent set on a tree), each person reports two numbers:

  • inv[v] = best for v's subtree with v invited = fun[v] + Σ out[child]
  • out[v] = best without v = Σ max(inv[child], out[child])

The answer is max(inv[root], out[root]). Each node is touched once: O(n).

Recursion depth. A tree can be a long chain: 100,000 levels deep blows Python's stack. For big trees, get a top-down order with BFS, then process it reversed (children before parents). The prelude's bfs_order does this.

blocks.code:
parent = [-1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2]
fun = [3, 2, 5, 4, 1, 6]
kids, order = bfs_order(parent)
print("top-down order:", order)
inv, out = [0] * 6, [0] * 6
for v in reversed(order):
    inv[v] = fun[v] + sum(out[c] for c in kids[v])
    out[v] = sum(max(inv[c], out[c]) for c in kids[v])
    print(f"person {v}: invited {inv[v]}, not invited {out[v]}")
print("best party:", max(inv[0], out[0]))
blocks.title: Bottom-up without recursion

blocks.q: In the party DP, why does out[v] take max(inv[c], out[c]) for each child?

opts.t: If v stays home, each child is free to come or not, so take whichever is better

blocks.why: If v is invited, children must stay home: only out[c] is allowed.

blocks.prompt: LeetCode 543. The diameter is the most edges on any path between two nodes. This version only measures paths through the root, but the longest path can bend at a node deep inside one subtree. Fix it by checking left height + right height at every node and keeping the best.

blocks.html:
The hard part is deciding what a node reports. Ask: "what does my parent need to know about me to make its choice?"

  • Robbing houses on a tree: (best if I'm robbed, best if I'm not).
  • Cameras that watch their neighbours: three states: I have a camera, I'm watched without one, I'm not watched yet (my parent must fix that).
  • Paths: report the best path going down from me; combine the two best children at me to update a global answer.

blocks.title: sum_of_distances
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 834, a hard one asked at Google and Amazon. For every node, return the sum of its distances to all other nodes. Two passes: bottom-up, size[v] and down[v] (sum of distances to nodes in v's subtree); then top-down re-rooting: moving the root from parent p to child v, size[v] nodes get 1 closer and n − size[v] get 1 farther, so ans[v] = ans[p] − size[v] + (n − size[v]).
blocks.tests:
assert sum_distances(6, [[0, 1], [0, 2], [2, 3], [2, 4], [2, 5]]) == [8, 12, 6, 10, 10, 10]
assert sum_distances(1, []) == [0]
assert sum_distances(2, [[1, 0]]) == [1, 1]
N = 20000
out, t = timed(sum_distances, N, [[i, i + 1] for i in range(N - 1)])
assert out[0] == 199990000 and out[N // 2] == 100000000
assert t < 1.0, f"too slow: {t:.2f}s"
hints: Running BFS from every node is O(n²). Every child's subtree hangs one edge below its parent, which adds size[child] to the parent's down.

blocks.q: In what order are nodes processed in tree DP?

opts.t: Children before parents (post-order), so each node's children are already solved

blocks.why: Re-rooting adds a second, top-down pass after that.

blocks.q: Why use a reversed BFS order instead of recursion in Python?

opts.t: A long chain is as deep as it is long, and deep recursion overflows Python's stack

blocks.why: Reversed BFS order still puts every child before its parent.

blocks.q: For a diameter, why is there a variable outside the recursion?

opts.t: The function returns a height (what the parent needs), but the answer is a path that bends at some node, checked at every node

blocks.why: What you return and what you're looking for are different things.

blocks.q: How many states does each node report in binary tree cameras?

opts.t: 3: has a camera, watched without one, not watched yet

blocks.why: "Not watched yet" tells the parent it must place a camera.

blocks.q: What does re-rooting give you?

opts.t: The answer with every node as the root, in O(n) total instead of O(n²)

blocks.why: Moving the root across one edge changes the answer by a formula you can apply in O(1).

blocks.title: Who manages whom, and who should hear first
blocks.client: An HR analytics startup that receives a company's org chart (each employee's manager) and builds team insights and announcement plans
blocks.brief: Build orgchart.py. From a parent list (-1 for the CEO), compute every person's team size (themselves plus everyone under them, directly or not). Then plan an announcement: brief as few people as possible so that every employee is briefed or works directly with a briefed person (their manager or one of their direct reports). That's a minimum dominating set on a tree; it needs three states per person.
blocks.why: Org charts, file system folders (sizes), comment threads, network trees and phylogenetic trees all get analysed this way, and the charts can have hundreds of thousands of nodes, so no recursion.
skills: minimum dominating set on a tree
milestones: Three states per person for the announcement
Combine children correctly when one of them must be briefed
stretch: Return who to brief, not just how many
Weighted version: briefing a VP costs more than briefing an intern

blocks.title: team_sizes
blocks.prompt: Return a list where entry v is the size of v's team: v plus everyone below them. Bottom-up over bfs_order.
hints: The starter counts direct reports only. A child's whole team is part of its parent's team.

blocks.title: min_briefings
blocks.prompt: Return the fewest people to brief so everyone is briefed or adjacent (manager or direct report) to a briefed person. For each v keep three numbers for v's subtree: a = v is briefed; b = v isn't briefed but a direct report is (so v is covered); c = v isn't covered yet (its manager must be briefed). For b, every child takes min(a, b), and if none chose a, force the cheapest one to a. A leaf can't have b (use infinity). Answer: min(a[root], b[root]).
blocks.tests:
assert min_briefings([-1, 0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]) == 2
assert min_briefings([-1]) == 1
assert min_briefings([-1, 0]) == 1
assert min_briefings([-1, 0, 1, 2, 3, 4]) == 2
assert min_briefings([-1, 0, 0, 0, 0]) == 1
hints: If v is briefed, its children can be in any state, even "not covered yet", because v covers them. If v relies on a child, that child must be briefed.
blocks.solution:
def min_briefings(parent):
    kids, order = bfs_order(parent)
    n = len(parent)
    INF = float("inf")
    a, b, c = [0] * n, [0] * n, [0] * n
    for v in reversed(order):
        ks = kids[v]
        a[v] = 1 + sum(min(a[k], b[k], c[k]) for k in ks)
        c[v] = sum(b[k] for k in ks)
        if ks:
            base = sum(min(a[k], b[k]) for k in ks)
            extra = min(a[k] - min(a[k], b[k]) for k in ks)
            b[v] = base + extra
        else:
            b[v] = INF
    r = order[0]
    return min(a[r], b[r])

blocks.q: Explain DP on trees: why subtrees are good subproblems, how to choose what each node reports, the global-best pattern for paths, re-rooting, and how to avoid deep recursion.
blocks.a: A tree has no cycles, so each node's subtree is an independent subproblem; solve the children first (post-order) and combine their answers at the node. The key decision is what a node reports to its parent, usually a small tuple covering each situation the parent might need: for the maximum independent set or house robber on a tree, the best with the node taken (its value plus children not taken) and without it (each child's better option), giving O(n) overall where greedy fails. Covering problems like cameras or briefing need three states: has a camera, covered without one, or not covered yet so the parent must act. For paths and diameters, a node returns the longest downward path but updates a global best by joining its two longest child paths, since the answer may bend deep inside the tree. Re-rooting computes an answer for every node as the root in O(n): a bottom-up pass gets subtree sizes and sums, then a top-down pass adjusts across each edge, such as ans[child] = ans[parent] − size[child] + (n − size[child]). In Python, long chains overflow recursion, so process a BFS order in reverse instead.

chapters.title: Digit DP
chapters.tagline: Count numbers up to 10¹⁸ by walking their digits
goals: Count numbers ≤ N with a digit property using (position, state, tight)
Explain why "tight" is needed and when it switches off
Handle leading zeros and ranges [lo, hi] with f(hi) − f(lo − 1)
Combine digit DP with masks and remainders
chapters.prelude:
import time
from functools import lru_cache

def timed(fn, *args):
    t = time.perf_counter()
    out = fn(*args)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - t

blocks.html: "How many numbers from 1 to 10¹⁸ have digit sum 90?" "How many 1s are written in all the numbers up to N?" You can't loop to 10¹⁸. But you can build the number digit by digit, from the left, and count how many ways each partial choice can be finished.

blocks.name: ds-digits
blocks.title: Numbers up to 4,327 with digit sum 13
blocks.goal: Run check every number to the end, then run digit DP and compare the work.
blocks.intro: The DP never lists a single number.

blocks.html:
While you write digits from the left, there are two situations:

  • tight: every digit so far equals the limit's digit. The next digit can only go up to the limit's next digit.
  • free: some earlier digit was smaller, so the number is already below the limit. Every later digit can be 0–9.

The template, memoised on (pos, state, tight):

`` def go(pos, state, tight): if pos == len(digits): return 1 if state is good else 0 hi = digits[pos] if tight else 9 return sum(go(pos + 1, new_state(state, d), tight and d == hi) for d in range(hi + 1)) ``

The state is whatever the property needs: a digit sum, a count of 1s, a remainder mod k, a mask of used digits. States × positions × 10 is tiny: 19 positions × 163 sums × 10 for digit sums up to 10¹⁸.

blocks.title: The template on the sim's question

blocks.q: When does tight become False?

opts.t: When the digit sum gets too big
As soon as you place a digit smaller than the limit's digit at that position
When you reach the last digit

blocks.why: Once smaller, always smaller: every later digit is free.

blocks.title: digit_sum_count
blocks.prompt: Return how many integers in [0, n] have digit sum exactly s, for n up to 10¹⁸. Memoise go(pos, sum, tight) with lru_cache; stop early when the sum passes s.
blocks.tests:
assert count_digit_sum(4327, 13) == 310
assert count_digit_sum(100, 1) == 3
assert count_digit_sum(0, 0) == 1
assert count_digit_sum(55, 10) == 5
assert count_digit_sum(10 ** 18, 90) == 24918647231083239
hints: Leading zeros are harmless here: 0042 has the same digit sum as 42.

blocks.title: forgot_tight_bug
blocks.prompt: This digit DP lets every position go up to 9, so it counts all numbers with that many digits, ignoring the limit: for n = 55, s = 10 it returns 9 (it counts 64, 73, 82 and 91 too). Add the tight flag back.
blocks.tests:
assert count_digit_sum(55, 10) == 5
assert count_digit_sum(4327, 13) == 310
assert count_digit_sum(1000, 27) == 1
hints: Start tight; the cap is the limit's digit while tight, 9 otherwise; stay tight only if you placed exactly that digit.

blocks.title: Count numbers in [0, n] that never use the digit 4
blocks.tests:
assert without_four(10) == 10
assert without_four(44) == 36
assert without_four(1000) == 730
lines: return sum(go(pos + 1, tight and d == hi) for d in range(hi + 1) if d != 4)
distractors: return sum(go(pos + 1, tight) for d in range(hi + 1) if d != 4)

blocks.html:
The state can be anything small:

  • a count (how many 1s so far)
  • a remainder (digit sum mod k, or the number itself mod k)
  • a mask of digits used (all digits distinct): 2¹⁰ masks
  • the previous digit (no two equal neighbours; no "11" in binary)
  • started (have we placed a non-zero digit yet?) when leading zeros would break the property

For a range, count f(hi) − f(lo − 1).

blocks.title: count_digit_one
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 233, a hard one asked at Google and Amazon. Return the total number of digit 1s written in all the integers from 0 to n. Carry the count of 1s so far as the state and return it at the end.
blocks.tests:
assert count_ones(13) == 6
assert count_ones(0) == 0
assert count_ones(99) == 20
assert count_ones(2023) == 1613
assert count_ones(10 ** 12) == 1200000000001
hints: The starter only counts 1s in the last position. Each finished number contributes how many 1s it used.
blocks.starter:
def count_ones(n):
    return n // 10 + (1 if n % 10 >= 1 else 0)

blocks.title: digits_from_a_set
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 902, a hard one asked at Amazon. Using only the digits in digits (strings, sorted, no 0), how many positive integers ≤ n can you write? Shorter numbers are all fine: k¹ + k² + … + k^(L−1). Then walk n's digits: count the smaller allowed digits times k^(remaining), and stop if n's digit isn't allowed. Add 1 if all of n was allowed.
hints: Here "free" has a closed form: k choices per remaining position. The tight walk ends early when the limit uses a digit you can't.
blocks.solution:
def at_most(digits, n):
    s = str(n)
    L = len(s)
    ds = sorted(int(d) for d in digits)
    k = len(ds)
    total = sum(k ** i for i in range(1, L))
    for i, ch in enumerate(s):
        c = int(ch)
        total += sum(1 for d in ds if d < c) * k ** (L - i - 1)
        if c not in ds:
            return total
    return total + 1

blocks.title: distinct_digit_numbers
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 2376, a hard one asked at Google. Count the integers in [1, n] whose digits are all different. The state needs a mask of used digits and a started flag: leading zeros don't count as using the digit 0.
blocks.tests:
assert count_special(20) == 19
assert count_special(5) == 5
assert count_special(135) == 110
assert count_special(1000) == 738
assert count_special(10 ** 9) == 5611770
hints: The starter treats the leading zeros of 007 as real zeros, so it throws away every short number with a 0 in it... and 7 itself. Track whether the number has started.

blocks.title: no_consecutive_ones
blocks.prompt: LeetCode 600, a hard one asked at Pocket Gems. Count the integers in [0, n] whose binary form has no two adjacent 1s. Digit DP in base 2; the state is the previous bit.
blocks.tests:
assert no_adjacent_ones(5) == 5
assert no_adjacent_ones(1) == 2
assert no_adjacent_ones(100) == 34
assert no_adjacent_ones(10 ** 9) == 2178309

blocks.starter:
def no_adjacent_ones(n):
    return n // 2 + 1

blocks.q: Why is digit DP fast even for n = 10¹⁸?

opts.t: The state is (position, small state, tight): about 19 positions × a few hundred states × 10 digits

blocks.why: The free part only depends on how many digits are left and the state, not on which number it is.

blocks.q: How do you count numbers in [lo, hi] with some property?

opts.t: Run the DP from lo to hi
f(hi) − f(lo − 1), where f(x) counts [0, x]

blocks.why: f(lo − 1) removes everything below lo.

blocks.q: When do you need a "started" flag?

opts.t: When leading zeros would wrongly affect the property, such as "all digits distinct" or "no zero digits"

blocks.why: For a digit sum, 0042 and 42 agree, so no flag is needed.

blocks.q: What's the state for "numbers ≤ n divisible by 7"?

opts.t: The remainder of the prefix mod 7: new remainder = (r · 10 + d) % 7

blocks.why: Remainders compose digit by digit.

blocks.q: Why is the tight flag needed at all?

opts.t: While the prefix equals the limit's prefix, the next digit can't exceed the limit's digit; otherwise you'd count numbers bigger than n

blocks.why: Forgetting it counts every number with that many digits.

sections.title: Real-world project: permit numbers without unlucky digits

blocks.title: Statistics for a permit numbering scheme
blocks.client: A city council that issues numbered parking permits and wants to skip numbers containing 4 (unlucky in several cultures), and to audit number ranges for a checksum rule
blocks.brief: Build permits.py. First: how many permit numbers from 0 to N contain no digit 4? (That tells the council how many usable numbers the scheme has.) Second: the council's old checksum rule says a number is valid if its digit sum is divisible by k. Count the valid numbers in a range [lo, hi], for ranges up to 10¹⁵.

Digit sum mod k as the state
stretch: Return the k-th usable permit number (walk the digits, using the counts to skip)
Ban the substring "13" as well

blocks.q: Explain digit DP: what it counts, the (position, state, tight) template, why tight is needed, leading zeros, ranges, and its cost.
blocks.a: Digit DP counts the numbers up to a huge limit N, such as 10¹⁸, that have some digit property, without listing them. It builds numbers from the left one digit at a time with a memoised function go(pos, state, tight). While tight, every digit so far equals N's digit, so the next digit can go only up to N's digit; as soon as a smaller digit is placed the number is below N and every later digit is free, 0 to 9. Forgetting tight counts every number with that many digits. The state is whatever the property needs and must stay small: a digit sum, a count of 1s, a remainder (r + d) % k or (r · 10 + d) % k, the previous digit, or a mask of used digits; a started flag stops leading zeros counting as real zeros when that matters, as for distinct digits. At the end the function returns 1 if the state is good, or the accumulated count. Ranges use f(hi) − f(lo − 1). The cost is positions × states × 10, a few thousand to a few million steps, and the free part often has a closed form, like k choices per position for a digit set.
